title: Cultivating Relationalities: On Refuge/Refuse
authors: Heidi Amin-Hong; Evyn Lê Espiritu Gandhi; Emily Hue
abstract: This introduction elaborates on the key terms of our special issue: refuge, refuse (verb), and refuse (noun). First, we define refuge in relation to critical refugee studies and critical militarism studies to understand how refuge for humans and nonhuman species can be shaped by militarized goals and processes. Secondly, we follow refuse (verb) through genealogies of refusal at the intersection of critical refugee studies and Indigenous studies to highlight the generative potential of refusal and Indigenous-refugee relationality. Finally, routing through new materialisms and transpacific Asian American studies, we track refuse (noun) and its entanglements with refugee environments, as well as its ideological and material implications.

title: The Water Remembers: The Eco-Occupation of the Jordan River and Palestinian Refusal
abstract: This article examines the transformation of the Jordan River from a life-giving source central to Palestinian ecological and spiritual practices to a militarized border shaped by Zionist infrastructure. Once vital to Indigenous Palestinians, the River embodies a broader colonial strategy, severing connections to land and water. Drawing on archival research, Palestinian poetry, and oral histories, I trace how Zionist projects such as marsh draining, the National Water Carrier, and dam construction produced a decaying landscape. The analysis highlights how manipulations of the River fuel Palestinian dispossession and underscores the enduring significance of memory, resilience, and resistance in the struggle for return and liberation.

title: Cans, Crates, and Concrete: Refuse Archaeology
abstract: The remains of the Gila River Incarceration Camp, which confined over 16,000 Japanese Americans during World War II, lay within Gila River Indian Community land. Japanese Americans incarcerees made homes and continued to care for one another through the exchange of goods, practices of comforting, and the making of homespaces. In this article, I discuss multiple modes of refuse archaeology – the reappropriation of objects by incarcerees, the afterlives of the camp on the landscape, and the methods of analyzing these materials. Throughout, I look to not only the refuse itself, but the acts of refusal which suffuse these histories.

title: Coral Refugee Refusals in the Shadow of Climate Resilience Finance
abstract: Speaking to this special issue on “Between Refuge and Refuse,” this essay analyzes how resilience and refugee narratives prime corals for recruitment into global racial capitalism as nonhuman climate disaster workers. Coral resilience finance underwrites the development of “super corals” through selective breeding (which produces “refuse” by discarding species deemed to be noncompetitive) and the rescuing of “coral refugees” (through coral arks that offer “refuge” to endangered lifeforms). The essay draws on critical refugee, finance, and disability studies to argue for coral futures that prioritize survivance over maximum productivity and radical interdependency over liberal independence.

title: “This Poison Broke the World”: Ri-Ṃajeļ (Re)mappings of Colonial Fallout on Hawai‘i Island
abstract: This essay theorizes the colonial fallout of U.S. nuclear weapons testing by tracking how fallout has atomized across the lives of ri-Ṃajeļ (Marshall Islanders) displaced to the Big Island of Hawai‘i. Through poetic narration, ri-Ṃajeļ refuse colonial fallout’s disintegrative logics, connecting across time and space to trouble what is considered a consequence of fallout and where these consequences are taking place. In the face of nuclear colonialism and settler militarism’s mutual reinforcement, these ri-Ṃajeļ (re)mappings also demonstrate how Hawai‘i and the Marshall Islands are imbricated in each other’s struggles, and how refuge can be found with or without return.

title: Còn Dùng Được: A Refugee Guide to Salvage
authors: erin Khuê Ninh; Nguyên Khôi Nguyen
abstract: A graphic essay collaboration about everyday creative re-use, and more.

title: War’s Aftermath and the Living Landscape in Tuấn Andrew Nguyễn’s The Unburied Sounds of a Troubled Horizon
abstract: This conversation with artist and filmmaker Tuấn Andrew Nguyễn explores the concepts of refuge and refuse as intertwined conditions shaped by war, displacement, and the effort to make visible what is often invisible. Through engagement with The Unburied Sounds of a Troubled Horizon, we discussed how objects and landscapes carry unresolved pasts into the present. Our dialogue explored the connection between imperial violence, considering what justice might look like in terms of healing and continuity, and how we might learn to see beauty in the aftermath of war and the possibility of what is yet to come.

title: Palm Oil Geographies: Storying Refusal Amid Deforested Futures in the Poetics of Barokka, Gebze, and Musa
abstract: Palm oil production is booming in Borneo and West Papua, where it predominantly impacts Indigenous peoples. Poems by Khairani Barokka (Indonesia–UK) and Omar Musa (Malaysia–Australia) and a song by Marcus Gebze (West Papua), set in such geographies, take what capitalism frames as disposable or worthless and give it new life. These three authors refuse the unstorying and erasure enacted by palm oil and insist on storied Indigenous futures as a form of refuge, even as those futures may be deforested. Read together, these literary works reflect how conversations about oil extend further than thinking solely of oil extracted from the ground.

title: Excerpts from Primordial : Poems
abstract: These poems examine Hmong identity in connection to the ecological, political, and spiritual repercussions of the U.S.’s secret war in Laos.Publication Information:“Battalions of Irregular Force,” Primordial: Poems, Graywolf Press 2025.“Autonomous Sky,” Primordial: Poems, Graywolf Press 2025.“Evolution, Absence,” Primordial: Poems, Graywolf Press 2025.“Node: Between literary and unlettered,” Primordial: Poems, Graywolf Press 2025.Poems reprinted courtesy of the author and Graywolf Press.

title: Intra-Korean Refugees and Mountain Refuges: Literary Environments of the Jeju Island 4.3 Uprising and Massacres
abstract: Jeju Islanders’ experiences and memories of the April 3, 1948 Uprising and massacres (4.3) are embedded in Jeju’s environmental features – especially the central volcano Hallasan. Focusing on two stories by Hyun Ki-young, this article asks how fiction serves as textual terrain for Jejuans to work out the dynamic between refuge(e), refusal, and refuse in their 4.3 retrospectives. Countering the post-Korean War reconstruction of Hallasan as a sanctuary for biodiversity, tourist pleasure, and peace, this article employs a guerrilla reading of the mountain as a material site of struggle and a refuge for insurgent environmental memories.

title: More Work Than Can Be Accomplished in One Lifetime: Refuge and Refusal at Kaloko Inlet
abstract: This essay examines the entanglements of refuge and refusal that emerge through Kanaka Maoli-led restoration at Kaloko Inlet. Analyzing the use of cultural practices and the treatment of invasive and endangered plants, I suggest that restoration practices offer lessons in cultivating place-based belonging. I ask what must be refused to produce Kaloko as an Indigenous place of refuge and for whom Kaloko provides sanctuary. I assert that Kaloko restoration invites Kanaka and nonnative, human and more-than-human relatives into working toward decolonial futures in which ‘āina (often translated as land, but literally “that which feeds”) can once again feed community.

title: Gai’ase’: Trans-Indigenous Refusal and Global Indigenous Solidarities from the Mariånas to Palestine
abstract: Building on the anti-imperial critique at the heart of critical refugee studies, I articulate “trans-Indigenous refusal” as a mode of global Indigenous solidarities. This notion captures the material and discursive practices bridging differential Indigenous vernaculars and relational accountabilities to place, in order to reject the central tenets of imperialism – including militarism, Westphalian statehood, and the global relations of domination and subordination. To demonstrate the analytical utility of trans-Indigenous refusals, I consider the case of Mariånas for Palestine, a Chamoru- and Palestinian-led collective fighting for an immediate ceasefire in Palestine and for the intertwined resurgence of Chamoru and Palestinian nationhood.

title: Mississippi to the Mekong: Capital and Plantation/Refugee Ecologies Across Two Deltas
abstract: This article examines how the Mississippi and Mekong Deltas, and the production of Black and Southeast Asian refugees out of them in the 1920s and 1960s/’70s, respectively, are imbricated by the U.S. imperial deployment of engineering knowledge meant to discipline sub/tropical ecologies. This article argues that this knowledge fuels plantation capitalist extraction in the Mississippi Delta and U.S. imperial warfare in Southeast Asia, producing refugees throughout. This is illustrated by the transformation of the Waterways Experiment Station, a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers research campus, from the study and control of Mississippi Delta floods to techniques of U.S. warfare abroad.

title: sunny day flooding fund: A Process Piece for HANDS IN THE DIRT, an Eco-Storytelling Project
abstract: Decades of environmental catastrophe have radically transformed coastal Southeast Louisiana, a region once known as Bayouk, still called Bvlbancha. State-designed restoration projects meant to build land and slow storms have been unevenly vetted and implemented, deepening uncertainty in a region already referred to as the nation’s environmental sacrifice zone. Lost in the churn are coast-interdependent peoples who know the coast best. HANDS IN THE DIRT (HID) is an ongoing digital mapping and oral history project that partners with the area's Southeast Asian refugee fisherfolk to archive knowledges about an ecosystem being disappeared from view. This process piece about HID reflects on its fraught development and the possible shapes the project might take as it works to illuminate the violences of western environmental expertise and the potentialities of fisherfolk agency, memory, and placemaking.

title: Finding Refuge in Refugee Archives: Eric Nguyen’s Things We Lost to the Water and Abdulrazak Gurnah’s By the Sea
abstract: This essay explores refugee archives in terms of refuse, refusal, and refuge by examining two novels, Eric Nguyen’s Things We Lost to the Water and Abdulrazak Gurnah’s By the Sea, and placing them in conversation with institutional archival practices related to refugees. I focus on how refugee characters construct alternative archival imaginaries in the absence of refugee-centered infrastructures. The essay concludes by considering how Vietnamese American scholar-archivists are working toward more equitable archives that refugee literature imagines.

title: Corridor Stories: Refuge and Resistance in Archival Filipina/x Counternarratives
abstract: “Corridor Stories” is a series of poems that narrate stories of Filipina/x migrants and labourers in North America as recorded in archival and media documentation (e.g. “Towards Social Justice for Overseas Filipinos” by Kalayaan Resource and Training Centre, public articles from the Philippine Canadian Inquirer, and government documents). This series explores how shape poetry is able (or unable) to persist as not only refuge for these narratives, but also as a form of remembering and un-forgetting critical migrant narratives for Filipino/a/x communities. What the poetics offer here is a method of “unburdening” the text and the counternarratives so that there are new opportunities of hapticity with the texts and lived experiences of migrants. Perhaps the pages where these poems are formed can become “new countries” that transcend boundaries, geographies, and liminalities—expanding as refuge and resistance, and as acts of solidarity with other migrant communities—to reimagine, with agency, futures and environments that do not include exporting and exploiting the Filipina/x body.Access the Corridor Stories audio here: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1hKjIAddUQxYQqtPS3tz9KcICjlFuoh4?usp=sharing

title: Sight, Sound, Movement: Aesthetic Departures from the Migrant Documentary in Shelter: Farewell to Eden (2019)
abstract: In Shelter: Farewell to Eden, an undocumented transgender woman named Pepsi left the militarized landscapes of Mindanao, found work as a caregiver in Libya, and applied for asylum in Italy. Throughout the documentary, the film creatively engages with passages, caves, and bridges to contemplate the contradictions of “refuge,” “refugee,” and “asylum” during the period of anti-migrant policies in Europe in the 2010s. Guided by anti-militarist interventions in feminist visual studies, Filipinx studies, refugee studies, and queer and trans of color studies, this essay posits that Shelter uses sight and sound to foreground how war, oil, and export labor economies furnish the Filipino caregiver’s path. The essay concludes with ways that Pepsi erodes the refugee documentary’s generic impulse to smooth and simplify, breaking open a pathway to consider migrant crossings in their ethical complexity.

title: The Eco-Politics of Voice and Refugee Environments in Ritwik Ghatak’s The Cloud-Capped Star
abstract: Drawing on critical refugee studies and environmental humanities, this essay reads voice in Ritwik Ghatak’s 1960 film Meghe Dhaka Tara as an eco-political archive of Bengal Partition’s afterlives. It argues that vocal timbre, breath, and song mediate relations between bodies, infrastructures, and landscape, refusing humanitarian “rescue” scripts and state-developmental narratives of progress. Moving between sociopolitical contexts and close attention to the film’s shifting soundscape, from domestic address and everyday coercion to moments of song, recitation, and rupture, the essay shows how Ghatak makes audible the gendered economy of obligation that governs refugee survival across postcolonial spaces.

title: Gut Displacements: Race, Migration, and Settler Colonialism in Refugee Health Discourse on the Microbiome
abstract: The reported rise in metabolic disorders among South and Southeast Asian refugees in North America is increasingly described in medical literature as a transition within the refugee body from a capacious to a sanitized, “Westernized” microbiome. Drawing from critical theories in food studies, fat studies, environmental studies, and disability studies, as well as from historical consideration of how wars and U.S. empire in Asia have transformed food systems, the article argues that a focus on obesity and mobility causes researchers to miss a larger set of structural contexts in the politics of refugee health and foodways. It proposes that critical refugee studies can incorporate cross-community approaches to agricultural, health, and environmental justice that configure refugee health against an ableist settler binary of emaciated/fat racial form.

title: Dissecting Militarized Refuge: Between the Archive and Repertoire of refuse/REFUSE
abstract: This essay meditates on the interplay between material archives and refugee repertoires by revisiting a performance I created and performed about my grandfather’s life as a militarized refugee titled refuse/REFUSE. On the tenth anniversary of the performance, I examine the remains of this embodied experiment to parse the materials that constitute refuge(e) life, death, waste, and futures.

title: Journeys in Asian American History: A Forum on Gordon H. Chang’s War, Race, and Culture
(Anti-)Imperial Intimacies: Tracing the Settler Colonial Ties That Bind Iran and Hawaiʻi
abstract: I use the telling and retelling of my grandmother’s unconventional migration journey – from Iran to the U.S. by way of Hawaiʻi – as an entrypoint to uncovering historical connections between Iran and Hawaiʻi. My grandparents’ migration experience invites us (1) to decenter the Global North and instead consider how sugar plantations link Iran and Hawaiʻi, and (2) to rethink dominant narratives of Iranian diaspora and diasporic subject formation and instead highlight relational formations of race and solidarity. Intimacy is both a theoretical framework and methodological tool to explore an array of archival sources and music by Hawaiʻi-based, diasporic Iranian artist Illnomadic.

title: California’s Historical Alien Land Law: Racial Xenophobia and Home Ownership
authors: Paul Ong; Jonathan Ong; Chhandara Pech
abstract: This article uses a racial xenophobia framework to examine the impact of California’s Alien Land Law on home ownership of Asians during the early part of the twentieth century. Racial xenophobia is a compounding of two forms of marginalization, which led to the enactment of a law targeting Asian immigrants. Drawing on historical micro-level data, the analysis finds that the law adversely hurt all Asian groups, although the motivation for the prohibition was rooted in the anti-Japanese movement. Moreover, the law created differences in home ownership among people of color, with Asians being at the bottom during the study period.

title: The Uses and Abuses of Asian American History in Responses to Anti-Asian Violence
abstract: This article examines how historical narratives were deployed by Asian American advocates in responses to anti-Asian hate and violence during the COVID-19 pandemic. We identify and critically analyze three commonly-used historical narratives: “racial injury” accounts that posit anti-Asian racism as singular and unchanging; “contribution” narratives that glorify the role Asian migrants played in American history; “solidarity” narratives that elevate racial figureheads while sanitizing their politics. We argue that the continual use of these narratives is more so about political scripts than about the history itself, which may ultimately narrow the possibilities for more capacious understandings of Asian American identity and solidarity.

title: Yuntaku Interview with Laura Kina: On Being Part of Many Universes All at Once
abstract: Laura Kina, a queer, disabled, and mixed-race Okinawan American artist and scholar, is interviewed by Cassie M. Miura. Both share Okinawan ancestry and are part of the contemporary movement to revitalize Okinawan ancestral tattoos. As a familiar form of intimate exchange, yuntaku enables Kina and Miura to reflect on Okinawan cultural identity, queer diasporic aesthetics, and Indigenous time. Their friendship, as well as Kina’s recent diagnosis with stage four cancer, gives shape and life to the conversation. Offering a retrospective look at their career and evolving sense of self, Kina considers what their work makes possible for future generations.

title: “Why can’t one of us write tragedy?”: The Unpublished Correspondence of Maxine Hong Kingston and Frank Chin
abstract: This article presents unpublished 1970s correspondence between Maxine Hong Kingston and Frank Chin, reframing the “Chin-Kingston debates” as an evolving dialogue over genre, representation, and literary authority rather than a zero-sum contest over authenticity. Read alongside Chin’s exchanges with Diana Chang and both writers’ correspondence with Aiiieeeee! co-editor Shawn Wong, these letters illuminate the aesthetic and political fault lines shaping early Asian American literature. Disputes over New Criticism, racialized genre, publishing, and artistic autonomy reveal overlapping commitments to craft and community, while showing how tensions between being a “minority writer” and “just a writer” were experienced both ideologically and personally.

title: An Absent Mother between Two States
abstract: Motherhood—one of the most important and yet mundane social institutions—is central to understanding the rise and decline of Third World internationalism. This article focuses on Francisca Casparina Fanggidaej (1925–2013), a left-wing Indonesian activist in the Afro-Asian solidarity movements that developed out of the Bandung Conference. She is also a mother of seven who endured decades of forced separation from her family. Based on a close reading of Fanggidaej’s diaries, personal letters, and oral history interviews with her family and friends, I discuss the politics of maternal absence in Indonesia and China—two of the leading countries in the Afro-Asian movements. I explore how these two countries shaped the public and self-perceptions of nonresidential mothers through their welfare provisions and reproductive policies. Against this backdrop, I examine how a transnational figure like Fanggidaej navigated motherhood within frameworks of revolutionary anticolonialism in Indonesia, state socialism in China, and the global rise of capitalist neoliberalism, which ultimately displaced the Third World internationalist vision once championed by both nations. I argue that the fall of Third World internationalism signaled not only a missed opportunity to reconfigure global geopolitics but also a lost chance to redefine motherhood—not as the individualized enterprise of the birth mother alone but as a communal effort involving a diverse assemblage of caretakers including both kin and non-kin, men and women.

title: Camera Time
abstract: In the early decades of the twentieth century, scores of men, women, and children around the world used the camera to enact their aspirational selves. While the power relationship inherent in some photographic encounters has been amply theorized, historians have been less concerned with a deeper understanding of ordinary personal portraiture, and especially its mimetic and ludic character. This essay focuses on such ordinary photographs commissioned or produced by middling urban Egyptians in order to make several methodological and historiographical interventions. First, I argue that these photographs ought to be understood as creative productions, rather than reflections or documentations of a self, and are best approached as dense social performances through which their subjects cultivated and realized some of the key desires unleashed by processes of urban modernity. Second, I employ these photographic acts to intervene in several recent debates, such as the place of enchantment in modern societies, the production of the Modern Girl around the world, and the articulations of local modernity in colonial situations. Paying attention to ordinary photographic practices brings new insights into these debates, as it also highlights the centrality of the camera to the emergence of modern forms of selfhood.

title: The Python God and the Empty Chair
abstract: This article explores how African royal power over the slave trade shaped transatlantic and cross-cultural interactions around sovereignty in the early eighteenth century. Employing an interdisciplinary approach, it analyzes the rich visual and material culture archive produced by the coronation ceremony of King Hufon of Hueda. This event offers a window into how Africans and Europeans negotiated, displayed, and subsequently reinterpreted cross-cultural relationships as part of competing political projects. By tracing the evolution of the story of Hufon’s coronation in Europe over many decades, the article shows how authors, artists, and publishers altered the memory and thus the archival imprint of Hufon’s power, obscuring the political subservience European merchants experienced in the kingdom. This formation of European imperial ideology occurred in parallel with a distinct but connected political process in West Africa, as the Dahomey kingdom overran and incorporated Hueda territory in response to the kingdom’s position within the Atlantic slave trade. The article argues that Hufon’s statecraft reverberated across African-European, inter-European, and inter-African relationships, demonstrating that the deep reconstruction of actual African-European relations in West Africa is necessary for understanding both Hufon’s coronation ceremony and how African power projected through Atlantic commerce shaped European and African imperialism.

title: Inside the History Lab
abstract: The September 2026 History Lab focuses on the imaginative ways in which historians are using archives and other primary sources in their research and teaching to transform our understandings of the past. It opens with “Reading Nature’s Archives,” a forum that foregrounds new approaches to the research and writing of environmental history. Organized by David Biggs, the forum brings together a team of distinguished environmental historians who each offer short essays centered on a reading of a particular object or visual form of documentation. Their “archives” range from ivory figurines, whale bones, roof tiles, porcelain earthenware, and botanical prints to a colonial era cattle census, photographs of the sun, aerial imaging of former warscapes, and a twenty-sided golden cosmic box. Together, the contributors provide a set of novel critical methods for reading these sources attuned to how situated forms of knowledge about nature are often shaped by longer histories of borrowing, theft, erasure, and resilience. As Biggs argues in his introduction to the forum, the essays model what Achilles Mbembe calls “a planetary library or archive” that can remake historical apprehensions of the intertwined worlds of human history, nature, and technology.

title: Reading Nature’s Archives
abstract: Recent changes in Earth’s climate and the rise of AI are driving a “planetary turn” in education and the humanities as traditional boundaries between history, technology, and natural processes dissolve. This text introduces a “planetary library” framework built on the idea that the world’s textual and material archives are inseparable. This History Lab forum demonstrates how the method is the argument, using scientific and other methods to interpret non-traditional archives such as ivory, whale bones, solar photos, and aerial imagery.

title: Archive of the Seven Spheres
abstract: During the last decades of the eighteenth century, the Kingdom of Mysore in southern India became immersed in reading the stars to ascertain its fate in times of war against the British East India Company. Seeking to know the order of the universe and its influence on the Earth, advisors and astrologers in the court of Tipu Sultan, the nawab of Mysore, compiled a library of Persian and Arabic manuscripts on the planetary sciences of astronomy (ʿilm al-nujum) and astrology (ʿilm ahkam al-nujum), including original texts synthesizing Persianate and Sanskritic knowledge of the celestial sphere. In the pages of this planetary archive, the cosmos—comprised of the seven planets of Islamic astrology—was mirrored by the climes of the Earth. Through knowledge of the stars and their movements and the use of talismanic objects to mediate planetary influences, the kingdom could divine and shape its future. This essay introduces this archive of the astral sciences, and explores elements of its visual and material culture, to trace views of the Earth and its place in the cosmos from the eighteenth-century Deccan.

title: Archiving Asia
abstract: Blue-and-white porcelain-inlaid earthenware, found exclusively in the 1600 San Diegoshipwreck and the Philippines, represents a distinctive material convergence within early modern global trade networks. However, the motivations behind the production of these objects and the perceived value attributed to them during that period remain unclear. Through integrated archaeological, visual evidence, and extant craftsmanship, this study investigates the cultural significance of the ware. While the production technique follows the barros Estremoztradition, the essay suggests that the ware’s creation was not merely driven by European nostalgia. Instead, drawing on the knowledge of búcaros’ sensory qualities among early modern European elites, it posits that the sensory experiences these objects offered provided Iberians with an alternative means to archive and engage with Asia, reflecting broader colonial ambitions and highlighting how the material properties of clay, minerals, and porcelain shaped early modern engagements with the natural world.

title: Cattle Censuses
abstract: Colonial historians have analyzed how human population censuses were instrumental for state-making and ethnic categorization, and how they can be used for demographical reconstruction. By contrast, they have thus far ignored the significance and analytical potential of livestock censuses. This essay teases out their potential for historical analysis by focusing on cattle censuses in French colonial Madagascar (1896–1960). It argues that colonial authorities went to great lengths to count cattle, deemed a key economic resource of the island, and showcase their numerical evolution in statistics, graphs, and maps. Due to context- and species-specific limitations of the data, historians cannot easily use these censuses to reconstruct cattle demography. Yet, they offer a fruitful lens to analyze cattle policies and knowledge regimes under colonial rule. Censuses were both an instrument of knowledge, used to monitor the evolution of the herds and reconceive policies, and an instrument of extraction, on which the annual cattle head tax was based. In both cases, cattle censuses were also sites of contestation. Tax extraction warranted strategies of dissimulation from the part of cattle owners, making knowledge even more unstable and causing epistemological anxieties within the colonial administration.

title: Ivory as Archive
authors: Jonathan Schlesinger; J Ryan Kennedy; Kristine Korzow; Vicky M Oelze; Peter E Sauer
abstract: This paper explores how historians might read ivory as an archive of environmental history. Using six figurines from Ming and Qing China held at the Eskenazi Museum of Art as a case study, it situates them within three histories: one of modern collecting; one of early modern production; and one that foregrounds elephants themselves. Ivory itself is a kind of archive. Biochemical signatures within it record key aspects of elephant lives, including their diet, lineage, and geographic origin. In the case of the Eskenazi figurines, these signatures showed that the collection derived from elephants from six different regions, two different continents, and two different eras. Connecting the elephants’ histories to human ones requires a participatory and omnivorous approach to environmental history: building partnerships with museums and citizen-historians, interpreting historical texts, and collaborating with scientists. The approach affords the opportunity to relate human histories to the history of life on Earth on the one hand, and to grow the community invested in environmental history on the other.

title: On the Uses of Whale Bodies for History
abstract: Whales are participants in history. While they do not create written archives, whales capture in their bodies the specific details of their individual lives as well as the societies in which they have lived. Fortunately, the long history of whaling has left behind an underappreciated, globe-spanning archive of whale history in the form of biological artifacts, like bones, teeth, baleen, and ear wax plugs. Through a survey of some of the latest research into paleobiology, this paper highlights how historians can use the information bound up in these natural archives to recount the journeys, diets, companions, and emotional states of whale societies across years, decades, and centuries. In doing so, historians can expand our spectrum of analysis to include non-human animals in their own right; to see how certain creatures shaped human history, but to also consider whale histories of the world.

title: Reading Conflict Landscapes
abstract: Intervisual analysis, using Geographic Information Systems to compare historic satellite imagery with ground-sourced information and maps, offers new methods for analyzing changes in conflict landscapes over time. By pairing visual data with local studies, oral histories, and texts, one may better appreciate visual biases in imagery and reveal hidden landscapes and histories. Intervisual approaches demonstrate how modern conflict sites like Phu Bai airfield often overlap with more ancient conflict zones and their spatial footprints can linger long after hostilities have ended.

title: Solar Photography
abstract: The mid-nineteenth century adoption of the new technology of photography transformed astronomical and meteorological practices. Today, there are upwards of ten million astronomical photographic negatives in observatory collections—a fraction of which are undergoing digitization to contribute to growing online databases of the astronomical archive, such as Germany’s Archives of Photographic Plates for Astronomical Use (APPLAUSE) and Digital Access to a Sky Century at Harvard (DASCH). As scientists revisit these images for time-domain astronomy, historians too are attuned to their significance to understanding the material conditions of their production. Focusing on a specific sunspot group, this essay situates these surviving plates in the visual and material cultures of astronomy and meteorology in the British colonies in the early twentieth century. It argues that such photographic plates, used in conjunction with more conventional documentary sources, can shed light on contemporary cultures of weather watching and forecasting.

title: Emerald Sea and Red Roofs
abstract: Red tile roofs are the icon of the Chinese coastal city, Qingdao, favored by German colonizers, Japanese invaders, and, most importantly, millions of Chinese who have resided in and built the city. This essay argues that, rather than treating them merely as cultural symbols, the red roofs, along with the cityscape they adorn, are a material artifact that blends both natural and cultural elements. They form a type of nature’s archive, recording the entangled environmental and cultural past of the city. We can learn to read and interpret these archives by analyzing our shared biological roots, the clay, the fuels, the tile-making process, the material sediments stored in the roofs, and the disposal process at the end of the tiles’ lifespan. By approaching the red roofs this way, they are no longer simply a German colonial heritage imposed on this Chinese city. On the contrary, we come to recognize a more complex history of the city, shaped by both external natural materials and our own inner desires and practical needs.

title: Reading Ramie from Plant to Fabric
abstract: Focusing on ramie, a fiber plant widely grown in the history of Asia, and its illustrations (from plant to fabric) produced in Asia and Europe, this essay compares knowledge in historical imagery with twenty-first-century botanical knowledge to show how botanical artists and early observers understood this understudied yet important fiber plant. These drawings in many ways correlate with modern botanical knowledge, but they also differ in distinctive ways. How illustrators chose to represent the plant and the fiber extraction process indicates not only their perception of the plant and the industry but also their aims—scientific, political, and commercial—in producing the illustrations.

title: Teaching Authoritarian History
abstract: Authoritarianism 101: A Global History is a set of thirty primary source-driven teaching modules designed to offer teachers and students a broad perspective on the history of authoritarianism. The AHR commissioned historians working on authoritarian histories in Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, and North America to write teaching modules that explored a singular instance of an authoritarian past. Temporally, they range from the seventeenth to the early twenty-first centuries, with the bulk of modules concentrating on the long twentieth century. In this issue of the journal, we feature a selection of modules from the project that explore authoritarian histories in China, the United States, Egypt, Cube, India, Argentina, and Korea. All thirty of the modules that make up Authoritarianism 101: A Global History, along with additional teaching materials, are free to access on the project website. Among the supplementary materials highlighted on the pages that follow are a set of short videos and podcast interviews with some of the contributors to the project that explore how they came to create their modules, the larger issues around the history of authoritarianism they want to raise, and ideas for successfully teaching their modules in the classroom.

title: How Cold War Populism Can Promote Authoritarianism
abstract: Tonight as we celebrate the 141st birthday of one of the great men in American history, I would like to be able to talk about what a glorious day today is in the history of the world. As we celebrate the birth of this man, who with his whole heart and soul hated war, I would like to be able to speak of peace in our time, of war being outlawed, and of worldwide disarmament. These would be truly appropriate things to be able to mention as we celebrate the birthday of Abraham Lincoln. Five years after a world war has been won, men’s hearts should anticipate a long peace, and men’s minds should be free from the heavy weight that comes with war. But this is not such a period—for this is not a period of peace. This is a time of the Cold War. This is a time when all the world is split into two vast, increasingly hostile armed camps—a time of a great armaments race. Today we can almost physically hear the mutterings and rumblings of an invigorated god of war. You can see it, feel it, and hear it all the way from the hills of Indochina, from the shores of Formosa right over into the very heart of Europe itself. Today we are engaged in a final, all-out battle between communistic atheism and Christianity. The modern champions of communism have selected this as the time. And, ladies and gentlemen, the chips are down—they are truly down. Lest there be any doubt that the time has been chosen, let us go directly to the leader of communism today—Joseph Stalin. Here is what he said—not back in 1928, not before the war, not during the war—but two years after the last war was ended: “To think that the communist revolution can be carried out peacefully, within the framework of a Christian democracy, means one has either gone out of one’s mind and lost all normal understanding, or has grossly and openly repudiated the communist revolution.” And this is what was said by Lenin in 1919, which was also quoted with approval by Stalin in 1947: “We are living,” said Lenin, “not merely in a state but in a system of states, and the existence of the Soviet Republic side by side with Christian states for a long time is unthinkable. One or the other must triumph in the end. And before that end supervenes, a series of frightful collisions between the Soviet Republic and the bourgeois states will be inevitable.” Ladies and gentlemen, can there be anyone here tonight who is so blind as to say that the war is not on? Can there be anyone who fails to realize that the communist world has said, “The time is now”—that this is the time for the showdown between the democratic Christian world and the communist atheistic world? Unless we face this fact, we shall pay the price that must be paid by those who wait too long. Six years ago, at the time of the first conference to map out peace—Dumbarton Oaks—there was within the Soviet orbit 180 million people. Lined up on the anti-totalitarian side there were in the world at that time roughly 1.625 billion people. Today, only six years later, there are 800 million people under the absolute domination of Soviet Russia—an increase of over 400 percent. On our side, the figure has shrunk to around 500 million. In other words, in less than six years the odds have changed from 9 to 1 in our favor to 8 to 5 against us. This indicates the swiftness of the tempo of communist victories and American defeats in the Cold War. As one of our outstanding historical figures once said, “When a great democracy is destroyed, it will not be because of enemies from without but rather because of enemies from within.” The truth of this statement is becoming terrifyingly clear as we see this country each day losing on every front. At war’s end we were physically the strongest nation on Earth and, at least potentially, the most powerful intellectually and morally. Ours could have been the honor of being a beacon in the desert of destruction, a shining, living proof that civilization was not yet ready to destroy itself. Unfortunately, we have failed miserably and tragically to arise to the opportunity. The reason why we find ourselves in a position of impotency is not because our only powerful, potential enemy has sent men to invade our shores, but rather because of the traitorous actions of those who have been treated so well by this nation. It has not been the less fortunate or members of minority groups who have been selling this nation out, but rather those who have had all the benefits that the wealthiest nation on earth has had to offer—the finest homes, the finest college education, and the finest jobs in government we can give. This is glaringly true in the State Department. There the bright young men who are born with silver spoons in their mouths are the ones who have been worst. Now I know it is very easy for anyone to condemn a particular bureau or department in general terms. Therefore, I would like to cite one rather unusual case—the case of a man who has done much to shape our foreign policy. When Chiang Kai-shek was fighting our war, the State Department had in China a young man named John S. Service. His task, obviously, was not to work for the communization of China. Strangely, however, he sent official reports back to the State Department urging that we torpedo our ally Chiang Kai-shek and stating, in effect, that communism was the best hope of China. Later, this man—John Service—was picked up by the Federal Bureau of Investigation for turning over to the communists secret State Department information. Strangely, however, he was never prosecuted. However, Joseph Grew, the undersecretary of state, who insisted on his prosecution, was forced to resign. Two days after, Grew’s successor, Dean Acheson, took over as undersecretary of state, this man—John Service—who had been picked up by the FBI and who had previously urged that communism was the best hope of China, was not only reinstated in the State Department but promoted; and finally, under Acheson, placed in charge of all placements and promotions. Today, ladies and gentlemen, this man Service is on his way to represent the State Department and Acheson in Calcutta—by far and away the most important listening post in the Far East. Now, let’s see what happens when individuals with communist connections are forced out of the State Department. Gustave Duran, who was labeled as, I quote, “a notorious international communist,” was made assistant secretary of state in charge of Latin American affairs. He was taken into the State Department from his job as a lieutenant colonel in the Communist International Brigade. Finally, after intense congressional pressure and criticism, he resigned in 1946 from the State Department—and, ladies and gentlemen, where do you think he is now? He took over a high- salaried job as chief of Cultural Activities Section in the office of the assistant secretary-general of the United Nations. This, ladies and gentlemen, gives you somewhat of a picture of the type of individuals who have been helping to shape our foreign policy. In my opinion the State Department, which is one of the most important government departments, is thoroughly infested with communists. I have in my hand 57 cases of individuals who would appear to be either card-carrying members or certainly loyal to the Communist Party, but who nevertheless are still helping to shape our foreign policy. One thing to remember in discussing the communists in our government is that we are not dealing with spies who get 30 pieces of silver to steal the blueprints of new weapons. We are dealing with a far more sinister type of activity because it permits the enemy to guide and shape our policy. This brings us down to the case of one Alger Hiss, who is important not as an individual anymore but rather because he is so representative of a group in the State Department. It is unnecessary to go over the sordid events showing how he sold out the nation which had given him so much. Those are rather fresh in all of our minds. However, it should be remembered that the facts in regard to his connection with this international communist spy ring were made known to the then-Undersecretary of State Berle three days after Hitler and Stalin signed the Russo-German Alliance Pact. At that time one Whittaker Chambers—who was also part of the spy ring—apparently decided that with Russia on Hitler’s side, he could no longer betray our nation to Russia. He gave Undersecretary of State Berle—and this is all a matter of record—practically all, if not more, of the facts upon which Hiss’ conviction was based. Undersecretary Berle promptly contacted Dean Acheson and received word in return that Acheson, and I quote, “could vouch for Hiss absolutely”—at which time the matter was dropped. And this, you understand, was at a time when Russia was an ally of Germany. This condition existed while Russia and Germany were invading and dismembering Poland, and while the communist groups here were screaming “warmonger” at the United States for their support of the Allied nations. Again in 1943, the FBI had occasion to investigate the facts surrounding Hiss’ contacts with the Russian spy ring. But even after that FBI report was submitted, nothing was done. Then, late in 1948—on August 5—when the Un-American Activities Committee called Alger Hiss to give an accounting, President Truman at once issued a presidential directive ordering all government agencies to refuse to turn over any information whatsoever in regard to the communist activities of any government employee to a congressional committee. Incidentally, even after Hiss was convicted, it is interesting to note that the president still labeled the expose of Hiss as a “red herring.” If time permitted, it might be well to go into detail about the fact that Hiss was Roosevelt’s chief adviser at Yalta when Roosevelt was admittedly in ill health and tired physically and mentally … and when, according to the secretary of state, Hiss and Gromyko drafted the report on the conference According to the then-Secretary of State Stettinius, here are some of the things that Hiss helped to decide at Yalta: (1) the establishment of a European High Commission; (2) the treatment of Germany—this you will recall was the conference at which it was decided that we would occupy Berlin with Russia occupying an area completely encircling the city, which as you know, resulted in the Berlin airlift which cost 31 American lives; (3) the Polish question; (4) the relationship between UNRRA and the Soviet; (5) the rights of Americans on control commissions of Rumania, Bulgaria and Hungary; (6) Iran; (7) China—here’s where we gave away Manchuria; (8) Turkish Straits question; (9) international trusteeships; (10) Korea. Of the results of this conference, Arthur Bliss Lane of the State Department had this to say: “As I glanced over the document, I could not believe my eyes. To me, almost every line spoke of a surrender to Stalin.” As you hear this story of high treason, I know that you are saying to yourself, “Well, why doesn’t the Congress do something about it?” Actually, ladies and gentlemen, one of the important reasons for the graft, the corruption, the dishonesty, the disloyalty, the treason in high government positions—one of the most important reasons why this continues—is a lack of moral uprising on the part of the 140 million American people. In the light of history, however, this is not hard to explain. It is the result of an emotional hangover and a temporary moral lapse which follows every war. It is the apathy to evil which people who have been subjected to the tremendous evils of war feel. As the people of the world see mass murder, the destruction of defenseless and innocent people, and all of the crime and lack of morals which go with war, they become numb and apathetic. It has always been thus after war. However, the morals of our people have not been destroyed. They still exist. This cloak of numbness and apathy has only needed a spark to rekindle them. Happily, this spark has finally been supplied. As you know, very recently the secretary of state proclaimed his loyalty to a man guilty of what has always been considered as the most abominable of all crimes—of being a traitor to the people who gave him a position of great trust. The secretary of state, in attempting to justify his continued devotion to the man who sold out the Christian world to the atheistic world, referred to Christ’s Sermon on the Mount as a justification and reason therefore, and the reaction of the American people to this would have made the heart of Abraham Lincoln happy. When this pompous diplomat in striped pants, with a phony British accent, proclaimed to the American people that Christ on the Mount endorsed communism, high treason, and betrayal of a sacred trust, the blasphemy was so great that it awakened the dormant indignation of the American people. He has lighted the spark which is resulting in a moral uprising and will end only when the whole sorry mess of twisted warped thinkers are swept from the national scene so that we may have a new birth of national honesty and decency in government. In 1950, on the anniversary of Abraham Lincoln’s birthday, junior US Senator Joseph McCarthy (R-WI) delivered a speech to the Republican Women’s Club in Wheeling, West Virginia. The lecture launched him into the national spotlight, largely because of his audacious claim that he possessed a list of 205 names of State Department personnel who were “communists” and “traitors.” He would subsequently revise his allegation to 57 names prior to publishing an official transcript of his speech in the Congressional Record. Vacillation aside, McCarthy remained adamant that Soviet sympathizers inside Washington were shaping “our foreign policy.” McCarthy’s Wheeling speech triggered the second Red Scare in America, and it established “McCarthyism” and its warring spirit of anti-communism as the dominant ethos of the early Cold War era. The history of McCarthyism is well known, but revisiting the senator’s Wheeling address also offers fresh insights into wider authoritarian impulses in US politics. To be sure, McCarthy’s political playbook was not entirely different from the populists of the 1930s, such as Huey Long and Father Coughlin, who professed to speak for “the people” in defense of “America First” democratic values against an overbearing federal state and foreign regimes. Both Long and Coughlin tapped a left-wing tradition of populism in the United States that targeted the wealthiest powerbrokers in society (“robber barons,” monopolists, and Wall Street) as the enemy of “the people”—average Americans toiling in the working- and middle-classes. As both a political style and a language, populism has enjoyed traction across the political spectrum. Yet amid the unprecedented uncertainties of the Cold War, intensified by Soviet communism’s global expansion, populism became decidedly right-wing in its political persuasion. title: Psychologies of Popular Support for Authoritarianism
Conscience and a Student Challenge to Authoritarianism
Forever in Fiction
abstract: Against a backdrop of ongoing harm, this essay interrogates the limits of closure—in grief, nuclear decommissioning, and academic scholarship. I draw from an unexpected moment in my research on the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant’s sixty-year closure in which I discovered part of my personal history at the public library that caused me to reexamine how closure and containment operate in both the oral histories that people told me, and the academic training that calls for me to construct a tidy narrative from them. I compare this narrative form of closure in oral histories with the plant’s more subtle impact on everyday life, as well as my own endeavor to frame these fragments in ways that do not sacrifice their incoherence for a logical retelling of them. This essay challenges closure as a useful concept or method not only for nuclear decommissioning and grief but also for scholarship, and proposes the politics of resisting closure, particularly in the climate of late industrialism and capitalism.

title: From There to Here
abstract: Combining an expansive view of family with a limited source base, this essay for History Unclassified examines a small collection of materials originating from the family members of the author’s mother-in-law: objects that they made and left behind, pictures that they sent into the world to call loved ones home, and papers that established or masked identities and granted passage or prevented movement. Transnational in scope and microhistorical in scale, it reveals the multistage, multigenerational, and gendered migrations of an ordinary Chinese American family over extended periods of separation and reunion in the second half of the twentieth century.

abstract: The principal goal of Ted Binnema’s The Vancouver Island Treaties and the Evolving Principles of Indigenous Title is simple: present a “disciplinarily historical perspective” on a series of fifteen land purchase agreements drawn up between 1850 and 1854 that are today known as the Vancouver Island Treaties (6). As the only such agreements between Indigenous communities and colonial authorities in British Columbia before the colony joined Canada in 1871, these “treaties” have occupied an outsized place in the complicated landscape of Canadian jurisprudence. Binnema argues, however, that the legal importance of these purchases has tainted modern examinations with “juridical preoccupations” and “other presentist concerns,” leading him to conclude that “the scholarly literature on the Vancouver Island treaties is badly flawed” (5). The thirteen chapters of this book present Binnema’s ambitious efforts to right this state of affairs. Chapters 1 to 7 delve into the deep history of these purchases, examining the land policies of the Hudson’s Bay Company (HBC) going back to its first trading expeditions in 1668 (chapters 1 and 2), the evolution of human societies on Vancouver Island since time immemorial (chapter 3), and the interactions between newcomers and Indigenous communities from the arrival of Spanish explorers in 1774 to the first purchase agreement in 1850 (chapters 4 and 5). Chapters 6 and 7 place developments on the northwest coast of North America in the context of the British imperial world, with a particular emphasis on debates surrounding New Zealand and the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi. The particular histories of the fifteen Vancouver Island Treaties are discussed in chapters 8 to 11, while chapters 12 and 13 are dedicated to shifting policies after 1854 and the evolving memories of the treaties to 1934.

abstract: Education histories about Indigenous students in the United States increasingly contend with the agency of families, students, and community members, even as they also document the schools’ violent policies and tactics. Robert W. Galler, Jr.’s Taking Charge, Making Change: Native People and the Transition of Education from Stephan Mission to Crow Creek Tribal School joins the growing collection of such histories by examining how the relationships between Catholic leadership and Dakota families influenced the local landscape at Stephan Mission boarding school from the early nineteenth century through the mid-twentieth century. As a local history situated within federal policy and international Catholic developments, Taking Charge seeks “to understand the connection between Native people and American education in a particular place” (19). Accordingly, it accounts for the holistic nature of establishing and running a school: the buildings, staff, curriculum and textbooks, funding, programming, and parental engagement. Galler has meticulously examined missionary sources, including letters between priests across a number of Catholic archives and priests’ own diaries. While reading for Native agency, this emphasis on Catholic sources also results in a deep engagement with the records of the priests themselves and a significant focus on their vantage points, positioning the book as a useful contribution to missionary school histories. Student writings and oral histories also guide later chapters; methodologically, the attention to these sources positions this book alongside recent boarding school histories from Denise K. Lajimodiere and Jacqueline Emery. Footnotes in Taking Charge are unusually and usefully robust.

abstract: In How the New World Became Old, Caroline Winterer provides “a new history of the United States” by exploring the geological and paleontological studies that led to the realization of deep time, the multimillion-year-old history of life on Earth. “For many [present-day] citizens of the United States,” she writes, “the antiquity of the land is a core feature of their national identity.” Although a debatable point, this does not diminish her well-written and thought-provoking account of “how and why this view of ancient America came to be” over the course of the nineteenth century (1). Whereas many histories of American geology and paleontology have focused on specific controversies, such as the rivalry between paleontologists and fossil hunters Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, Winterer offers a sweeping narrative that defies easy characterization. She does not provide readers with an argument per se; rather, she weaves together a compelling and well-researched account of the men and women who studied and artistically represented deep time as well as the meaning(s) they assigned to it.

title: Karin Wulf. Lineage: Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America
abstract: For far too long, the history of the family has been relegated to a secondary field of interest or even an area for genealogists rather than professional historians. In Karin Wulf’s adept hands, however, family history is essential for unpacking key historical questions about power, race, law, and gender. Lineage: ­­Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America offers a multi-layered, sweeping study of the way ­­eighteenth-century Americans deployed family histories as tools of governance and hierarchy. This richly illustrated, meticulously researched and argued book weaves together the latest innovations in cultural history to read a wide range of “texts.” Wulf’s voluminous source base ranges from a silver plate engraved with a family story to illustrated bibles to mere scraps of paper in archives across the eastern United States and England. Her mastery of the scholarship of “vast early America” (a term Wulf herself coined) allows her to contextualize her evidence in historiographies of family, law, religion, material culture, sexuality, and slavery. While this is primarily an Anglo-American story, Wulf situates the work in conversation with scholarship on the broader Atlantic world in this era.

abstract: There is a long tradition of caution among Roman historians. Anachronism, modern terms, values, and frameworks can all easily overwhelm our fragmentary source base, creating false, overly modern interpretations. Our hesitancy has generated steady, but admittedly very slow, progress, especially on lesser-documented segments of the Roman population. We have struggled to effectively characterize, let alone categorize, some of these groups, as we seek to avoid importing baggage from other periods and fields of study. As Sarah Bond powerfully argues in Strike: Labor, Unions, and Resistance in the Roman Empire, we needn’t tie ourselves into knots to work on these portions of the populace. Anachronism, properly acknowledged and employed strategically, can be another tool in our kit, and it can be deployed to “return a voice of collective action to a conversation about labor in the ancient world” (5). Strike explores the power that existed within and was sometimes utilized by associations of workers in the Roman Republic and Empire. Bond begins in the near-mythological past of the city and guides the reader to the early Middle Ages in a comprehensive look at seven periods, each with distinct expressions of resistance from and attempts to control working people. The result is an accessible history of the Roman world that centers the experience of working people.

abstract: In Finding God in the Gulag, Jeffrey S. Hardy tells the story of religious believers in the Soviet prison camp system. Although the Gulag—the system of forced labor camps in the Soviet Union—has been extensively researched, the story of religious faith in the Gulag is far less well known. Scholars have explored how faith and a sense of higher meaning and purpose helped people survive the dehumanizing environment of Nazi concentration camps. Although the history of Soviet atheism has received significant recent attention, the history of Soviet mass repression of religious believers has not. The Soviet regime did not simply disestablish the Russian Orthodox Church and institute atheist propaganda; it expended enormous effort to eradicate religion. Yet religion did not disappear: According to the suppressed 1937 census, over half of the Soviet population believed in God twenty years after the revolution, and the Soviets continued to battle against religious belief until the end. This book contributes to an important facet of that story.

Shulamit Volkov. Germany through Jewish Eyes: A History from the Eighteenth Century to the Present
abstract: Since the beginning of “modernity,” Jews have repeatedly been an object of inquiry by non-Jews who evaluated and disparaged their subjects’ religion and lives. The sheer volume of ink spilled on discussing Jewish emancipation and Jewish rights during the long nineteenth century (and beyond) demonstrates how central Jewish lives and religion were to self-definitions of Germanness; however, the writing of German history has struggled mightily to incorporate Jewish lives in anything but a peripheral manner—right up to the present. Often, Jewish lives—if they are presented at all—revolve around suffering, discrimination, and the Holocaust. Furthermore, the view from the historians of German history rarely reflects the views of German Jews and the times, places, and spaces in which they lived. The field of German-Jewish history has thus flourished where German history has lagged behind, and such scholarship has provided a lens through which we can view how Jews lived in the German states and in the context of the events of their time. Yet these historiographical traditions are in an asymmetrical relationship—the latter relies explicitly on the former, but the former can pick and choose when, where, and how to incorporate the latter.

Surekha Davies. Humans: A Monstrous History
abstract: Surekha Davies declares that “[m]onsters are category problems that have to be defanged” (67) in her dazzling new book Humans: A Monstrous History. This politically engaged work shows how and why humans have “monstrified” other people across many different settings, deploying examples from histories of colonialism, gender, religion, science, and the environment in a deliberately wide-ranging work of accessible scholarship. Some of the most compelling and detailed examples come from the author’s background in the global history of the early modern period, but Davies adeptly juggles case studies ranging from the classical world to science fiction. She does so in order to ask the reader to assess the ethical implications of stereotyping others as “monstrous,” and to simultaneously argue for a positive, inclusive way of thinking about monstrosity through the lens of difference. These two strands are held in productive tension throughout the book. Davies’s aim is to build on the work of scholars like Saidiya Hartman: to engage with the challenges of foregrounding experiences too often lost (in Hartman’s phrase) to “the silence in the archive” (227). In practice, here, that often means empathetically centering stories of people who were exploited, condemned, or marginalized in their lifetimes for their perceived monstrosity. It also means showing the reader how to interrogate and contextualize the ways that individuals and groups were “monstrified” in cultural artifacts: artworks, court records, treatises, maps, advertisements, and news media, amongst other sources. The book unfolds in a loosely chronological format, and most frequently utilizes case studies from western Europe and the Americas. It also at times takes a wider perspective, from cholera epidemics in nineteenth-century Japan to categories of gender in the early-modern Ottoman court. This is the kind of work that necessarily involves drawing on a very wide range of scholarship alongside Davies’s own specialist research. Many subsections function as neat introductions to the much larger fields of knowledge that Davies expertly weaves together with her lively, incisive prose.

abstract: Scholars of French or Indian history (or indeed of European imperial or Indian Ocean history more broadly) might be puzzled by the book’s subtitle. They have not forgotten the history of French India. But Glorious Failure is not written for them. It is presumably a book written for the wider public, particularly in India and in France, which, as Robert Ivermee argues, have erased and forgotten this history, or worse, still believe in the myth of France “as a ‘good’ coloniser” (9). There are, of course, a whole host of studies about French India, but as the author points out, they are more focused or written in French, so this is an English-language book “chart[ing] the origins, development and ultimate failure of French imperialism in India from the late seventeenth to the early nineteenth century” (4). Works for public are often works of synthesis, and works of synthesis need to simplify. This monograph is not afraid to do so. Ivermee makes some bold statements (“the fiasco of American world leadership since 1945” [9]) and is clear in his own ambition: He wants to tell not only the story of intra-European conflict on the subcontinent, and that of French engagements with various Indian powers, but also to weave in the story of life in the French colonies, the negative impact of French rule, and particularly the persistence of slavery throughout the French Indian Ocean possessions. He insists that, from the very outset, French ambitions were not simply commercial or colonial, but imperialist, driven by the French monarchy’s insatiable thirst for glory. As a consequence, the role of the monarchy is stressed even in the first privately funded and organized trading voyages to India in the seventeenth century. By contrast, after the Napoleonic Wars, Ivermee argues, when the French presence in India was reduced to a few territories and trading posts (Pondichéry, Karikal, Yanaon, Chandernagor, and Mahé), it ceased to be “imperialist” and became solely “colonial” (264). Despite the geopolitical importance of these possessions to the French colonization of Vietnam or its rivalry with Britain, these 150 years of history only get a 13-page epilogue. Ivermee tells an unambiguous story of inevitable French failure, of “a defeat that was ultimately emphatic, crushing and almost absolute, in which the vain pursuit of power and glory led to overstretch and collapse” (10).

abstract: At first glance, Jack Neubauer’s The Adoption Plan: China and the Remaking of Global Humanitarianism appears poised to trace the transnational history of child adoption from China. But readers expecting an account of Chinese children adopted into families abroad will soon find themselves on a different track. Instead, Neubauer examines the early days of a now widespread fundraising strategy: international child sponsorship, through which individuals send money to support children in welfare institutions, focusing on creating relationships between donors and child recipients via the exchange of personal letters, gifts, and photographs. This program in China, which Neubauer refers to as “The Adoption Plan,” forms the book’s central subject. Neubauer follows the early twentieth-century histories of organizations employing this tactic in China—such as the National Association for Refugee Children, the China’s Children’s Fund, Foster Parents Plan for War Children (PLAN)–China Branch, and the American-Oriental Friendship Association—drawing on Chinese- and English-language archives and monographs, as well as eclectic English sources. Touching on topics including Chinese charitable traditions, the American Red Cross in China, overseas Chinese remittances and epistolary practices, the psychological testing of orphans in China (a curious digression), the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration and the China National Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, and the US turn to Korean adoptions, Neubauer makes his narrative about these institutions an entertaining one. He stops along the way to include gossip about Madame Sun Yat-sen’s love affair with the US head of PLAN; the story of a Chinese orphanage funded by a famous female assassin; a discussion of so-called jeep babies (interracial babies born after World War II in China); and insights into a contemporary Chinese campaign to discourage Sino-American love affairs potentially leading to espionage. The majority of Neubauer’s case studies focus on work done in the early 1940s. Related discussions span from the nineteenth century through the current day. These studies form the basis for his critique of humanitarianism.

abstract: The Conquest of the Mountains places particular emphasis on the Sasun massacre of 1893–1894 as a microhistory in the broader context of the Ottoman government’s protracted efforts to assert its modern statehood in the mountainous regions. Owen Robert Miller interprets this violent history as the history of the conquest of the mountains and places it in a larger history of “upland conquest, control, and colonization,” which he defines as a phenomenon encompassing the French campaigns in the Atlas Mountains, the Russian conquest of the Caucasus, and the British campaigns in the tribal areas (5). The book discusses the absence of mountains in general historiography, and dialogues with recent works on the history of violence in the Ottoman east. Ottoman strategy during the nineteenth century centered on the military’s efforts to eliminate the Kurdish power holders (mirs) in Eastern Anatolia, while cultivating new alliances with the less powerful Kurdish tribal heads as local intermediaries. The implementation of this policy in Sasun resulted in the imposition of double taxation, the perpetration of acts of plunder, and the continuation of violence by certain tribes against Armenian villages. The Armenian revolutionaries, specifically the Hnchak members, successfully organized self-defense units of peasants as networks in the Sasun mountains to counter Kurdish attacks. In response, the Ottoman army intervened, potentially exacerbating the conflict between the Kurdish tribes and the Armenian peasants. The military operation culminated in a significant Armenian massacre.

abstract: Reports of the violence in Warri in 1997 often got mired in the international condemnation of the execution of Ken Saro Wiwa in 1995 and news of the environmental devastation of the Niger Delta caused by petroleum. The Warri crisis over the creation of local governments was explained in terms of ethnic conflict: whether Olu, the Itsekiri monarch, was suzerain over a very heterogeneous region. Ethnic conflicts of this type were so commonplace that save for its widespread violence and devastation, the Warri crisis amounted to a blip and did not attract sustained national conversation or even much scholarly rationalization. In Minority Identities in Nigeria, Oghenetoja Okoh argues for the uniqueness of the Warri crisis even as it was set within a historically established pattern of political ethnicization by which the peoples of the Niger Delta were forged into colonial subjecthood and Nigerian citizenship. Scholarly disinterest, Okoh argues, is typical for a colonial and Nigerian historiography that considers minority populations as tangential to colonial purposes and to the structure of the postcolonial state. Yet, minorities have driven the most significant changes in Nigeria’s political history, both through efforts of the state to restrict their political participation and from how minorities have used their statuses to navigate adverse colonial and postcolonial exclusions. Minority Identities in Nigeria recovers the historical process by which the peoples of the western Niger Delta were marginalized by colonial and imperial policies aimed at political incorporation and economic exploitation, and how they responded to marginalization.

Everyday Bureaucratic Authoritarianism under South African Apartheid
abstract: The standard by which the police operate is cruelly simple: every black man is a criminal suspect. In a technical sense, the police are not far off the mark to be so suspicious. The laws of apartheid are a far-reaching tangle of restrictions, reaching so deeply into everyday life that it is a rare African who does not violate some law. A policeman may at any time call upon any African who is sixteen or older to produce his reference book. If the African fails to produce it, or if his papers are not in order, he is committing a criminal offence and is liable to a fine or imprisonment. This is the nub of the infamous “pass laws,” a complex mesh of rules and regulations that restrict the freedom of movement of Africans. Compared to some of the other oppressive statutes of apartheid, the pass laws on paper seem modest enough. But in practice they are the keynote on which enforcement of the entire apartheid system is based.

abstract: The study aimed to (a) compare Korean American U.S. citizens and Korean American permanent residents studying in U.S. colleges in their experiences of everyday discrimination, parental ethnic–racial socialization (PERS), depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms and (b) investigate whether different PERS practices (namely, cultural socialization–pluralism, preparation for bias, and promotion of mistrust) moderate the effects of everyday discrimination on depressive and anxiety symptoms. Survey data were collected from 415 full-time undergraduate students in the United States who self-identified as Korean American (citizens n = 223; permanent residents n = 192). The results revealed that compared to Korean American U.S. citizens, Korean American permanent residents reported more everyday discrimination, PERS practices, depressive, and anxiety symptoms. Everyday discrimination was associated with more depressive and anxiety symptoms for both groups. For Korean American citizens, the associations with both depressive and anxiety symptoms were buffered by cultural socialization-pluralism. On the other hand, for Korean American permanent residents, the association between discrimination and depressive symptoms was buffered by preparation for bias. Despite differential rates of everyday discrimination across the two groups, these experiences are similarly detrimental to their mental health. Also, the findings highlight distinct protective mechanisms conferred by specific PERS practices that can help shield these groups from the adverse impacts of discrimination. title: Transnational activism and civic engagement among Burmese American refugee youth.

abstract: Research on refugee youth has predominantly centered on challenges and deficits, often overlooking their resilience, contributions, and the positive roles they play in their new communities, including activism and civic engagement (ACE). This study addresses that gap by focusing on Burmese refugee youth, one of the largest resettled groups in the U.S. in recent history. Specifically, we examined four types of activities—protesting, donating, distributing information, and signing petitions—across three domains: ethnic/local (Burmese American causes), transnational (Myanmar causes), and general (other causes). The sample comprised 99 Burmese American adolescents from refugee backgrounds. Over half engaged in at least one ACE activity in the last six months. Transnational engagement was most common, followed by ethnic and general ACE. An explorative person-centered analysis revealed three profiles: moderately engaged (60%), transnationally engaged (11%), and highly engaged (20.7%). Results were discussed in the context of the global refugee crisis and the 2021 February 1 Myanmar coup d'état. These findings have important implications to expand the current conceptual model of activism and civic engagement among refugee and migrant youth.

title: Archaeology of the “Self”: Kenneth Tam Standing in Discontinuous Becoming(s)
abstract: This article examines contemporary artist Kenneth Tam’s recent body of work, focusing on a series of sculptural pieces in his larger project, Tender is the Hand Which Holds the Stone of Memory. It explores how the artist engages with past moments of atrocity and violence through his artmaking, incorporating research components such as archival and site visits as a basis for his processes of casting, manipulation, and juxtaposition of objects purchased online. Through close analysis of the visual and material properties of the objects he crafts, as well as the historical and institutional contexts within which they are enmeshed, this article suggests that Tam’s works serve as his “self-portrait.” I argue that he leverages his artmaking as a means to explore a changing sense of “self,” acting as a co-constitutive force in reshaping the dynamics of custom, ritual, and memory—dynamics that have not only enabled but also delimited his aspiration for navigating the discontinuities in his becoming.

abstract: This article explores how painter and collagist Jimmy Tsutomu Mirikitani (1920–2012) narrated his life through art, alongside his collaboration with Linda Hattendorf, the director of the 2006 documentary The Cats of Mirikitani . Drawing on scholarship in life writing studies and art history, it examines the ways in which Mirikitani’s street art and life narratives—created in collaboration with pedestrians while he was unhoused in New York between the late 1980s and 2001—challenge conventional forms of auto/biography. The article also analyzes The Cats of Mirikitani as a collaborative project between Mirikitani and Hattendorf, revealing the political potential of such collaborations. Through the case study of Mirikitani’s collaborative life narration, it emphasizes the significance of cross-ethnic collaboration and intersubjective modes of life narration in fostering new forms of community and understanding across social and racial divides.
