title: Migration and Memory: Navigating Intersectional Identity Through Sarindar Dhaliwal’s Triple Self-Portrait with Persimmons and Pomegranates
abstract: This article analyzes Sarindar Dhaliwal’s autobiographical artwork, Triple Self-Portrait with Persimmons and Pomegranates (1988) , exploring how her life, marked by geographical transitions, shaped her identity and artistic vision. By engaging with critical scholarship on memory, place, and identity, this study discusses how Dhaliwal’s use of landscape imagery connects her emotionally to the colonial legacy as a member of the South Asian diaspora. Simultaneously, through the multilayered visual language and techniques employed in the artwork, Dhaliwal engages with shifting post-colonial theories, offering a decentred, globalized view of her art and identity. This paper argues that through self-portraits embedded in the artwork, Dhaliwal imparts a sense of temporality, mirroring the evolution of her identity as an artist. As one of the first South Asian female artists in Canada with a career spanning over 40 years, Dhaliwal’s contributions to Canadian and the diaspora South Asian visual cultures are path-breaking.

journal: Asian Diasporic Visual Cultures and the Americas
title: How Could One Paint a Self Portrait! Identity and Erasure in the Work of Rasheed Araeen
abstract: Throughout the late 1970s and early 1980s, the contemporary Pakistani artist Rasheed Araeen created a series of self-portraits in response to the institutional racism he experienced in London. Araeen described one such self-portrait as “trying to deal with my own existential reality, the reality of a [B]lack person living in a white (racist) society.” 1 A careful analysis of his work reveals that not only was he barred from participating in discourses of minimalism, but that self-portraiture—as it is conceived of in Eurocentric discourses—is also foreclosed to Araeen. His work thus underscores the strict definitional boundaries of art historical categories, which inherently and unconditionally exclude the voice of the Other. Read through the work of Franz Fanon, Araeen’s self-portraits reveal how the Black, colonized body is denied any notion of a fully embodied self, but rather how their identity is fixed and determined by the white gaze.

journal: Asian Diasporic Visual Cultures and the Americas
title: Beyond Japanese Crafts: Kōgei in Brazil from a Transcultural Perspective
abstract: As craftspeople migrated between Japan and Brazil, Japanese crafts ( kōgei ) underwent negotiations, adaptations, and transformations. This article explores the transference of kōgei from Japan to Brazil, beginning with a historical examination of the term within the context of East-West dialogues at the turn of the nineteenth century and the challenges of translation. In the twentieth century, as Japanese immigrants formed a discrete community in Brazil, kōgei, as a category of objects and a system of value, was introduced in the country. We document the institutionalization of kōgei through an exhibition and association and trace the professional paths of four ceramic practitioners: two Japanese migrants and two Japanese Brazilians. These trajectories illustrate how kōgei , through its integration into Brazilian society, has evolved from a distinct Japanese cultural practice into a transcultural phenomenon that crosses national, cultural, and ethnic boundaries.

journal: Asian Diasporic Visual Cultures and the Americas
title: Extending Ornamentalism: Yellow Woman as Decolonial Object/Plant/Land/Person in Kelly Akashi’s Formations Exhibition
abstract: This article engages with ornamentalism, a critical theory often presented as a problematic condition of feminized Asian personhood/objecthood. In this article, I argue that ornamentalism can disrupt settler colonialism and geontopower, as well as the dominant social and epistemological construction of Life and Nonlife. By examining Kelly Akashi’s Formations exhibition at the Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego, I extend ornamentalism as an opportunity for Asian Americans to witness their historical and present conditions on Indigenous land, specifically through Japanese American incarceration. In this article, I examine the exhibition and the ways in which Akashi entangles objects, plants, land, and bodies; share my racialized and gendered encounter as an object at the museum; and discuss how Akashi’s work challenges viewers to see the liveliness of “nonliving” “objects” through their slow witnessing and low activity. Akashi's disruption of the boundaries around land-based materials and “humans” questions geontological and economic discourses that uphold settler colonialism.

title: Trilateral Relations in Northeast Asia
abstract: The aim of this introductory essay is to both discuss the overall topic of this Special Issue – trilateralism in Northeast Asia – and briefly present the five research articles that follow. The Introduction begins by explaining the choice of the theme for the Special Issue, and why there are empirico-policy and theoretical reasons to examine trilateral relations in Northeast Asia through a series of dedicated research articles. The second part of the Introduction covers several of those empirico-policy and theoretical reasons in depth, including how trilateral relations in Northeast Asia contribute to power balancing and how information asymmetries within trilateral groupings can make cooperation challenging. Special attention is placed on examining how trilaterals (as a form of minilateral) have the upside of filling some gaps in the international security architecture, while nonetheless also representing potential downside risk through heightened security dilemma dynamics. The penultimate section of the Introduction provides a brief synopsis of the main argument of each research article in the collection. Finally, the fourth section concludes the Introduction by tying together the main points, contextualising them within the evolution of contemporary Northeast Asia, and signposting the value of the articles for scholars and policymakers.

title: Trilaterals and the Reorganisation of Northeast Asia’s Regional Order
authors: Sung Chul Jung; Jagannath Panda; Jae Jeok Park
abstract: In an era of intensifying competition over the international order in Northeast Asia, both major and non-major states have increasingly sought to use trilateral mechanisms distinct from bilateral and multilateral forms. In this context, this article aims to discuss various types, origins, and influences of trilateral relations in international politics, as well as current and historical trilateral relations that have contributed to the emergence and transformation of regional orders. First, it categorises trilateral relations into four types: (1) three partners, (2) three rivals, (3) two partners against one rival, and (4) two rivals competing for one (potential) partner, encompassing cooperative and conflictual relationships among both three parties and three bilateral relations and clarifying each type’s characteristics and dynamics. Then, it offers a comprehensive way to understand the origins of trilateral relations, identifying three different, but complementary, sources for the formation of trilateral relations: structural balance of power, strategic interests, and a mix of structure and strategy. Lastly, it explores power dynamics both of and within trilateral relations, focusing on three dimensions of power: the trilateral’s collective power as a group, the power dynamics within trilateral relations, and the structural power exerted by the trilateral over its individual component states.

title: Minilateralism and Trilateral Cooperation in Northeast Asia: Implications for Regional Security and Order-Building
authors: Daewon Ohn; Er-Win Tan; Hyun Chung Yoo
abstract: This article examines the evolving dynamics of minilateralism and trilateral cooperation in Northeast Asia, and assesses their implications for regional security and order-building. It traces the development of minilateral frameworks in the region since the end of the Cold War, focusing in particular on two key trilateral cases: security cooperation between the United States, Japan, and South Korea, and functional cooperation between China, Japan, and South Korea through the Trilateral Cooperation Secretariat (TCS). It is argued that US–Japan–South Korea trilateralism, which was initially shaped by the need to address the North Korean nuclear challenge, has become a core element of the US-led security architecture aimed at balancing China’s growing influence in the Indo–Pacific. By contrast, the TCS reflects a pragmatic form of minilateralism centred on economic and technical cooperation. Yet its effectiveness has been constrained by deep-seated geopolitical tensions and institutional limitations, particularly amid intensifying US–China rivalry. The article concludes that while trilateral minilateralism offers new avenues for coordination, it also risks exacerbating security dilemmas. Strengthening institutional mechanisms for strategic communication, confidence-building, and risk reduction will be essential to supporting regional stability and order-building.

title: A Comparative Analysis of the China Policies of Japan and South Korea Amid Sino–US Confrontation, 2017–2024: An Ontological Security Perspective
abstract: This study compares the China policies of Japan and South Korea under escalating US–China strategic competition and asserts that both states’ policy approaches reflect ontological security pursuits. The analysis illustrates how Tokyo and Seoul formulate policies that align with their self-perceived identities within established relational frameworks with the two superpowers to preserve ontological security. The findings reveal that ontological insecurities stemming from abrupt systemic changes or contentious interactions by China drive both states towards strengthened US alignment. Conversely, when ontological insecurities originate from problematic engagements with the US or when there is no insecurity, both states demonstrate an inclination to revitalise economic cooperation with China. The respective patterns of China-engagement strategies and US-aligned balancing against China differ markedly, rooted in distinct identities and interactions among states that generate varying levels of ontological insecurity. By integrating ontological security theory with an empirical analysis of East Asian strategic adaptations to great-power rivalry, the article enhances the theoretical understanding of state behaviour in international relations.

title: How China, the ROK, and DPRK Balance Each Other’s Security Interests: Dynamic Analysis of Conflict and Cooperation
abstract: This article draws on typological approaches to trilateral relations to construct three models characterising the China–South Korea–North Korea triangle. These models – the confrontational alignment model, mediation model, and limited cooperation model – represent different patterns of interaction within this trilateral relationship. To understand why and how these models evolve, the article employs a level-of-analysis framework that identifies key explanatory variables at three interrelated dimensions: systemic, processual, and unit-level factors. By integrating international structure, interactional processes, and domestic actor attributes, this framework reveals the complex dynamics shaping trilateral relations. Given intensified US–China strategic rivalry and North Korea’s accelerated nuclear development, this combined approach highlights emerging and evolving characteristics in China–South Korea–North Korea relations.

title: What Minilateralism Can and Can’t Do in Cross-Taiwan Strait Conflict Management
abstract: What can – and can’t – minilateralism contribute to the management of cross-Taiwan Strait conflict? Although US-linked minilateral mechanisms have multiplied across the Indo–Pacific, their concrete relevance to Taiwan’s security has not been systematically assessed. To address this gap, the study develops a comparative framework focused on policy signalling, deterrence by punishment and by denial, and escalation dynamics, and applies it to three prominent cases: the US–Japan–South Korea trilateral, the Quad, and TSD. The analysis finds that these minilaterals generate distinct and uneven security effects. The US–Japan–South Korea trilateral provides the strongest signalling and denial leverage due to institutionalised intelligence-sharing and operational coordination. Across all mechanisms, escalation risks persist and domestic political constraints hinder consistent implementation. The article clarifies the mechanisms through which minilateralism shapes China’s cost–benefit calculus, and delineates the boundaries of what minilateral settings can realistically achieve. Minilateralism cannot substitute for Taiwan’s self-defence, but it meaningfully shapes China’s cost–benefit calculus by raising uncertainty, reducing vulnerabilities, and reinforcing a more resilient Indo–Pacific security environment.

title: The Politics of Regionalism in the Mekong: Institutional Bypass and Bricolage
abstract: Regionalism in the Mekong has continued to proliferate over the last three decades, despite some ups and downs, but the reasons for this persistent proliferation remain under-explained. The hypothesis of this study is that ‘institutional bypass’, a concept originally developed by international lawyers, provides the logic behind the proliferation of regional institutions in the Mekong. This is a top-down force to bypass existing institutions, often exercised by states in forming regionalism at the international level. In addition, the study draws on the insights of geographers, who have argued that ‘institutional bricolage’ helps to explain how regionalism is rooted in local communities. This is a bottom-up force to re-use and re-shape existing institutional elements associated with regionalism, rather than creating new ones. After analysing the politics of regional institution-building in the Mekong, which seems to support the institutional bypass hypothesis, this article considers how best to synthesise the two seemingly opposing logics – namely, institutional bypass and institutional bricolage. The article proposes an integrated analytical framework that explains the coexistence of various types of regionalism in and beyond the Mekong.

title: Speaking Back to National History in Thailand: Lanna Historiography and the Question of Colonialism
authors: Tinakrit Sireerat; Søren Ivarsson; Waraporn Ruangsri
abstract: This article examines how the term ‘colonialism’ has been employed in the historiography of Lanna, a historical region in Northern Thailand. It traces the evolution of scholarly debates surrounding Siam’s incorporation of Lanna and analyses how the colonial lens has influenced interpretations of state domination and local resistance. Some scholars explicitly adopt colonialism as a critical lens to highlight asymmetrical power relations and cultural suppression. Some regard it as mere contextual background or a neutral temporal marker for economic branding. Others reject it altogether, instead emphasising the unevenness of modernisation and its socioeconomic consequences. Recent studies have increasingly used the colonial lens to critique Siamese policies, drawing parallels between Siam’s state-building strategies and European colonial practices. However, this article also highlights the potential pitfalls of replacing the teleology of nationalism or modernisation with that of colonialism by overemphasising Siam’s colonising agency, which risks obscuring the uneven, negotiated, and at times resistant engagement of Lanna actors with the Siamese state.

title: Classical Music Education as National Inculcation: The Case of Crypto-Colonial Thailand
abstract: Thailand, a ‘crypto-colony’ that has officially never been colonised but has been heavily dependent on Western powers, boasts a so-called ‘classical music tradition’ that has endured periods of neglect and even prohibition before being revived and officially embraced as part of national culture. Education has played a key role in broader civilising movements and, since the 1970s, in the revival of Thai classical music. Through fieldwork and interviews conducted in schools across central Thailand, I examine how Thai classical music is taught and learned in institutionalised educational settings. From making documentation to practising the music, appropriate manners and behaviours are embedded into both teachers’ and students’ daily lives. Education thus functions not only as a means of transmitting traditional musical knowledge and skills, but also as a tool for inculcating and (re-)constructing notions of Thai civilisation, culture, and tradition, within the habitus of institutionalised education in modern Thai society. Using Thai classical music education as a case study, I argue that in crypto-colonial contexts, the (re-)invention of continuous cultural traditions functions not only as a strategy for cultural preservation, but also as a means of asserting civility and modernity independent of Western influence, thereby claiming equivalent status with colonial counterparts.

title: The Adaptation of Silang Tanmu : Cultural Censorship, Performance Governance, and Negotiation in Cold War Taiwan
abstract: This article examines two state-sanctioned adaptations of the Peking opera Silang Tanmu (四郎探母, Fourth Son visits His Mother) in Taiwan to illuminate the interaction of political ideology, grassroots pressure, and cultural governance under Kuomintang (KMT, Nationalist) rule. After retreating to Taiwan in 1949, the KMT promoted Peking opera as an instrument of cultural orthodoxy and a means of politically mobilising waishengren (mainlander) soldiers and civilians. However, Silang Tanmu became politically contentious when some critics argued that its narrative did not embody anti-communist values. This coincided with the harshest phase of martial-law authoritarianism and led to the first official adaptation in the 1950s. Produced under intense political repression, this version left no meaningful space for artistic agency and was ultimately rejected by performers and audiences. By the 1970s, however, Taiwan’s gradual political opening provided space for cultural workers and audiences to exercise greater agency in shaping the opera’s form and messaging, resulting in a second, more accepted adaptation that preserved the original structure while modestly aligning itself with state ideology. The contested revisions of Silang Tanmu thus reveal both the limits of top-down cultural control and the historically contingent negotiations among state, society, and cultural producers in Taiwan.

title: Learning to be Feminists from Their Own Lives: Interpreting Feminist Identity Among Female Chinese College Students
abstract: This study focuses on the identity and subjective experience of female Chinese college students who self-identify as feminists, adopting an interpretive qualitative method to explore their interpretation of feminist identity and related experiences. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 16 female college students, and the interview data were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings conclusively reveal that these students’ identity construction is rooted in daily embodied practices, whereby continuous dialectics between subjective experiences and critical reflexivity foster dynamically fluid feminist frameworks. Female Chinese college students generally self-identify as feminists rather than subscribing to specific theoretical definitions of feminism. Feminist identities are shaped by their learning experiences, are dynamic and fluid, and serve as a means of navigating real-life situations. In their feminist practices, the research participants interpret and fight against their situation as ‘outsiders-within’. They strategically use feminist identities as a means of learning and a way of reconstructing their lives. We show that the participants’ intersectional identities and feminist consciousness developed embodied standpoints from the margins. This study therefore contributes to the field of Chinese feminist knowledge by offering a perspective on the development of feminist identity among female college students.

title: Equalism Among Young South Korean Men: A Localised Form of Antifeminism
abstract: Young men and women in South Korea have increasingly divergent views on gender equality, with more young men openly expressing antifeminist sentiments. This study examines the prevalence of antifeminism among young Korean men by analysing their perceptions of feminism and the underlying reasons contributing to their antifeminist attitudes. Based on interviews with 23 Korean men in their 20s, we find that while these men acknowledge gender inequality in Korea, they reject Korean feminism and instead advocate for an alternative ideology called equalism. Distinct from, yet overlapping with, modern sexism, we argue that their stance of equalism is grounded in four interrelated beliefs: 1) acknowledgement of gender inequality and nominal support for gender equality as an ideal, 2) support for gender equality, only insofar as it does not challenge existing male privilege, 3) belief in fairness and meritocracy as the primary pathways to gender equality, while overlooking structural causes of inequality, and 4) critique of perceived extreme feminist methods and endorsement of a more moderate, merit-based approach reflected in equalist discourse. Through this research, we contribute to the literature on antifeminism, misogyny, and modern sexism by offering a nuanced understanding of its local manifestation in South Korea.

title: Framing the Crisis: The Chinese Mainland’s Guidance of Popular Nationalism in the Context of Nancy Pelosi’s Visit to Taiwan
abstract: This study examined whether the Chinese government could guide nationalism to its benefit in a sovereignty-related incident. To answer this question, it used the case study of the visit to Taiwan in 2022 by the former Speaker of the US House of Representatives, Nancy Pelosi, and an innovative framework that combines framing theory and social identity theory, alongside indicators to measure the extent to which the government achieves its goals in guiding nationalism. Based on more than 6,000 comments on the visit, the research finds that the Chinese mainland maintained a certain degree of control over nationalism even in a high-stakes case such as the Pelosi visit. However, the article also highlights the limitations to the government’s guidance of nationalism. Moving beyond the binary conclusions of the existing literature, the study offers a more nuanced account by identifying factors influencing public acceptance of official narratives and by proposing concrete measures for assessing the effectiveness of attempts to guide state-led nationalism.

title: Reframing Hong Kong: Legitimation in the Post-National Security Law Era
abstract: In 2020, the Chinese government imposed the National Security Law (NSL) in Hong Kong, which transformed the liberal authoritarian regime into an illiberal one. This article examines how the government has tried to legitimise this regime change while promoting the growing integration of the territory into the Chinese state. It does so by analysing a newly created National Security Exhibition Gallery unveiled in 2024, which displays the new political narratives that are used to justify the changes. The article argues that the regime’s legitimacy discourse has shifted from institutional and procedural foundations to one centred on nationalism and the Chinese Communist Party, while continuing to invoke the longstanding rhetoric of ‘stability and prosperity’. Through a critical reading of the exhibit’s visual and textual narratives, the article shows how the state seeks to reshape public memory, reframe dissent, and align Hong Kong’s identity with the ideological norms of the mainland.

title: Cigarette Girl , Netflix, and Soft Commodity Nationalism in Indonesia
abstract: With its 2023 Indonesian historical fiction series Cigarette Girl, Netflix sought to grow its market in the world’s fourth most populous country. Based on a novel by Ratih Kumala, the Netflix series sets personal drama and business intrigue against a historical backdrop of postcolonial nationalism, political violence, and rapid growth in the clove-laced tobacco cigarette (kretek) industry. The series condemns 1960s-era patriarchy and state-sponsored violence but ultimately creates a redemptive arc for the nation and positive representations of the kretek industry, disengaging from the political nature of state massacres and the tobacco-related diseases killing more than 250,000 Indonesians a year. Analysing the series as a ‘commodity nationalist’ text that closely identifies kretek with Indonesian national history and culture, this article illuminates how commodity nationalism – like other nationalist projects – entails forms of forgetting and exclusionary class, gender, and racial dynamics.

title: What Needs to be Governed? Hip-Hop Cultural Governance in China through the Lens of Modifications to Rap Music Lyrics
authors: Tianyi Yang; Ge Zhu; Yilin Luo; Fang Wu
abstract: Rap music, as a core element of hip-hop culture, is often celebrated for its subcultural resistance but has undergone significant transformation in China amid processes of mainstreaming and state cultural governance. While previous research has highlighted the localisation and commercialisation of Chinese hip-hop, limited attention has been paid to the micro-level textual shifts in the mainstreaming of Chinese rap music. This study investigates how Chinese state ideology exerts an explicit and subtle impact on popular culture through the case of The Rap of China, a widely viewed hip-hop competition show. By analysing 934 pairs of live and studio versions of songs using thematic and critical discourse analysis, the study identifies three major patterns of lyrical modification: explicit depoliticisation, subtle depoliticisation, and the elimination of ‘badness’. We find that content perceived as politically sensitive or morally inappropriate is systematically altered, transforming hip-hop from a rebellious subculture into an ideologically compliant tool for moral education and social harmony. These transformations are not solely top-down; they reflect a negotiation between state agencies, streaming platforms, and artists under China’s model of cultural governance. This study contributes to understanding how subcultural forms are restructured to serve both market logics and ideological purposes in contemporary China.

title: The Maoist Roots of China’s Extreme Income Inequality
abstract: China today has more extreme income inequality, according to some measures, than the United States, the most unequal advanced capitalist society. The conventional view is that when Mao Zedong was in charge, he relentlessly pursued greater social equality, even at the expense of China’s growth rate. However, a closer look at the contours and drivers of current inequalities tells a different story. The cardinal feature of income inequality in China today is a very large, and generally increasing, gap between the household incomes of rural origin citizens and their urban origin counterparts. China’s unusually large urban-rural income gap is rooted in, and perpetuated by, the system of household registration ( hukou ) that was institutionalized under Mao in 1958. By perpetuating the hukou -based division of Chinese into lower caste rural origin citizens and favored urban origin citizens, while relaxing the Mao-era restrictions on rural to urban migration, China in the reform era benefited by exploiting the undercompensated labor of millions of rural migrant laborers, arguably the major engine of the China boom. Despite some modest reforms of the hukou system in recent years, most of the more than 250 million rural–urban migrants in large cities today still face considerable obstacles and discrimination in trying to gain access to urban public goods and benefits for themselves and their children. But today the stubborn persistence of hukou -based discrimination poses major obstacles for China’s future. Three concrete obstacles are discussed: the low human capital levels of China’s adult population, the difficulty of shifting the economy to emphasize consumption over savings, and the declining number of babies being born each year. Each of these obstacles has roots in the hukou system institutionalized under Mao.

title: Who Will Deliver Common Prosperity in China? A Look at Policy Instruments
abstract: This article examines how Xi Jinping’s common prosperity agenda has been translated into policy practice in China. Using the PKULaw database, we construct two original datasets: 194 common prosperity policies (CPPs), whose titles explicitly include “common prosperity,” and 10,180 common prosperity-linked policies (CPLPs), whose texts reference the term. Combining descriptive analysis, structural topic modeling, and dictionary-based keyword searches, we show that explicit CPP branding is limited and that it is highly concentrated in Zhejiang, the designated demonstration zone, with limited uptake elsewhere. Within the broader Xi-era CPLP corpus, the dominant themes are public service delivery and political signaling, while more ambitious redistributive, disciplinary, and regulatory domains are weakly represented or absent. These findings suggest that common prosperity in formal policy practice has been much narrower and more welfare administrative than its expansive political rhetoric implies, and they highlight the limits of a province-led approach to implementing an agenda that would require stronger central commitment and more substantial fiscal and regulatory support.

title: The Rise of China’s Electric Vehicle Industry: Strategic Alliances Between Local Governments and Private Capital
abstract: This article challenges the prevailing view that China’s electric vehicle (EV) boom is primarily the result of top-down industrial policy. Drawing on the history of China’s automotive sector since the 1990s, it shows that stringent central regulations and entrenched state-owned enterprises (SOEs) excluded most localities from lucrative joint ventures. In response, local governments forged strategic alliances with private manufacturers, leveraging capital markets, policy loopholes, and post-2008 credit expansion to attract investment, upgrade industries, and diversify regional economies. These partnerships, initially in traditional automotive manufacturing, proved pivotal to China’s EV takeoff after 2015, enabling private firms to outcompete SOEs in innovation, responsiveness, and market expansion. Comparative cases in steel and pharmaceuticals illustrate the broader applicability of this dynamic. The study highlights the enduring adaptability of Chinese local governments and private capital in navigating central constraints, offering new insights into industrial policies, industrial upgrading, and local developmental states.

title: Historical Nihilism: The Rise of a Political Technology
abstract: This article interrogates the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) evolving struggle over the past by tracing the career of the concept of historical nihilism (历史虚无主义), from polemic to a fully institutionalized yet diffuse political technology under Xi Jinping. Through close analysis of historical documents, Party resolutions, laws, disciplinary codes, court rulings, propaganda circulars, and digital governance directives, it identifies two phases: a pre-2013 rhetorical stage, during which the term remained discursively unstable and primarily served to stigmatize heterodox scholarship, and a post-2013 institutional stage, in which it was recast as an existential threat and embedded across four domains of Party-state power: law, discipline, education, and cyberspace. To account for this transformation, the article draws on Althusser’s concept of interpellation, along with Bourdieu and Butler’s insights on performative authority, to show how historical nihilism evolved from a polemical label into a political technology capable of triggering juridical, bureaucratic, and algorithmic sanctions. This shift exemplifies the CCP’s transition from narrating history to governing its possibility, and from rhetorical contestation to epistemic sovereignty: the sovereign power to determine what history is, who may speak it, and how it must be remembered.

title: Urban Investment and Development Companies in China’s Local Governance: The Paradox of Marketization
abstract: As financing platforms and construction agents for local governments, urban investment and development companies (chengshi touzi fazhan gongsi 城市投资发展公司), or UIDCs, play a crucial role in China’s urbanization and local governance. Existing research has often treated UIDCs as static instruments of local governments while overlooking their evolving, and at times conflicting, objectives and their complex governance roles within local administrations. Drawing on 15 months of fieldwork within a district government and its affiliated UIDCs, this article examines UIDCs within the broader dynamics of state capitalism and central-local relations. First, it argues that despite marketization reforms promoting corporate governance and substantive business operations, UIDCs remain deeply embedded in local governance structures, particularly in less developed regions, where they continue to serve as key vehicles for local governments’ developmental and fiscal objectives. Second, rather than clarifying the boundary between the state and the market as officially intended, marketization has further intensified tensions between the two. To navigate both the central government’s reform agenda and local political imperatives, UIDCs often adopt adaptive strategies to reconcile multiple and conflicting pressures. These practices offer short-term remedies, while also introducing unintended financial and governance risks. By examining the paradoxical outcomes of UIDCs’ marketization at the local level, this article contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how state and market interact amid central-local tensions in contemporary China.

Social Work on the China-Myanmar Border: State-NGO Synchronization
abstract: This article investigates the evolving relationship between the Chinese state and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) through the case of Ruili, a county-level city on the China-Myanmar frontier. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and extensive archival records, we develop an analytical framework of synchronization for the Chinese state and NGOs to capture how the relationship between them has changed. The analysis identifies four stages: a compensatory phase, in which foreign NGOs filled governance gaps and nurtured local capacity; a parallel growth phase, in which domestic NGOs and local governments expanded activities together; an alignment phase, in which NGOs reoriented themselves to implement national strategies such as rural revitalization and public health security; and a global outreach phase, in which selected NGOs extended their services abroad within the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). We present a case in which a welfare NGO working on cross-border social problems developed its operations alongside local state agencies. This article contributes to current debates on the adaptation of Chinese NGOs to a new environment by showing how coproduction, strategic alignment, and bounded negotiation have unfolded over time in a politically sensitive frontier setting.

The Resilience of Self-reliance in China: Autonomy, Interdependence and Order-shaping
abstract: The idea of “self-reliance” has endured in Chinese political discourse for nearly a century, transcending profound changes in China’s political, economic and strategic circumstances. Although it is frequently misinterpreted as economic isolation or autarky, the idea of self-reliance in China has always acknowledged the country’s engagement with the global economy. Drawing on the discursive institutionalist concept of ideational resilience, we show that self-reliance comprises three interlocking elements: autonomy, interdependence and order-shaping. While these sit in tension with one another, they have also accommodated one another since the earliest articulations of the idea. This tripartite structure has enabled Chinese leaders since the Republican era to reinterpret and usefully deploy the idea of self-reliance. Our findings underscore the resilience of Chinese foreign economic policy ideas, as well as the ideational logic behind Xi Jinping’s seemingly contradictory pursuit of technological self-reliance, open global markets and greater connectivity with the developing world.

title: Ideology Without Unity: The Rhizomatic Logic of Xi Jinping Thought
abstract: This article reconceptualizes Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics (Xi Thought hereafter) not as a coherent doctrine but as a rhizomatic ideological formation. Drawing on the work of Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, it treats Xi Thought as a configuration in which coherence is not presupposed but produced through the continual recombining of fragments across institutional sites. Based on an analysis of official publications, including collected works, excerpt volumes and study readers, the article shows how Xi’s speeches are disassembled and reassembled across domains such as law, economy, diplomacy and culture. These recompositions render ideology modular and resilient, allowing elements to be activated, re-weighted or sidelined without destabilizing the system as a whole. The article further argues that ideological coherence is generated through distributed and compulsory participation by Party and state actors, who are required to embed fragments of Xi Thought into institutional practice. Conceptualizing Xi Thought as a rhizome shifts analysis from doctrinal meaning to the operational logic through which ideology acquires administrative force within the Chinese party-state.

title: Bureaucratic Restructuring and the State-led (De-)Financialization of Local Governance in China
abstract: State-led financialization has emerged as a salient feature of local governance in China, yet it remains underexplored through the lens of bureaucratic restructuring. This paper traces the evolution of local financial agencies since 2002 through four distinct stages: local financial offices ( jinrongban ), financial bureaus ( jinrongju ), financial regulatory bureaus ( jinrong jianguanju ) and financial commissions ( jinrongwei ). Initially, local governments established jinrongban to harness financial capital for regional development. By proactively connecting local firms with capital markets to facilitate corporate listings, they embedded financial logic into local governance, reflecting local state-led financialization. Subsequently, the central government formalized these bodies into jinrongju with expanded mandates, deepening state-led financialization. Later, it systematically devolved regulatory responsibilities and renamed them jinrong jianguanju , elevating regulatory functions to a top priority, illustrating how the central government selectively steered the direction of financialization. Ultimately, provincial agencies were reorganized into jinrongwei and stripped of development functions, while city-level counterparts were largely closed, signifying a shift towards central state-led de-financialization. This trajectory was driven by shifting central–local dynamics, as early bottom-up initiatives were superseded by top-down control. The bureaucratic restructuring examined in this study offers new insights into the state-led (de-)financialization of local governance in China.

title: Explaining China’s High Welfare Spending: Local Models and Drivers of Fiscally Oriented Affordable Housing
abstract: While the world has been undergoing a global wave of welfare retrenchment since the turn of the 21st century, China’s spending on welfare provision has grown remarkably. Through a comparative study of the public housing provision programmes in two districts within the same municipality, this paper explores models of fiscally oriented public housing provision and their underlying driving forces. Drawing on data from archives, interviews and intensive fieldwork conducted in south-west China from 2014 to 2018, we identify two prominent public housing models: the entrepreneurial model and the extractive model. We propose that the choice of different welfare provision approaches is linked to local fiscal pressures and the target responsibility system. This paper sheds light on the structure of political incentives within China’s local governments in relation to public service provision and explores how local leaders improve public welfare in a non-Western setting.

title: Governing through Visibility: Local Government Experimentation with Internet Celebrity Cities in China
abstract: The rise of internet celebrity cities has become one of the most striking phenomena in China since 2021. How do local governments respond and harness this trend to advance their development goals? This study focuses on local experimentation in creating such cities, drawing on the case of the Village Football Super League ( Cun chao 村超) in Guizhou. We identify policy entrepreneurship as a key driver of local experimentation and highlight three core strategies for creating internet celebrity cities: crafting local symbols, co-producing viral content and mitigating public opinion risk. Further analysis shows that this experimentation, by attracting massive public attention, simultaneously promotes economic growth, strengthens social cohesion, reinforces state narratives and projects China’s national image onto the global stage. Overall, the findings suggest an emerging model in which public attention becomes a core resource for local development and governance in China’s digital era.

title: From Contention to Clientelism: Evidence from the Ten-Year Fishing Ban in China
abstract: How do ordinary Chinese people circumvent unpopular state policies? The existing literature primarily focuses on resistance against local bureaucrats. Drawing on ethnographic research on the ten-year fishing ban in the Yangtze River Basin, this article finds that fishermen (clients) continue to fish by maintaining patron–client relationships with the enforcers of the fishing ban (patrons). Ordinary fishermen seek the protection of enforcers through bribery. Enhanced state monitoring under the fishing ban facilitates bribery-based clientelism by weakening the fishermen’s everyday resistance, but it also constrains the power of enforcers by increasing the risk that their corruption will be discovered by upper-level authorities. For extremely poor fishermen, who are barely able to afford to pay bribes, their daily acts of resistance are morally justified by the need for subsistence safety, presenting enforcers with a dilemma: they must fulfil their law enforcement duties while also ensuring the survival of these individuals to maintain social stability. Therefore, cultivating a clientelist relationship with impoverished fishermen enables enforcers to manage their noncompliance, thereby balancing these conflicting goals. While clientelism protects people from unpopular policies to some extent, it more fundamentally strengthens the power of local bureaucrats, creating the potential for greater exploitation and larger-scale popular grievances in the long run.

title: Promoting Meritocracy through Recognition: The Post-recognition Career Trajectories of China’s Model County Party Secretaries
authors: Weilin Xiao; Haoyue Hu; Cai (Vera) Zuo
abstract: The increasingly proactive role of central authority in managing subprovincial leaders is understudied and our understanding of the function of political recognition in contemporary China remains inadequate. By adopting an expanded view of political meritocracy and using difference-in-differences analysis of original data about China’s model county Party secretaries, we demonstrate the ramifications of political recognition in generating a merit-based fast track and find that the recognition of model county Party secretaries has a lasting positive impact on recipients’ subsequent career advancement, although this impact is uneven. These findings enhance our understanding of the role of centrally bestowed political honours in promoting meritocracy, the non-institutionalized soft measures in shaping political incentives and the central–local interaction in the dynamics of political recognition in contemporary China.

title: Solving Agency Problems in Chinese Universities: Academics in the Shadow of the Party’s Declared Leadership
abstract: How does the party-state exercise leadership over universities and manage the individuals embedded in the university system without restraining their capacity for excellence and innovation? I argue that the presidential responsibility system has resolved a fundamental agency problem in Chinese universities. The system is supported by a set of mechanisms designed to enforce loyalty to the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party. It can easily adapt to political changes and thus maintain authoritarian rule without compromising the overarching agenda of research excellence.

title: Political Satire and the Decline of Discourse Quality: Evidence from China’s Online Public Sphere
abstract: Extensive research has examined whether political satire promotes or suppresses political discussion, but far less attention has been paid to how it shapes discourse quality. This study investigates the impact of political satire on discourse quality by scrutinizing the substance of online discussions in a non-democratic context. Drawing on manual content analysis of discussions on a major Chinese social media platform surrounding China’s controversial policy to raise the age of retirement, we analysed original posts and subsequent replies (N = 3,400) to assess the impact of satire on online political talk. The results show that political satire significantly decreases topic relevance and rationality, while exerting no significant effect on civility, and virtually precludes argument reciprocity. These findings contribute theoretically by shifting the focus from whether satire stimulates political engagement to how it influences the substantive quality of deliberation. They also invite a reassessment of the often-overemphasized optimistic role of political satire, highlighting its potential to erode rational and constructive discourse.

title: Desperate Acts of Democracy: Identity Threat, Autocratization and Voter Turnout in Hong Kong
authors: Lev Nachman; Nathan Kar Ming Chan; Chit Wai John Mok
abstract: How does identity threat affect mass political participation during times of autocratization? Building on social identity and group threat literatures, we theorize that perceived threats to Hong Konger identity increase voter turnout; however, the political salience of this threat is contingent on the degree of autocratization. We test this argument utilizing the case of Hong Kong, whose ongoing incorporation into the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has entered an unprecedented era of autocratization. We argue that threats to Hong Konger identity came to mobilize voter participation, especially as autocratization progressed in Hong Kong. Hong Kongers resisted during this period of political change through their intention to turn out to vote. We conducted three original experiments during different transitionary periods of Hong Kong’s autocratic shift. We find that priming identity threat had no effect on voter turnout before Hong Kong’s autocratic divergence. However, once more extreme forms of autocratization began, Hong Kongers assigned to an identical identity threat treatment were substantially more likely to report a higher likelihood of voting. This mobilizing effect persisted in a third experiment. Our results suggest a paradox where citizens’ propensity to vote increases when faced with perceived shrinking opportunities to participate in elections during times of authoritarian transition.

title: China’s Internal Security Spending: An Assessment of New Data
abstract: Internal security has been a governance priority under Xi Jinping. How does China’s budget reflect this prioritization? This research report presents updated data on China’s internal security spending, 1992–2022, revealing a mix of continuity and change. Domestic security expenditure continues to rise, more than doubling from 2012 to 2022, but has risen mostly in proportion to the People’s Republic of China’s overall expenditure. The balance between central and local expenditure has shifted further towards local spending, which, in the context of rising local fiscal constraint, may increase pressure on local public security bureaus. The Ministry of Public Security continues to receive the largest share of domestic security spending, while the proportion of internal security spending allocated to the People’s Armed Police (PAP) has decreased, probably reflecting the reorganization of the PAP in 2017–2018. Spending per capita and relative to GDP continues to be higher in locations that are politically sensitive, including Beijing, Tibet and Xinjiang.

title: Discovering Controversies through Reversions: A Text-based Analysis of China’s Two-phase Bill Changes
abstract: This study uncovers hidden disputes in China’s law-making process by systematically tracking bill changes across executive and legislative phases. Utilizing an original dataset of 45 executive-initiated bills (2008–2023), it identifies a consistent pattern of reversions – instances where executive-approved changes to draft bills were overridden in the legislature – revealing the National People’s Congress to be a key policy battleground. Reversions are concentrated in bills concerning health, safety and environment, often involving scope, regulatory frameworks and legal liability. Combined with qualitative case studies, these findings demonstrate the legislature’s crucial role in facilitating monitoring and negotiation in the policy process, offering new insights into executive–legislative dynamics in China’s single-party regime.

title: How the Chinese Public Perceives South-East Asia: Affinity, Annoyance and Apprehension
abstract: This article explores how the Chinese public perceives South-East Asia. Using original survey data collected in China, it suggests three perceptual frames. The “affinity” frame, which is rooted in historical Chinese migration and diaspora ties, generates feelings of kinship and cultural connection. Conversely, the “annoyance” frame stems from contemporary geopolitical tensions, particularly South China Sea disputes, where several South-East Asian countries are viewed as provocateurs challenging China’s regional authority. The “apprehension” frame characterizes the region as exotic yet dangerous, a perception reinforced by recent cyber scams and criminal activities targeting Chinese citizens, creating stereotypes of South-East Asia as lawless and unsafe. The article analyses the survey data for the statistical distribution of these frames and discusses their political implications. By exploring how historical ties, geopolitical tensions and security concerns simultaneously shape Chinese public opinion, the article illuminates the complex perceptual landscape that may influence China’s diplomatic and economic relations with South-East Asia.

title: Forever Hong Kong: A Global City’s Decolonization Struggle Ching Kwan Lee. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2025. 344 pp. £37.95 (hbk). ISBN 9780674290198
abstract: Forever Hong Kong offers a bold reinterpretation of the city's contentious political trajectory from the handover era to the present.The book is masterfully written and meticulously researched.It is a unique and valuable contribution to Hong Kong studies and beyond.Lee's core question is how Hong Kongers transformed from "colonized subjects" complacent with the status quo into "decolonizing subjects" willing to take action and chart their own history.Her answer is that Hong Kong's successive waves of contention -from the 2003 Article 23 protests through the 2014 Umbrella Movement to the 2019 Anti-Extradition movement -are best understood as a decolonization struggle, rather than a conventional fight for democratization.The colonialism to be unravelled, she argues, was not purely British.It was a "double coloniality" co-produced by London and Beijing, held together by four interlocking "colonial myths" that constrained Hong Kongers' political agency and imagination: stability and prosperity, free-market capitalism, rule of law, and China as destiny.The first chapter reconstructs how each pillar was manufactured and hardened into common sense; the rest of the book traces how various political and economic ruptures pushed activists and ordinary citizens to challenge each pillar in turn, culminating in the 2019 uprising that Lee calls both "the peak of the city's ongoing decolonization struggle decades in the making and the opening salvo of a new era of confrontation between Western neoliberal capitalism and Chinese state capitalism" (p.2).The book's empirical depth is impressive.Lee draws on ethnographic fieldwork from 2019 through 2023, in-depth interviews with a wide cross-section of participants -from frontline militants and student leaders to bankers, medics, accountants and diaspora organizers -as well as archival materials and intellectual writings.Chapters four and five provide particularly illuminating details about militant frontline protesters and the international front, which had remained obscure to outsiders.By recasting Hong Kong's political history as a quest for decolonization, Lee offers a refreshing perspective.Most scholarship on Hong Kong's politics -including much of my own -works within contentious politics or democratization theory, privileging topics such as hybrid regimes, electoral authoritarianism, opportunity structures and repertoire shifts.These works focus on both structure and dynamics: what explains protest participation, how movements escalate and how political opportunities open and close.Lee poses a different question: how did people come to understand what they were doing, and why?The payoff is most visible in her analysis of protest violence.While contentious politics scholars tend to explain radicalization through state repression and organizational dynamics, Lee reconstructs how "brave warriors" themselves theorized and negotiated the use of violence.These accounts capture emotional, ethical and calculative dimensions that analyses on structure and dynamics tend to flatten.

Managing Hydro-dependence and Risk: Hong Kong’s Water Insurance Policy, 1967–1982
abstract: Using archival and unofficial sources, this article examines how political calculations, economic considerations, local consumption patterns and international dynamics shaped the colonial administration’s water governance strategies in Hong Kong. It focuses on how the 1967 water emergency prompted the colonial government to recalibrate its approach, from a policy of manageable dependency to one of risk aversion. After 1967, an “insurance policy” ensuring a “basic ration” was pursued. This led to the construction of the Lok On Pai desalination plant. The article then traces developments from 1976 to 1982, when Hong Kong gradually moved to a regionally integrated strategy, driven not only by improved Sino-British relations but also by economic considerations, growing public intolerance of water rationing and the Middle East oil crisis. By 1982, Hong Kong’s water insurance policy had officially ended; Chinese water was classified as “reliable.” By exploring these understudied developments and factors, the article contributes to the histories of water management, colonial Hong Kong and China.

Balancing Accommodation and Authority: Husbands’ Family Strategies in Transnational Marriages in North-East China
abstract: This article examines South–South transnational marriages between Vietnamese women and Chinese men in North-East China, focusing on the strategies husbands’ families employ to sustain these unions. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of family strategies and in-depth interviews with 26 households, it develops a “departure-restraint” framework to explain how receiving families respond to the persistent possibility of a bride’s marital exit. The findings show that these strategies rest on a balance between limited accommodation and selective authority: Vietnamese brides are granted a degree of autonomy in everyday matters, while husbands’ families retain control over major household decisions. The article further argues that the relatively narrow economic gap between sending and receiving regions in South–South marriages reshapes household dynamics in distinctive ways. Under conditions of limited economic opportunity, husbands’ families maintain marital stability not through outright domination, but through calibrated negotiations over everyday autonomy and household authority.

title: Feminized Revival: Han Chinese Dress, Gender and Cultural Nationalism in Contemporary China
abstract: Women hold disproportionate authority in China’s contemporary Hanfu revival, where Han-ness operates through implicit cultural codes rather than explicit ethnic claims. Recent scholarship highlights how Han-ness circulates as a moral, etiquette-centred grammar of “proper culture.” Drawing on 18 months of ethnography across six sites in China, this article shows how gender mediates that grammar and shapes the performances of Han-ness. Women, as arbiters of taste and propriety, enact an assertive banal nationalism through aesthetic and organizational labour. Men, marginal within the field, perform defensive overt nationalism through didactic historical narratives and moralized claims to legitimacy. To explain this pattern of identity formation and boundary making, I advance the notion of gendered everyday nationhood. The article contributes to scholarship on nationalism by showing how embodied practices sustain national belonging, and how mundane evaluation and boundary policing reproduce nationhood in everyday life.

title: The Origins of Land Finance: Local Resistance and Top-Down Imposition
abstract: Land sales have been a significant source of revenue for Chinese local governments since the early 2000s. Contrary to popular belief, local governments did not turn to land finance to make up for lost tax revenues after the 1994 tax sharing reform. Rather, both before and after 1994, corrupt land sales were widespread, as officials sold land far below market prices in return for bribes. Even as the fiscal incentives for local governments to adopt land finance increased in the 1990s, state agents continued acting on their own personal interests rather than the institutional interests of local governments. Local governments only began to sell land at higher, market prices when an anti-corruption campaign launched by the central government made doing so a political imperative in the early 2000s. Local governments were much more responsive to political imperatives than to fiscal incentives.

title: Subversive Amplification: Online Dissent and the Limits of Information Control in China
abstract: Intensified information control severely constrains digital contention in China, yet online mass events occasionally occur. Using a dataset of 274,721 Weibo messages, this study examines mobilization, coordination and grievance articulation during a two-day episode of online dissent in the aftermath of the 2022 Urumqi residential building fire, which preceded the White Paper protests. It argues that users were activated by public communication failures that transformed manifold grievances into outrage, and that the associated hashtags provided anchors to which criticism could be attached. In a process this study terms “subversive amplification,” concentrated engagement amplified the hashtags’ visibility, and with it the critical content attached to them. However, absent the unifying function of opinion leaders, grievance articulation remained fragmented and did not converge on unified demands. The case illustrates the inherent vulnerabilities of information control but also the conditions and limits of their exploitation.

title: Rising Engagement and Substantive Responsiveness: 13 Years of Online Petitioning in China
abstract: The Chinese government has invested heavily in online petition platforms to channel public grievances, yet systematic longitudinal evidence on citizen–state interactions within these venues remains limited. This research report presents nationwide evidence showing that both public participation and government responsiveness through e-petition institutions have increased markedly since Xi Jinping took office. Analysing more than four million citizen appeals submitted to the country’s largest online petition portal, Message Board for Leaders, from January 2011 to January 2024, we find a twelvefold rise in petition volume and a fivefold increase in users, largely driven by urban residents in eastern provinces. Appeals have also diversified, with notable growth in housing-related issues and more strategic appeals directed at Party secretaries. Meanwhile, local governments have raised response rates from 50 per cent to 98 per cent, shortened average wait times from 176 to 19 days, and increased the substantive resolution rate from 17 per cent to 31 per cent over the past decade.
