Introduction: Expanding the History of Chinese Food Culture
abstract: The consumption of food is simultaneously one of humanity’s most basic necessities and one of its greatest luxuries. It has, appropriately, both inspired and reflected cultural activities, from agricultural rituals and ascetic practices to epicurean banquets and poetry. At the present moment, we seem to be living in an era of peak food obsession, fueled by extremely popular food culture, the rapid rise of “foodie” life on social media, and heated debates over the authenticity and identity of cuisine in a multicultural context. Chinese societies have been equally obsessed, with food being a central theme of ancient bronzes, Confucian classics, religious practices, and literary works. For this reason, the study of Chinese food culture naturally brings one through a wide array of disciplines, including cultural studies, history, religion, medicine, and aesthetics. However, with a few notable exceptions, major research in humanistic food studies has tended to emphasize recent time periods, European and American cultures, or both (the “modern west”). The result has been a strong emphasis on “cultural studies” approaches, usually adopting structuralist, culturalist, or Gramscian critiques of power brokers in the past century. 1 This special issue shows how attention to Chinese food history may bring to light many new questions and methods in the study of food culture.

title: Tummy Troubles: When Chinese Healers Administered Milk
abstract: Received scholarship by H.T. Huang and others has argued that the high incidence of lactose intolerance in East Asians discouraged the Chinese from adopting dairy on health grounds before the twentieth century. However, such wisdom overlooks Chinese medical literature that prescribes fresh dairy to treat chronic diarrhea. This essay considers what famed healer Sun Simiao (581–682) had to say about the uses of dairy products in treating digestive ailments. Towards this end, we consider the Essential Formulas Worth a Thousand Pieces of Gold for Emergencies ( Beiji qianjin yaofang 備急千金要方) and the Supplemental Formulas Worth a Thousand Pieces of Gold ( Qianjin yifang 千金翼方). We then compare the uses of dairy in the Sun corpus to both contemporary and earlier texts. Our analysis shows that Tang-dynasty (618–907) healers regarded milk products as generally good for the gut, and, in some cases, recommended using fresh dairy for cases of flux.

title: Mycological Mania: Foraging the Mushroom Catalogues of Imperial China for Recipes, Remedies, and Rituals
abstract: This article reconsiders three of the most iconic mushroom catalogues of classical China, which underscored the culinary value of local fungi, in light of indebtedness to medical and self-cultivation literature. Through this re-examination of mycological sources and the imbrication of discourses that they exhibit, mushrooms emerge as richer, more complex, objects of gastronomic interest.

title: Poisoned Meals: Toxic Food, Epistemic Standards, and Retributive Justice in Twelfth-Century Judicial Cases and Anecdotal Narratives
abstract: This article examines case studies and anecdotal narratives in which murderers used poisoned food as a weapon, and government officials used their epistemic authority to solve these crimes and bring the perpetrators to justice. Drawn from Zheng Ke’s 鄭克 (fl. 1124–1149) legal compendium Tortoise and Mirror for Judging Cases ( Zheyu guijian 折獄龜鑑) and Hong Mai’s 洪邁 (1123–1202) anecdote collection Record of the Listener ( Yijian zhi 夷堅志), these narratives reflected the violent threat that poisoners posed to the preservation of gender, familial, social, and political hierarchies. In the Mirror ’s legal realm, astute officials used abductive reasoning to expose poisoning plots, thereby restoring the moral fabric of society; in Hong Mai’s Record poisoners are punished by imperial judges as well as by retributive mechanisms of cosmic justice. These six selected case narratives illustrate the permeability of the boundaries that divide the conceptual categories of food, medicine, and poison, and the connections amongst medical, legal, and socio-moral systems of knowledge.

title: Savoring Beauty and Cultivating a Poet’s Spleen: The Plum Blossom as a Delicacy in Southern Song China
abstract: For a plant as renowned and beloved in China as the plum blossom ( meihua 梅花), there is conspicuously little written in English about eating it. However, without understanding the historical affection for consuming plum blossoms, our comprehension of it as a cultural icon misses an important dimension. This article explores the intriguing discourse surrounding plum blossom consumption in three sections. The first section introduces the key concept of qing 清 (“purity”) and its relation to the “poet’s spleen” ( shiren pi 詩人脾), which provides a theoretical framework for a relationship between eating it and writing poetry. The second section examines Song-dynasty poems on this eating practice, particularly those by Yang Wanli 楊萬里 (1127–1206) and the Rivers and Lakes poets ( jianghu shiren 江湖詩人). Their poetry was closely tied to new developments in the notion of qi 氣 and “poetic spleen” ( shipi 詩脾). The third section turns to culinary recipes, primarily from the Rivers and Lakes poet Lin Hong 林洪 (fl. 1224–1263), who promotes qing aesthetics in plum blossom dishes. I argue that the discovery of culinary value in a flower long regarded as more symbolic than edible marks a significant development in Song-dynasty (960–1279) literati culture, aesthetics, intellectual history, and medicine.

title: Seeking a Deadly Delicacy: Pufferfish, Regional Gastronomy, and Pharmacology in Middle Period China
abstract: Seafood gained prominence as a southern flavor in middle-period China. Among the southern products that piqued gourmets’ fancy, the pufferfish as a deadly delicacy presented a special case. How did it come to acquire its contentious reputation? This article traces the process that transformed it from a dangerous ancient killer to an alluring treat by the early twelfth century. Its shifting cultural stature was propelled by demographic and geographical reconfigurations, negotiations between northern and southern culinary traditions, and the literati effort to collect and classify natural knowledge. Along the way, diverse encounters and experiences with different pufferfishes were coalesced into one uniform category hetun (“river-piglet”), connoting at once danger and delicacy. The metamorphosis of the pufferfish demonstrated the interplay between literary, medical, geographical, and natural knowledge across genres in middle-period Chinese history.

title: The Chickpea in Premodern China: A Perpetual Foreigner in the Central Lands
abstract: In this paper, I explore the millennium-long presence of the chickpea in premodern China by highlighting three key historical moments. The legume had its first rise to prominence as a cosmopolitan “Muslim Bean” in the Mongol Yuan (1271–1368) imperial diet. It then experienced a phase of obscurity, as the most renowned Chinese herbalist, Li Shizhen 李時珍 (1518–1593), conflated it with the pea. A disparate identity of the legume emerged around the same time, as the bean garnered attention from famine relief specialists, consequently transforming into a source of sustenance. The multiple lives of the chickpea were characterized with a common emphasis on its foreignness, drawing connections to various Eurasian cultures beyond China. The plant’s enduring presence, coupled with ongoing allusions to its alienness, makes it a perpetual foreigner in the broad expanse of the Chinese empire.

title: Tea and Place: The Evolving Discussion about Terroir in Song China
abstract: This article employs terroir as an analytical framework to examine how a place-specific tea acquired its reputation and contributed to processes of cultural self-fashioning in Song China. Focusing on Fujian’s Beiyuan 北苑 tea—exceptionally well documented in Song sources—it explores the close connections among tea, landscape appreciation, and place-making. Drawing on tea manuals and connoisseur writings, the article shows how literati linked tea quality to both natural conditions and cultural practices, using such associations to articulate refined taste and produce place-based knowledge. The case of Beiyuan tea reveals the emergence of a distinctly Chinese rhetoric of terroir, one that transformed environmental description into a rhetoric that mediated between local expertise and imperial order. Within this framework, place itself came to embody quality, integrating physical environment, cultural identity, and sensory experience.

title: MSG, Vegan Soap, Meatless Restaurants and Buddhism in the Emergence of Modern Chinese Vegetarianism
abstract: This paper explores how traditional Chinese vegetarian concerns were adapted to exploit new possibilities in the early twentieth century. Specifically, I examine attempts to promote the vegetarian diet through monosodium glutamate, ventures to manufacture vegan soap, and the emergence of a vibrant culture of urban vegetarian restaurants, all of which were actively supported by the socially conservative monk Yinguang 印光 (1862–1940).

From Individual to Lineage Identity: Huizhou Merchants and the Rise of Genealogies in Ming China
abstract: This article examines how Huizhou merchants shaped their identities during their economic ascent from the fifteenth century onward. Because commerce carried a stigma in Confucian ideology, they shifted the basis of self-presentation from mercantile success to moral excellence. This produced a competition in virtue, where the moral capital accumulated in a single lifetime could not rival that amassed across generations. Merchants therefore redirected identity claims from personal virtue to membership in lineages where virtue had been cultivated over generations. In doing so, they moved the foundation of identity from individual achievement to collective lineage affiliation. This shift provides a new explanation for the rise of lineages and genealogies from the perspective of identity formation. By underscoring the initiative, creativity, and adaptability of merchants in driving these changes, the article also repositions them from the cultural margins to the center of identity-making in late imperial China.

The Sino-Soviet Alliance, the Korean War, and the Predicament of the CCP’s Attack Plans for Taiwan, 1949–50
abstract: Drawing on archival materials from the Republic of China (Taiwan), the People’s Republic of China (PRC), the United States, and the former Soviet Union, this article discusses why the PRC’s 1949–50 strike plans for Taiwan went unfulfilled. What prevented the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) from “liberating” Taiwan was the fact that it lacked sufficient naval and air power to overwhelm the comparatively better equipped Kuomintang (KMT). The only way to overcome this disparity in a timely manner was to call upon Soviet assistance. In early 1949, seeking to incorporate China into the Soviet Union’s sphere of influence, Joseph Stalin resolved to support the CCP’s seizure of power. At the same time, he adopted a policy of indirectly assisting the CCP’s preparations to take Taiwan. This was also when US strategy in Asia became focused on preventing the PRC and the Soviet Union from consolidating an alliance. The United States attempted to do so by using the occasion of Mao Zedong’s first visit to Moscow to publicly announce a policy of non-intervention on the Taiwan issue. To pull the PRC into the Soviet camp and prevent the CCP from turning to the United States and the West, as well as to maintain the Soviet Union’s ports and military bases on the Yellow Sea, Stalin responded by acquiescing to Mao’s demands that Dalian, Port Arthur (Lüshun), and the Changchun Railway be returned to China. However, he simultaneously halted indirect assistance for the CCP’s preparations for attacking Taiwan, instead giving Kim Il Sung the green light to launch an attack against South Korea. With the outbreak of the Korean War providing a legitimate pretext, and in response to the signing of the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance, and Mutual Assistance , the United States adjusted its policy of non-intervention regarding Taiwan. Thus, while the status of Taiwan and Fujian’s coastal islands was considered by both the CCP and the KMT to be China’s internal affair, by 1950, it had already, in Mao’s words, “turned into a complex and serious international struggle.”

The Price of Freedom: Lèse-majesté Prosecutions and the Politics of Bail in Thailand
abstract: In recent years, Thai courts have arbitrarily used the lèse majesté law to prosecute hundreds of defendants. This use of lèse majesté has been an important part of a reaction against a movement that had been mobilised nationwide during 2020–2021 calling for reform of politics. Breaking the kingdom’s biggest taboo, the movement explicitly criticised the monarchy and called for monarchy reform. Besides an unprecedented number of cases, what distinguishes the recent wave of persecutions is the way the court handles the question of bail. In the past, almost all lèse majesté defendants were likely to be imprisoned from an early stage of investigation, and they were constantly denied bail. Recently, however, granting bail has been more common. This research examines the politics of bail in lèse majesté cases, arguing that the trend of granting bail should be considered a political tactic of the courts while maintaining the prosecution of disloyal subjects. Setting bail so high means ordinary people cannot reach it. Despite this high price for freedom, the monarchy reform movement and several civic associations manage to secure bail for most defendants. This article examines fundraising role as a form of resistance against the power of the court and the crown.

title: Digital Defiance: Analysis of Public Responses to Youth Activism in Thailand, 2020–2023
abstract: During Thailand’s 2020–2023 wave of youth activism, once unsayable political topics moved into online debate, pushing the boundaries of public discourse. Anchored in the concept of Thai-Style Democracy, this article examines how discourse on Twitter/X shapes what becomes sayable, respectable, or sanctionable. The article argues that platformed talk did not merely reflect opinion but recalibrated legitimacy under Thai-Style Democracy. Using Critical Discourse Analysis of 4,705 tweets, five recurrent patterns were identified: (i) self-identification and labelling; (ii) rights, freedoms, and duties framed through a duty-first moral order; (iii) guardianist legitimacy and platform scaling; (iv) karmic idioms as moral justifications; and (v) conditional support and opposition tied to compatibility with duty and non-violation of royal authority. Together, these dynamics illuminated a paradox: expanding speakability around monarchy reform alongside a narrowing acceptability of youth activism. The analysis shows how online discourse participated in legitimating institutional responses and reshaping horizons of action. This study contributes to broader discussions of digital activism, generational conflict, and the resilience of Thai-Style Democracy under democratic pressure by linking the nuanced dynamics of online discourse to political events.

title: Illicit Parallel Trading, State Permission, and Legality: A Comparative Analysis in the Southern Chinese Seaboard
authors: Lawrence Ka-ki Ho; KuoRay Mao; Henry Hin-Yan Chan; Alexander Hagan
abstract: This article applies institutional and media content analysis to investigate the legitimation and criminalisation of cross-border trade within the "Southern Chinese Seaboard," specifically between Taiwan and China and between Hong Kong and mainland China, a region characterised by diverse taxation and legal jurisdictions, as well as rapidly evolving political-economic and regional geo-political dynamics. This study re-evaluates common media portrayals and simplistic perceptions of "illicit" and "parallel trading" as merely spontaneous actions by individuals embedded in criminal networks. Instead, we posit that such activities stem from deliberately vague taxation and legal definitions, as well as enforcement strategies resulting from collusion between state and non-state actors. Utilising the "Regime of Permission" framework, this study examines how political actors manipulate the definitions of licit and illicit trading to achieve political objectives, thereby creating loopholes that non-state actors exploit. The findings demonstrate that the delineation and oversight of illicit trade have evolved in response to shifting economic relationships and the development of enforcement institutions within a changing geo-political landscape, offering deeper insight into the state's role in creating and maintaining liminal spaces that regulate the boundaries between lawful, unlawful, and socially illicit trade.

title: Banditry in the Sundarbans: The Political Economy of a Mangrove Frontier
authors: Md. Tanvir Mahtab; M. Anwar Hossen; Md. Shihabul Islam
abstract: This study examines the political economy of forest-centred banditry in the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, where the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers meet. It focuses on the roles played by patronage networks in banditry. Employing a qualitative and case study approach, the research seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of the political economy of forest-centred banditry. The interviews were conducted in the Mongla and Rampal areas of Bagerhat district, Bangladesh. Findings reveal a deeply entrenched system of exploitation and control. Local business elites (mahajans) and political actors exploit individuals through the dadni debt system and political manipulation, coercing them into banditry. This system is sustained through hierarchical structures led by boro bhai (big brother figures) and enforced by violence. Bandits abduct fishermen for ransom, with local politicians acting as intermediaries, collecting significant amounts annually. Businessmen support bandit gangs to monopolise natural resources, resulting in fierce competition among traders. Additionally, powerful figures profit from illegal enterprises such as the arms trade and prostitution. Further, the study identifies a deep relationship between bandits and local government officials, highlighting systemic corruption through monthly payments for protection and information.

title: Unequal Chains: Global Value Chains and Income Disparity
authors: Kay Kiang Tan; Andrew Jia Yi Kam; M. Niaz Asadullah
abstract: As countries deepen their integration into global value chains (GVCs) to pursue industrial growth and economic advancement, a critical question remains unresolved: Who truly benefits from this participation? This study examines the effects of GVC participation on income disparities within the manufacturing sector. Three measures of income inequality are employed – value-added distribution, wage distribution, and labour income share – based on the World Bank Economic Enterprise Survey data for 44 countries and 16 manufacturing industries between 2006 and 2016. The results reveal that the choice of inequality measure is crucial. GVC participation reduces income inequality in value-added and wage distribution but increases inequality in labour income share. At the country level, backward and forward linkages reduce income inequality in lower-income economies, while effects are not significant in upper-middle- and high-income countries. Regionally, Asia shows more equitable value-added through backward linkages and equitable wages through overall GVC and forward linkages. However, overall GVC participation and forward linkages are also associated with a decline in labour income share, suggesting that while GVC integration may improve wage equality, the proportion of value-added accruing to labour tends to shrink.

title: Indonesia’s Illiberal Capitalism and the 2025 Protests: A Reply to Wijaya and Jayasuriya
abstract: Indonesia was less affected by the 2008 global crisis than many developed capitalist economies, but can it be said to have followed a similar path, leading to austerity that deepens disincorporation of the subordinate classes and the decline of liberal democracy as a source of legitimacy for capitalism? Wijaya and Jayasuriya suggest so. However, it cannot be forgotten that Indonesia’s capitalism has long relied on an illiberal political-legal order as a means of accumulation and legitimacy, despite post-1998 democratisation. This arrangement persists because there is neither a coherent progressive movement capable of shifting the balance of power nor a rupture within the capitalist fractions that introduces a new way to sustain bourgeois hegemony. Hence, characterising Indonesia as evolving towards Poulantzas’s model of authoritarian statism overlooks the specificity of the mode of capitalist accumulation. What has happened in Indonesia is the deepening of the already illiberal mode, often provoking mass protests. However, this new direction is not the result of a post-crisis re-organisation of capital but rather arises from the logic of accumulation in which sections of oligarchic alliance seek to further concentrate power and wealth in the absence of the organised left.

title: State, Capital, and the Crisis of Social Reproduction in Indonesia: A Rejoinder
abstract: This rejoinder to Mudhoffir (Citation2026) identifies three key theoretical points of disagreement in the response to our commentary on Indonesian protests of 2025 (Wijaya and Jayasuriya Citation2026). First, the “authoritarian continuity thesis” advanced by our critics misses the way in which the “rule of capital” is organised within the state apparatus. The response to our article rests on an instrumentalist reading of the Indonesian state, which is contrasted to a more structural understanding set out in our 2026 commentary. Second, this perspective enables a better comprehension of the shifts in the form of authoritarian political regimes in response to a variety of often overlapping crises. Third, protests must be understood not simply as a set of grievances about elite impunity but signify a fundamental shift in the structure of the working or labouring class, which is itself the product of capitalist transformation over the last decades. Here, it is contended that these conflicts now find expression in new forms of politics over access to means of social reproduction.

title: Invisible Brokers, Visible Haze: Value Chains and the Political Ecology of Northern Thailand’s Maize Economy
abstract: Each dry season, thick haze blankets northern Thailand. Maize cultivation, driven largely by demand for animal feed, is one of its most politically contested sources. Policy responses often target farmers through burning bans, technical fixes, and behavioural change campaigns. This article focuses on the middlemen who link upland maize fields to downstream feed markets. It shows that brokers, traders, and silo operators, by controlling access to credit, logistics, and markets, translate corporate demand, price volatility, and regulatory pressures into everyday farming practices. Moral economies of debt, reciprocity, and patronage intersect with buyer-driven value chain pressures to shape brokerage practices and disperse accountability for environmental harm. These practices reinforce farmers’ dependence on maize, and make burning appear the most viable option while displacing responsibility onto farmers and shielding large agribusinesses. The article demonstrates that market power operates through everyday social relations of credit, trust, and loyalty to reproduce unequal commodity relations. This helps explain why haze persists despite repeated policy interventions. The article integrates middlemen into environmental governance analyses, shows that value chain governance and moral economy combine to reproduce environmental injustice, and contributes to meatways scholarship, tracing the intermediary networks through which national and regional meat demand reproduces environmental harm.

title: The Contours Of Working-Class Debt: Precarity, Gender, And Labour Discipline In Cambodia’s Construction Sector
abstract: This article argues that in Cambodia’s construction sector, overall levels of precarity play a key role in shaping the extent to which debt functions as a mechanism of labour discipline. Building on LeBaron’s reconceptualisation of debt bondage as a class-based form of labour discipline, it situates worker indebtedness within the broader structural conditions through which it acquires coercive force. Drawing on data collected from 600 workers employed in cement factories and on construction sites, the article reveals that debt’s coercive power stems less from its absolute burden than from its interaction with employment precarity. Although workers in both sub-sectors faced significant indebtedness, cement factory workers benefited from relatively stable employment, monthly wages, and access to social security, whereas construction workers were paid irregularly, experienced wage theft, and were excluded from social protection. These dynamics operated in profoundly gendered ways, reflecting women’s household financial responsibilities and difficulties securing formal credit. By foregrounding the relationship between indebtedness and structural precarity, the article argues that it is the configuration of precarity itself that determines the depth of debt-based coercion in contemporary Cambodia.

title: Devouring the Pacific: Acapulco’s Fort of San Diego and its deadly repartimientos
abstract: In 1615, a Dutch fleet under the command of Joris van Spilbergen attacked the Mexican port of Acapulco. The port was the eastern terminus of the Manila galleons, the ships that linked Asia and the Americas during the early modern period. In the face of foreign incursion, Spanish officials in Mexico proposed to secure transpacific trade by constructing the Fort of San Diego to protect Acapulco. To build and later repair the fort, they mobilized thousands of Indigenous men through the repartimiento (rotational forced labour system) from what is now the Mexican state of Guerrero. Using the port’s accounting records, this article argues that the novelty of transpacific empire profoundly affected the social and economic lives of Mexico’s coastal and hinterland Indigenous peoples. However, the global histories of the Manila galleons and of early modern Asia–Latin American connections have overlooked the relationship between Spanish Pacific expansion and Indigenous labour in the Americas. Placing the fort’s Indigenous builders at the centre reveals not only the violent outcomes of imperial anxiety, but also how Indigenous people adapted to the advent of transpacific empire.

title: Rethinking global Catholicism from Ottoman Europe: Catholic missions and local agency in the early modern world
abstract: This article investigates the role of Catholic and non-Catholic local actors in shaping missionary activities in seventeenth-century Ottoman Europe. It examines jurisdictional conflicts and collaborations between Bosnian Franciscan friars, Ragusan merchants, Ottoman officials—particularly judges—and Serbian Orthodox clergy, whose interactions shaped the local landscape of Catholicism and defined the limits of Catholic engagement. Drawing primarily on Catholic missionary sources, the study argues that analysing missions through interconnected local, regional, and global lenses, while foregrounding the agency of local actors, provides a more nuanced understanding of early modern Catholicism. By expanding historiographical approaches that have primarily focused on Catholic missions outside Europe, the article advocates for the inclusion of Ottoman Europe as a significant yet understudied site of Catholic missionary activity. It further highlights the jurisdictional and institutional tensions within Catholic expansion and governance, revealing the complexities of missionary engagement in a politically fragmented and religiously plural environment.

title: Coextension of knowledge networks and technological infrastructures: The Jesuits and meteorology in late colonial Asia
abstract: This article challenges the traditional view of the linear causality of technological globalization in the history of modern predictive meteorology. According to this linear narrative, telegraphy, by enabling near-instantaneous communication over vast distances, was the causa efficiens that directly and inevitably produced large-scale weather forecasting. However, the role of Jesuit scientists in East Asia as pioneers of cyclone warning systems not only demonstrates that the linear narrative is too simple but invites a rigorous examination of the relationships between prior knowledge networks and technological infrastructures. This article contends that the expansion of technological networks does not inexorably imply the expansion of knowledge networks. There was not, therefore, a unidirectional causal relationship but a concomitant two-way interaction; that is, there was a coextension of knowledge and technological networks, where both Jesuit scientists and telegraph companies benefited from each other and shared common goals confronting a global threat—cyclones. This offers a new perspective not only on the history of meteorological services but also of science globalization.

title: Anthoine de Gogorza, Louis Lacharme, and the forgotten origins of the Panama Canal
abstract: The story of the Panama Canal is often framed as a morality tale juxtaposing French tragedy and American triumph (or imperialism). What gets lost in this depiction is a pair of adventurous entrepreneurs, Anthoine de Gogorza and Louis Lacharme, whose efforts led Ferdinand de Lesseps to his doomed canal project. This article shows how the roots of the Panama Canal emerged from the forests of Colombia’s Sinú River Valley, whose settlement, in turn, was fostered by the search for canal routes in the Darien. Yet despite the spatial proximity of these two regions, their overlooked connections were woven together through the ‘lifepaths’ of de Gogorza and Lacharme as they moved from France to Colombia and around the globalizing Atlantic of the nineteenth century. Following their movements, in turn, sheds light on the overlooked figure of the foreign speculator, the business of exploration, and marketing the tropics.

title: Beyond extraterritoriality: The Chengdu riot of 1895 and the politics of protection
abstract: Scholars often analyse Western–Chinese legal conflicts in the nineteenth-century Qing empire through the lens of extraterritoriality. This article examines the 1895 anti-missionary riot in Chengdu and the ensuing dispute over the responsibility of Qing officials. It highlights the protection of foreign lives and property as a key area of contestation between Western powers and the Qing empire. During the riot, Chengdu authorities exploited their discretionary power to challenge missionary presence and undermine treaty obligations. In response, Western powers began a concerted effort to hold local officials accountable by pressuring the Qing state to impose severe punitive sanctions. The riot and its aftermath reveal how a non-Western state negotiated and enforced obligations required by Eurocentric international law. Protection emerges as a multifaceted instrument for the projection of imperial power and a malleable component of the Western-imposed treaty system, mediating the asymmetrical international relations in the nineteenth century.

title: Sewing machines, intercommunal violence, and the economic order of things in the late Ottoman empire
abstract: The global diffusion of sewing machines required concerted efforts from manufacturers, sales agents, and, most significantly, local consumers, who rendered the machine legible and desirable across diverse social settings. As this article shows, however, in politically volatile contexts, it was manufacturers who most decisively shaped these processes. Focusing on the Singer Company—the largest and most influential of its kind—the article examines how this process unfolded in the Ottoman empire during the Armenian massacres of the 1890s. Occurring when ethnic and religious homogeneity was becoming central to the political order, the Ottoman case offers an especially important early example of global firms’ responses to the emerging pressures of exclusionary—and often violent—political and economic reordering. The article traces how Singer tested adaptive strategies that not only sustained its regional presence but also recalibrated its business model. In doing so, it contributes to global history by demonstrating how seemingly localized episodes of political violence became formative sites of adaptation, attuning global corporations to a world increasingly structured by systemic violence, warfare, and demographic homogenization.

title: Escaping Washington’s Tutelage: Latin America, the League of Nations, and International Law
abstract: Relying on a variety of archival sources, including the recently discovered private correspondence of the Uruguayan diplomat Enrique Buero, this article demonstrates that a Latin American bloc with a common agenda emerged in Geneva during the 1920s and transformed the codification of international law in both the League of Nations and the Pan-American Union. Key pressure groups previously thought to have operated exclusively in the Americas were created in the League by Latin American diplomats who wanted to reform international law to protect small states but had lost faith in Pan-Americanism. The article examines the ideological origins of this bloc and the obstacles that it encountered, including an initial tendency among some diplomats to prioritize status-seeking. It charts the Latin American bloc’s success in dismantling obstacles to the League’s involvement in the Americas. Finally, the article demonstrates that the bloc was able to leverage its influence beyond the League, including during the run-up to the 1933 Montevideo Conference.

title: Beyond the Cold War and decolonization: Nigerian foreign policy, French nuclear tests, and the politics of independence in West Africa
abstract: As the first foreign policy issue Nigeria debated, the controversy around France’s nuclear tests, conducted in Algeria during the War of Independence there, allowed Lagos to rehearse its envisioned African role even before formal independence in October 1960. Nigerian opposition to France eventually culminated in the expulsion of the French ambassador on 5 January 1961, after the third French atomic test in the Algerian Sahara. This seemingly straightforward anti-colonial and anti-nuclear act was in fact largely driven by inter-African dynamics, particularly Nigeria’s complicated relationship with Ghana. By reconstructing this episode, the article demonstrates how international affairs uniquely crystallized interactions between domestic and regional politics in decolonizing states. This in turn encourages us to look beyond the paradigms of the Cold War and decolonization when writing the Global South into world history.

title: Global Maoist optics among diaspora: The Indian Workers’ Association during India’s food ‘crisis’, 1965–69
abstract: This article considers the responses of the Indian Workers’ Association (Great Britain) (IWA) to food scarcities in India during the late 1960s. It reveals Maoist optics informed IWA critiques, departing from coexistent appraisals articulated in leftist circles in India. In doing so, the article demonstrates the relevance of worldviews, idioms, and paradigms emanating from global conjunctures beyond places of origin among diaspora. IWA luminaries were embedded in revolutionary anti-colonial networks shaped by decolonization and the global Cold War, and bestowed substance upon Maoism in these contexts. Ultimately, this informed IWA perceptions of causes and solutions to the food ‘crisis’: in their characterizations of reliance on external aid as indicative of post-1947 India’s semi-colonial status; in portrayals of Soviet ‘social imperialism’ in India during the Sino-Soviet split; or in demands for radical land reform based on a selective rendering of the Chinese model, which downplayed the consequences of the ‘Great Leap Forward’.

title: An American mosque and the migrating imam: The Shi‘i revival between Lebanon, Iraq, and the USA
abstract: This article reconstructs the religious and political activities of the Lebanese Shi‘i scholar Mohamad Jawad Chirri, who founded the first purpose-built Shi‘i mosque in the United States in 1963. It uses Chirri’s biography to explain the institutional, ideological, and political concerns structuring the global Shi‘i revival of the mid-twentieth century, as well as the strategies adopted by Islamic revivalist figures to achieve their institutional ambitions in a competitive and increasingly globalized religious marketplace. A hypermobile activist who lived and travelled between southern Lebanon, southern Iraq, Michigan, and West Africa, Chirri’s institutional initiatives and public activism took place outside the purview of the centres of Shi‘i religious authority in southern Iraq and Iran. The article argues that Chirri’s work, thought, and legacy complicate diffusionist understandings of Islamic revivalist activity as an ideologically coherent project of politicization or radicalization in the years surrounding the 1979 Islamic Revolution in Iran. The ‘global’ Shi‘i revival should instead be understood as an entanglement of institutional projects linked by transnational familial, professional, and financial networks emerging in the 1950s.

title: Unpacking the Emergency Health Kit of international humanitarian medical aid, 1978–90: How humanitarian standards and supply chains became global
authors: Maria Cullen; Bertrand Taithe; Janelle Winters
abstract: This article considers the history of Emergency Health Kits established by United Nations agencies and the larger medical non-governmental organizations of the 1980s to analyse the significance of standardized responses in humanitarian emergencies. We argue that, far from being a rigid and immutable response, the kits reflected a (not universally realized) desire to standardize and control both supplies and medical care from international organizations. As such, humanitarian medical practice remained a disputed field in which each object or drug was negotiated at the risk of creating innovation traps. Coming at a time of increasingly global logistics capacities, the Emergency Health Kits became a central feature of a more coordinated global marketplace of humanitarian aid. The kits’ promise to provide rapid transport of emergency supplies to crisis settings across the world was often experienced as a construct, with long delays and logjams in certain regions. Even so, humanitarian organizations were agents of globalization because they imagined a system of centralized production in the Global North and supply to isolated and/or insecure locations across the world.

title: Regionalising development: UN expertise and the making of a pan-Arab welfare field, 1949–59
abstract: In August 1949, the first Social Research Seminar for the Arab States convened in Beirut; five further seminars followed over the next decade. Drawing on Arabic-language seminar proceedings and UN archival records, this article recovers these largely overlooked gatherings to analyse how a distinct regional developmental field took shape in the post-war Arab East. UN institutional uncertainty in the late 1940s allowed the Arab League to capture this format, to authenticate global development through civilisational framing—most visibly in a lexical shift from emancipatory inʿāsh (reinvigoration) to custodial riʿāya (guardianship)—and to consolidate a self-sustaining professional field. The resulting regional arena mediated between global circulation and national implementation while proving durably compatible with the authoritarian welfare regimes emerging across the region.

title: Following East African cowries: Currency supply, transoceanic exchange, and monetary transformation in the nineteenth century
abstract: This article recentres East Africa in the global history of cowrie shells by tracing the trajectories of Monetaria annulus —the East African cowrie species—across interconnected monetary arenas in the nineteenth century. Situating African monetary history within transoceanic processes, it argues that the ‘great cowrie inflation’ in West Africa was closely tied to the reorganization of procurement networks, labour regimes, and commercial infrastructures in the Western Indian Ocean. Viewed from Zanzibar, the massive export of East African cowries emerges as the outcome of intersecting processes: price fluctuations in Maldivian shells, the expansion of the palm oil trade, extractive labour networks, and imperial interests. The article further shows that the same infrastructures were later reoriented toward the Great Lakes region, tracing how a single commodity connected East and West Africa, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic world. Following cowries across these overlapping spaces demonstrates that monetary history—wherever it is written—cannot be fully understood without attending to the supply-side infrastructures that made money available.

title: Come a long way: The global historian’s craft, twenty years on
abstract: Twenty years after the founding of the Journal of Global History , this anniversary article takes stock of global history: its trajectory, its markers of disciplinary maturity, its political sense of purpose, and the difficulties and limits of the enterprise. Concerns after 2016 that global history might lose its relevance in a changing political climate have, thus far, not been borne out. By many measures, global history is both a flourishing field and an influential sensibility. Its enduring contribution, this article argues, lies in how it has helped, and continues to help, bring about a fuller, more accurate, and more complete understanding of the ever-incomplete ‘selection of facts’ that constitutes history, our humble truth. Twenty years on, global historians know their field’s limitations but also its value. They know that they have brought the world into history—and that this is no small thing.

title: Knowledge uprooted: Transimperial forestry and the hiring of foreign experts in the Dutch East Indies, 1920s–1930s
abstract: This article examines the global networks underpinning colonial forestry in the Dutch East Indies in the interwar period. In the aftermath of the First World War, a renewed surge towards the internationalisation of the forest sciences served to open up imperial knowledge systems to a wider pool of outside expertise. This provided opportunities for smaller, thus far underresearched parties like the Nordic states, as explored here through a case study of a group of international foresters employed by the Dutch colonial administration in the 1930s. The article combines transimperial and global history approaches into a multisite analysis of both the scholarly exchanges that led to their initial hiring and their subsequent on-the-ground work in the colony. It is argued that an actor-oriented interrogation of the practical networks and internal frictions of colonial knowledge work reveals the hesitant emergence of a multilateral system that anticipated the post-1945 regime of international development.

title: The Right to Communicate: UNESCO and the politics of global communication, 1969–1987
abstract: The Right to Communicate (RtC) is the idea that individuals possess not only the freedom to ‘seek, receive and impart information’, as laid down in Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), but also the right to communicate horizontally with their peers, using technologies new and old. The brainchild of Jean d’Arcy, a French broadcaster and official who argued in 1969 that Article 19 should be updated to reflect the new technological possibilities, the concept inspired an international effort to write the RtC into human rights law. This article examines the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s (UNESCO) campaign to define this new human right, showing how initial enthusiasm was undermined by a widespread conviction that collective rights were a threat to individual rights; the difficulty of squaring the Global South’s state-led vision of communication with d’Arcy’s anti-statist ideals; and the vocal opposition of Western governments and NGOs, who increasingly saw the concept as a threat to freedom of information.

title: II. Chronologies
authors: Maria Framke; Maha Ali; Widya Fitria Ningsih; Adwoa K. Opong; Claudia Prinz; Iris Schröder
abstract: Despite a recent shift towards Global South-centred histories of development, women in and from Asia and Africa remain largely neglected in the historiography. In response, this Arenas issue examines the implications of situating the roles and experiences of women at the centre of historical analysis in this field. Bringing together scholars with diverse research expertise, the discussion reflects on the gendered meanings of development in twentieth-century colonial and post-colonial societies and emphasises the need for an expansive definition that takes in social welfare activities alongside industrial and economic projects. The forum explores some of the ways in which researching Asian and African women’s histories of development present particular challenges while at the same time offering conceptual and methodological insights that are relevant to the wider field. ‘Chronologies’ considers the question of periodisation and offers nuanced correctives to established narratives of continuity and rupture in the historiography of development.

title: IV. Sources
authors: Agnieszka Sobocinska; Anna Adima; Maria Framke; Kirsten Kamphuis; Adwoa K. Opong
abstract: Despite a recent shift towards Global South-centred histories of development, women in and from Asia and Africa remain largely neglected in the historiography. title: III. Scales
authors: Rosalind Parr; Claire Nicolas; Agnieszka Sobocinska; Darshi Thoradeniya; Jana Tschurenev
abstract: Despite a recent shift towards Global South-centred histories of development, women in and from Asia and Africa remain largely neglected in the historiography. In response, this Arenas issue examines the implications of situating the roles and experiences of women at the centre of historical analysis in this field. Bringing together scholars with diverse research expertise, the discussion reflects on the gendered meanings of development in twentieth-century colonial and post-colonial societies and emphasises the need for an expansive definition that takes in social welfare activities alongside industrial and economic projects. title: Unshackled?: China, the ‘unequal treaties’, and the limits of international law, 1919–1929
abstract: The post-1919 international order extended to China formal sovereign equality while offering few legal means to exercise it. The Sino-Belgian treaty dispute of 1926–29 reveals this: when China abrogated its 1865 treaty with Belgium and Brussels sued at the Permanent Court of International Justice, the institutions that promised peaceful revision could not deliver it without the consent of the powers whose privileges were at stake. The ‘unequal treaties’, a political category coined only in 1923, named the contradiction the order had built in. Four lawyer-diplomats—Wellington Koo, Wang Chung-hui, C.T. Wang, and Eugene Chen—were each caught between national autonomy and admission among the ‘civilised’ powers. The turn from legal argument to ‘revolutionary diplomacy’ was the structure’s doing, not a failure of nerve. Read beside Turkey, Persia, and the Latin American states, China’s case locates the obstacle: not semi-peripheral weakness as such, but the institutional position from which each engaged an order that subordinated its members through the very terms of their admission.

title: Humanitarianism, race, and the late colonial global order: Red Cross prison inspections in Apartheid South Africa
abstract: This article interrogates the politics of global humanitarianism and its entanglement with racial oppression during Africa’s decolonization by examining the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) first prison visits to Apartheid South Africa in the 1960s. Using newly available archives from liberation movements, anti-Apartheid collections, the Apartheid state, and the ICRC itself, it shows how a global humanitarian organization was appropriated as a legitimating façade in the governance of a late colonial global order. Rather than scrutinizing Apartheid policies or safeguarding prisoners of colour, the ICRC’s prison visits reframed collaboration as humanitarian neutrality, thereby enabling White minority rule. Afro-Asian critics, however, articulated alternative legal and humanitarian visions that challenged the Red Cross’s claims to impartiality, neutrality, and universality. The article unsettles triumphalist accounts that portray Red Cross humanitarianism as neutral, leading, and/or inherently progressive, and instead emphasizes its structural incorporation into Apartheid’s political order. In doing so, it contributes to a global history of humanitarianism and international organizations that calls for a more critical reckoning with how international organizations instrumentalize and memorialize their pasts.

title: Between disconnection and connection: The paradoxes of Cold War export controls
abstract: This article reinterprets Cold War multilateral export controls not simply as mechanisms restricting access to strategic technologies, but as sites of mediated connection within Cold War globalisation. Moving beyond a US-centred framework, it examines West Germany’s experience of the China embargo under ChinCom in the 1950s and the liberalisation of controls in respect of China within CoCom in the 1980s. It asks how regimes designed to enforce technological disconnection generated new forms of global connectivity, arguing that this transformation can be understood through Western alliance asymmetries and CoCom’s role as an institutionalised site of transit. In the 1950s, embargo enforcement produced alternative re-export routes and unintended transnational connections. In the 1980s, competitive alliance manoeuvring revealed CoCom’s regulatory architecture as a space of negotiation where technological circulation was enabled, delayed, redirected, or politically obscured. A case study of Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm illustrates how these dynamics operated in practice. By tracing mediated technological circulation across different phases of controls in respect of China, the article reframes Cold War globalisation as shaped by dis:connectivity: the mutually constitutive interplay of connection and disconnection.

title: Financing mission societies, capitalizing Protestantism: A transimperial history – ERRATUM
Coconut frontiers and ecological frictions in the Pacific World, c .1900–20: A multispecies history of capitalism
abstract: The copra industry that developed in the Pacific region from the mid-nineteenth century was a global, thriving enterprise. Imperial powers and trade companies jointly set up palm tree plantations that shaped the livelihoods of island societies and recruited Chinese contract labourers. Such monocultural territorialisations also radically transformed the environments and lives of non-humans (plants, insects, fungi), creating ecological conditions that challenged the same economic endeavours at work. ‘Economic entomology’, a novel branch of the scientific study of insects related to profit-oriented land management, emerged globally in the early twentieth century to protect plantations more efficiently from insect pests and other plant diseases. By focusing on the unprecedented outbreak of rhinoceros beetle ( Oryctes rhinoceros ) in the Samoan islands during German colonial rule and its aftermath in the Pacific world, this article examines the history of coconut capitalism in this region as a more-than-human history and explores the potential of reading the global archive against the grain while applying a multispecies ethnographic lens. In so doing, it reconsiders both the colonial anxieties exposed by the beetle outbreak and the kind of multispecies spaces that this insect opened up for Samoan resistance. This paradigmatic case of the global co-constitution of plantation economies and transimperial pest control research sheds light on the intersections of capitalist expansion in the modern era and the correlated environmental transformations that forged a new epistemic and ecological regime in commodity frontiers during the early twentieth century.

title: Financing mission societies, capitalizing Protestantism: A transimperial history
abstract: This article examines the transimperial fundraising practices of two major continental European Protestant missionary societies—the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society (PEMS) and the Basel Mission (BM)—between the end of the Napoleonic Wars and the 1870s. It proposes a meso-level approach to global history that focuses neither on individual actors nor on abstract categories such as capitalism or religion, but instead on organizations. By analysing the PEMS and the BM, the article shows how missionary societies connected specific subregions of British India and Southern Africa with Protestant regions across the northern transatlantic world. Drawing on rarely studied financial reports, it demonstrates how these societies mobilized hundreds of thousands of donors through global financial networks spanning Europe, North America, and the colonies. In doing so, the article reframes Protestant missionary societies not merely as cultural actors but as economic institutions that helped normalize capitalist practices in both Europe and colonial settings. It thus contributes to transimperial and global history by suggesting a way to study Protestant continental Europe, the United States, and the British empire as mutually constitutive partners.

title: Fraught friendships: East German experts, communist development, and environment in Mongolia during the Cold War
abstract: This article examines East German experts’ participation in development projects in Mongolia and their conceptions of environments during the Cold War. Starting in the 1950s, East Germany (German Democratic Republic, GDR) and Mongolia intensified economic ties that aimed to industrialise Mongolia and align with communist objectives. The endeavours were intended to provide development aid, though they also provided the GDR with access to natural resources it could not obtain domestically. Drawing on sources from numerous German archives, this article argues that East German development projects followed broader patterns of exploitation and consumption between Europe and the Global South after the Second World War. Communist trade relations dissolved with the end of the Cold War, but they set the stage for trade and environmental impacts that have continued to this day.

title: From Moscow to Cologne and across the Atlantic: Newspaper science and the global origins of Soviet mass communication
abstract: This article situates early Soviet studies of the press, a specific academic field called gazetovedenie , within the global history of mass communication research. While scholarship often portrays Soviet media theory as entirely subordinate to agitational practice, this situation only became established by 1930, when well-known Soviet orthodoxies on the nature and role of propaganda fully solidified. In the 1920s, Soviet press scholars actively engaged with contemporary global debates about the press’s role in mass society, how propaganda functioned, and why it often failed. Far from working in isolation, they drew upon thinkers such as Karl Bücher, Grant Hyde, and Walter Lippmann, while developing distinctive approaches, including applying Formalist methods to media texts, that resonated internationally. Viewing this intellectual activity as part of a global exchange redefines the origins of propaganda studies, not as a Cold War divide, but as diverging, yet deeply entangled, responses to modernity, war, and mass politics.

title: Citizenship and autonomy: Bilateral labour migration governance and its discontents in Malawi, Mexico, and Spain, 1919–75
abstract: During the 1930s, the International Labour Organization sought to establish standards for bilateral labour migration agreements on separate but parallel colonial and nation-state tracks. I interrogate the ramifications of these discussions across the subsequent half-century, integrating global structural scales of analysis with migrants’ perspectives on the ground. First, I trace the concept of the ‘temporary migrant worker’ in the bilateral migration agreements signed in the 1930s to the 1960s between Spain and France; Nyasaland (later renewed by independent Malawi) and South Africa; and Mexico and United States. I then show how common post-war ideas and pressures led Mexico, Spain, and Nyasaland/Malawi to invest local authorities with substantial control over emigration and deprioritize migrants’ comfort and safety. Migrant-generated sources, notably letters, petitions, and oral histories, point to a resultant convergence of experience unanticipated by international policy discourses: migrants coming to perceive their own states as a primary barrier to progress, dignity, and autonomy.

title: Dancing ambassadors: The Indian republic’s global cultural project
abstract: Beginning in the 1950s, emerging from the British empire’s shadow, the Indian government helped dancers become globe-trotting, state-sponsored cultural ambassadors, projecting a vision of the young nation’s art as ancient, sophisticated, and spiritual. Asserting a ‘national culture’ (understood by the formerly colonized as essential to decolonization) involved its reconstitution, despite claims to civilizational continuity. This article reveals how dance became the natural candidate for global cultural projection, the ways in which the state allied with artists in this endeavour, and the conflicts this engendered between them. It offers insights into the state’s anxieties about the nation’s image globally, debates within civil society and between politicians about Indian culture, and the logic underlying how Indian dance was presented differently across the world. The global projection of culture and its reception abroad was part of the contested process of defining it at home. National culture took shape as it travelled the world.

title: What is UNRWA for? The contested purposes of refugee relief in Gaza, 1948–1950
abstract: In the midst of the crisis of displacement caused by the 1948 war for Palestine, the newly minted United Nations contracted with the (Quaker) American Friends Service Committee to provide aid to Palestinian refugees in Gaza. Over the next eighteen months, as AFSC workers participated in the institutionalization of new and modern forms of internationalist refugee assistance, many of them came to think that the real goal of this regime was not protection or succour but order, containment, and prolongation—a conclusion that informed the AFSC’s decision, in 1950, to withdraw its provision of aid and turn over its operations to the new United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA). This article explores this brief and apparently minor historical interregnum in Palestine’s refugee regime with an eye to the enormously consequential questions it raises: who built these modern refugee regimes, what did they actually do, and to what ends?

title: Between commerce and sanctity: Ottoman policies and international boundaries in the early modern Red Sea
abstract: This article examines the transformation of the Ottoman empire’s maritime boundary policies in the Red Sea during the early modern period. It focuses on the dual character of the Red Sea, as both a religious frontier safeguarding the Holy Cities and a strategic maritime corridor within global trade networks. Drawing on Ottoman and British archival sources, the study analyses the period from 1517 to 1798 in three distinct phases: a closed sea era shaped by the Portuguese threat (1517–1608); a phase of negotiation with friendly European actors (1608–36); and a period of controlled openness (1636–1798), in which limited access was granted to merchants recognised as müsteʾmin (protected foreigners). The article argues that Ottoman maritime sovereignty in the region was not exercised through absolute control, but through a flexible and negotiable mode of boundary management. This perspective offers a contribution to early modern debates on imperial border-making and sovereignty by revealing how empires balanced ideological commitments with economic pragmatism.

title: A Businesswoman in Meiji Japan
abstract: Women are conspicuously underexamined in the business and economic histories of modern Japan. Although wives and widows played central roles in the financial management of their families and family businesses, they have typically remained hidden behind the names and accomplishments of their more visible male relations. This was true not only in Japan but also in other countries undergoing rapid industrialization in the long nineteenth century. Some women, however, did leave traces of their economic activity and leadership. As scholars encounter more and more of these so-called anomalies, the need grows for new, more inclusive historical narratives that can account for their existence and impacts. This article responds by studying the involvement of one especially visible married businesswoman in the development of her marital family’s coal mine in Kyushu’s Chikuhō region. More specifically we investigate the networking and management approaches of Hirooka Asako (1849–1919) and contextualize them with those of female business leaders working in male-dominated industries in and beyond Japan. Unexamined or understudied contracts, financial records, speeches, interviews, and editorials as well as private, unofficial sources like correspondence, memoirs, and eulogies reveal that she played a leading role in Uruno Mine’s development and management. Mobilizing determination, familial and professional networks with men, and direct management strategies, she personally oversaw the metamorphosis of this failing project into a successful, profitable enterprise. Her methods and achievements in fact resemble those of prewar modern Japan’s few famous businesswomen, of a few well-known Western women entrepreneurs, and, likely, of many less visible women. If, as we demonstrate, dynamic, enterprising women were active entrepreneurs, respected collaborators of men, and influential contributors to Japan’s economic and industrial development during the Meiji period (1868–1912), the inclusion of their stories can complicate scholars’ understanding of Japanese business and economic history.

title: The Hearts of People in the World
abstract: This article explores the economic dimensions of the late fiction of the seventeenth-century writer Ihara Saikaku, asking how the author’s understanding of the marketplace shaped his humanistic studies of “the hearts of people” (hito-gokoro). Applying methods of economic criticism to the posthumous Tying Off Saikaku’s Loose Ends (Saikaku oridome, 1694), I argue that the author’s late writings develop a formal homology between the imperfect rationality of the early market economy and the ineffable dynamism of the human heart.

title: Grounding Empire Through Burial Grounds
abstract: This article examines how the Japanese military, notably the Kwantung Army, used the acquisition and maintenance of military burial grounds to challenge Chinese sovereignty in Manchuria (currently Northeast China) and expand Japan’s territorial control in seemingly “peaceful” periods. The burial grounds became contested sites where debates over sovereignty and different groups’ claims of land use played out. With a close focus on the military-use land, this article challenges the previous depiction of Japanese imperialism in Manchuria as informal imperialism and enriches our understanding of how the military reshaped social and political relationships in the empire through the control of land. This article also enriches historical writing on the Kwantung Army, which tends to focus on its military roles. The Kwantung Army in Manchuria not only enacted its power through military actions but also far more extensively penetrated Manchuria’s local communities even before the Manchukuo era (1932–45).

title: To the Virtuous Go the Spoils
abstract: This article examines Taiheiki (Chronicle of Great Peace, fourteenth century) as a critical intervention in medieval Japanese historiography. It challenges conventional court-versus-rebel binaries, framing the fragmentation of authority during the Nanbokuchō age through Neo-Confucian concepts of virtue, such as the three bonds and five virtues, the Mandate of Heaven, and revolutionary reign change. Figures like Emperor Go-Daigo and his loyal general Kusunoki Masashige expose the erosion of imperial legitimacy through failed moral governance. Taiheiki offers a flexible, genre-defying model of historical change, challenging myths of imperial inviolability and anticipating early modern re-conceptualizations of virtue, sovereignty, and political order.

title: Ainu Handicrafts
abstract: This article examines the mass commercialization of Ainu handicrafts as Hokkaido’s official folk art and signature souvenir during the 1930s. Focusing on the political economy of these works, it analyzes how the Japanese empire constructed a colonial handicraft industry that promoted the popular consumption of Ainu woodcarvings and attus textiles as symbols of Japan’s civilizing mission over the Ainu people. Despite such appropriation, Ainu craftspeople repurposed these works as instruments of political mobilization to confront colonial inequalities. At Asahikawa, Ainu activists from the Third Chikabumi Land Dispute envisioned collective handicraft workshops as a centerpiece of their proposal to dismantle their reservation and construct a new village. In the Saru River basin, Ainu weavers also drew on community-based management of mountain forests to connect attus textile production to Indigenous land rights. By tracing Ainu cultural production across these sites, the article argues that Ainu handicrafts were critical sites for the articulation of Ainu demands for land recovery, local autonomy, and equitable resource use.

title: Acting Like Female Spirit Mediums
abstract: In 1913, Nakachi Kamado called for a public trial in Naha, Okinawa, to contest the accusation that she had acted as a yuta, or female spirit medium. The trial captivated city residents, drawing hundreds to the courtroom and even more to commercial theaters featuring plays about the trial. This article argues that the trial and plays articulated tensions of class and gender pulsating through the city of Naha. From police surveillance to the dispossession of the former ruling class and an influx of working-class women, tensions wrought by Japanese colonialism and urbanization found powerful expression in the trial and plays.
