title: Introduction to the Special Issue: Crossing Boundaries in Modern Korean Literature and Culture
Negotiating the Colonial Dilemma Through Science Fiction: Translating Jules Verne in Early Twentieth-Century Colonial Korea
abstract: This article examines the emergence of science fiction (SF) in early twentieth-century Korea by analyzing the first two Korean translations of Jules Verne—Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1907–8) and The Begum’s Fortune (1908). It argues that these relay translations, produced during the years between the Russo-Japanese War and formal Japanese annexation, reveal how Korean intellectuals navigated what the article terms the “colonial dilemma”: the challenge of rethinking national identity amid accelerated modernization and encroaching imperial domination. Rather than passively importing European SF, Korean translators actively reshaped the texts through genre relabeling, annotation, and selective adaptation, using them simultaneously as vehicles of scientific enlightenment and as tools for articulating Korea’s precarious place within global geopolitics. The article further contends that the early Korean use of the term “science fiction”—predating its standardization in the Anglophone world—calls for a reconsideration of global SF timelines and assumptions about the genre’s origins. By situating Korean SF within the broader East Asian circulation of Verne’s works and by highlighting the translators’ interventions into colonialist narratives, this study demonstrates that SF in Korea emerged not as an extension of European imperial imagination but through a complex interplay of colonial, anti-colonial, and nation-building impulses.

title: Translated Poetry in Younghill Kang’s The Grass Roof and the Tradition of Inset Poetry in Premodern Korean Fiction
abstract: Younghill Kang’s 1931 novel The Grass Roof, long taken as the first commercially successful novel by a Korean in English, is unusual for incorporating sixty-five of its author’s translations of East Asian poetry into its narrative fabric. These embedded translations represented one of the early mass audiences for Korean poetry in English. This article argues that The Grass Roof adapts the literary convention of inset poetry (sabipsi) from the premodern Korean novel, hybridizing it with English-language autobiographical fiction. It proves Kang knew traditional narrative models by analyzing his depictions in the novel of the Kuunmong and Ch’unhyang chŏn. It then examines two different uses of inset poetry in the novel: (1) retrospective ornamentation by the narrator and (2) dynamic plot advancement by characters. The second function, in particular, reflects classical uses of sabipsi to heighten scenes of courtship and erudition. Kang’s use of inset poetry gave Korean poetry an unusually early global audience at the same time as it drew Western and Korean novelistic techniques together in a new, shared experiment.

title: Reading O Changhwan Translating Sergey Esenin in Seoul, 1946
abstract: This article explores the allegorical layers of meaning that emerge from one translator-poet partnership in the aftermath of the collapse of the Japanese empire in Korea. The iconoclastic modernist poet O Changhwan’s first published book in a newly liberated Korea was a translation of poems by the deceased Russian poet Sergey Esenin. O was translating at a moment when the Korean language was returning to public life after suppression under colonial rule and amid escalating violence on the partitioned peninsula. Reading O’s translations and lengthy afterword opens a window onto the scene of Seoul in 1946, one year before O was to cross over the thirty-eighth parallel into the northern zone. With the aim of rethinking the creative legacies of the early Cold War, this article explores the many meanings created in and through O’s translation.

title: Milan Kundera’s Poetry in North Korea and Socialist World Literature in the 1950s
abstract: This essay examines Milan Kundera’s unexpected presence in 1950s North Korean literature, revealing a forgotten chapter of socialist world literature in the Cold War era. The study focuses on three of Kundera’s poems related to the Korean War: “The Gardener,” “Korean Ballad,” and his epic poem “The Last May,” which revolves around the anti-fascist martyr Julius Fučík. By analyzing North Korean literary journals including Chosŏn munhak, the essay traces how Kundera’s early socialist poetry arrived in North Korea as part of broader international solidarity efforts during and after the Korean War. Noting how the translation of these works occurred at a specific historical moment when North Korea was actively engaging with Eastern European literature before turning inward in the 1960s, the essay situates Kundera within North Korea’s evolving conception of “world literature,” which shifted from Soviet-centeredness through Eastern European engagement to eventual interest in the Tricontinental (Asia, Africa, Latin America) before closing off entirely. The divided reception exemplifies the broader fragmentation of world literature during the Cold War, gesturing to the power dynamic that shapes literary histories in conversation with but also beyond ideological boundaries.

title: Interpretive Praxis Under Pax Americana: Paik Nak-chung’s Reading of D.H. Lawrence in 1980s South Korea
abstract: This article examines Paik Nak-chung’s (Paek Nakch’ŏng’s) 1982 translation and reading of D.H. Lawrence’s Studies in Classic American Literature (1923) as a case of interpretive praxis under Cold War authoritarianism in South Korea. Situated between the aftershocks of the Kwangju Uprising and the intensification of anti-American student activism, Paik’s essay “The American Dream and the Burden of American Literature” appears, at first glance, anomalous: Why would a leading critic of literary engagement turn to Lawrence at a moment when dissident reading communities centered on Marx, Fanon, and other banned revolutionary texts? I argue that Paik’s sustained engagement with Lawrence is best understood as a metacritical strategy that converts reading and translation into a political intervention. Working through Lawrence’s symptomatic critique of “American democracy” and the ideological work of the American dream, Paik exposes US imperial duplicity while simultaneously resisting the nativist essentialism that could accompany virulent anti-Americanism in 1980s Korea. Lawrence’s insistence on stripping “democratic and idealistic clothes” from American utterance becomes, in Paik’s hands, a method for historicizing—one that links the contradictions of American nation-building to South Korea’s compressed modernization and US-backed authoritarianism. Tracing how Paik reframes Lawrence’s critique of the “whole soul” of America, I show how he articulates a decolonizing stance that resists simple binaries of foreign imperialist versus authentic minjung. Finally, situating Paik’s Lawrence within a longer genealogy of criticism shaped by Matthew Arnold and F. R. Leavis, I argue that Paik’s “double project of modernity” (ijung kwajeron) marks a commitment to hold aesthetic autonomy and political praxis in productive tension with each other.

title: Archaeological Translation: How to Translate Diasporic Korean Literature
abstract: Min Jin Lee’s Pachinko chronicles four generations of Zainichi (Koreans in Japan) from the colonial era to the 1980s. Its translation process remains enigmatic; Lee imagined the narrative in Korean and Japanese before writing the novel in English. Consequently, the English original and its two Korean translated versions produce divergent meanings. This article investigates the translational issues in the two Korean versions, questioning the hierarchical order between the original Anglophone text and its translations. Building upon postcolonial translation scholarship, we first examine restored dialects in the Korean versions that are absent in the English text, analyzing their intersection with discourses of class, gender, and ethnicity. Second, we compare the opening sentences of the three versions, unearthing distinct insights into colonial and postcolonial histories embedded within each text. By unsettling conventional notions of originality, this comparative analysis introduces a new framework termed “archaeological translation.” Through this lens, we critique Lee’s mode of representation that flattens cultural and historical specificity, while demonstrating how translated versions evolve into distinctive texts with their own historical, political, and cultural perspectives in the transnational age.

title: The Magical Agency of Parameters as Intent and Meaning: The Translation Application in Decision to Leave
abstract: This essay examines how the translation application in Park Chan-wook’s Heŏjil kyŏlsim (Decision to Leave, 2022) functions as a narrative agent and framework for parametric mediation. Semantic entropy designates information loss when neural translation compresses multivalent meanings into probable outputs; yet this entropy proves generatively productive, creating new possibilities in gaps between languages. Close readings examine scenes where the app mistranslates Chinese into Korean, transforming affective complexity into anatomical literalism, imposing unwarranted honorifics, and reducing Confucian ethics to suit consumer preferences. The screenwriters deliberately crafted these failures; paradoxically, such errors generate meanings exceeding both languages. Drawing on Walter Benjamin, Susan Bassnett, and neural translation research, this study shows how mistranslations illuminate both limitations and generative capacities in algorithmic and human understanding. These insufficiencies become narratively productive through a hermeneutics of irresolution: an interpretive mode refusing closure, locating meaning in interstices between competing translations. Characterizing this dynamic as parametric creativity, I argue that Decision to Leave transforms technical constraints into aesthetic method. As artificial intelligence increasingly mediates communication, the film reminds us of interstices arising from encounters between disparate entities: the tremor in voices, the weight of pauses, and the irreducible difference between heart as an organ and heart as feeling.

title: Between Eco-Governmentality and Forest Management Cooperatives: Reinterpreting South Korean Reforestation in the 1970s and 1980s from the Local Level
abstract: In 1973, the Park Chung Hee government launched its first Reforestation Plan to deal with the pressing issues surrounding forest loss, soil erosion, and forest management through countrywide tree planting and stricter control of forest use for logging. The top-down campaigns, often referred to as a “green Yushin,” can be understood as eco-governmentality with direct state intervention in the sylvan environment. However, to recognize the effects of reforestation on the local level, there is a need for further consideration of the role of forest owners. The West German and South Korean governments promoted the establishment of Forest Management Cooperatives (FMCs). After their introduction in Ulju County, the model was subsequently transferred to other regions all over the country throughout the 1980s. The cooperatives contributed to the economic livelihood of the rural population and enabled the transfer of forest management skills and practices to forest owners amid the government-led campaign. The forest owners could then actively participate in decision-making processes on the local level. This article proposes a new understanding of the reforestation campaigns that took place under the authoritarian government by engaging perspectives from the local level and introducing the new models of cooperatives that were carried out as rural development projects.

title: Cleared for Takeoff: The Economic and Environmental History of Incheon International Airport in 1990s South Korea
abstract: In 1990, the South Korean government announced the construction of a new international airport on reclaimed land to the west of Seoul. This proposal drew the ire of environmental groups and major newspapers as an environmental and economic disaster. The international airport construction proposal arrived at an inflection point of post-1987 democratization, government liberalization of travel restrictions, the growth of the aviation industry, rising environmentalism, and the beginning of a global recession. While large-scale infrastructure projects had enabled South Korea’s rapid economic rise, the high environmental costs sparked intense public interest among South Koreans. However, the openness of the post-1987 period was a double-edged sword for environmental groups. While they found greater freedom to organize and high public interest in environmental issues, the public also had the freedom to decide the type of environmentalism and lifestyle they wanted to pursue. This article examines the Incheon International Airport construction proposal as a case study of the intersection between economic history and environmental history, with popular sentiment as a key swing variable. This study argues that the Incheon airport proposal illustrates the contemporary nature of South Korean environmentalism, lifestyle objectives, and economic consciousness.

Intimate strangers: Shifting images and knowledge gap of Southeast Asia in Japan
abstract: Japanese people have a strong affinity for Southeast Asia as a region, yet they often know very little about it. This is particularly true for students in Japanese universities. The issue lies in the gap between what students believe they know and what they actually understand about Southeast Asia. This is concerning because perceptions based on a superficial understanding of the facts are vulnerable to political mood swings and propaganda, which can undermine sound judgements in international relations. It is not unreasonable to expect students at top schools, who are interested enough in the region to take related courses, to develop a deeper understanding. This paper approaches the problem from two angles: first, it reviews the evolution of scholarly literature on Southeast Asia in Japan, analysing the characteristics of the Japanese approach to Southeast Asian studies. Second, it traces the educational background of Japanese youth to examine how scholarly culture has influenced education from high school to college level. In doing so, we problematise the global perceptions of ordinary Japanese citizens and attempt to explain the disconnect between poor knowledge and rich awareness. We argue that a structural issue between the production and consumption of knowledge must be addressed.

title: HongKar experiences: Rethinking localisation in Southeast Asia through Teochew-Catholics in Singapore
abstract: The microhistories of three Teochew-Catholic parishes in Singapore challenge notions of localisation as conceived of in the studies of overseas Chinese diasporas. Despite hailing from the Guangdong province of China, these Catholic migrants reached Singapore under a myriad of circumstances, and the Catholic Church played a pivotal role in their coping with the experiences of migration. Triangulating between ecclesiastical archives, oral history interviews, and commemorative artefacts, this paper highlights three separate experiences of mobility between China and Singapore between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries: of sojourning, long-term migration, and refugees. Differing experiences hence prompted divergent modes of localisation, resulting in disassociation amongst fellow Teochew-Catholics. Even though Catholicism and similar geographical origins in China provided commonalities amongst these Teochew-Catholics, the dynamics of migrant-mission interactions contrasted drastically across the three parishes, resulting in distinctive traditions and communal identities. Rather than a single Teochew-Catholic community, these parishes evidence three localised overseas Chinese communities within the island of Singapore. The paper hence problematises understanding localisation across national boundaries and cultural assimilation, advocating for an experience-based model of analysis and inviting further comparisons across communities in Southeast Asia.

title: Mediums, mobility, migration: The religion of compassion in Southeast Asia
abstract: The Cijiao is a Chinese sectarian religion founded during the Malayan Emergency (1948–1960). Contrary to the common perception of East Asia as the cradle of Chinese religious movements, this study examines a movement that originated in colonial Malaya and subsequently spread to North America and China since the latter half of the twentieth century. This article proposes that different forms of migration and mobility among Malaysians and Singaporeans were quintessential to the Cijiao’s development within Southeast Asia and abroad. It argues that these diverse channels, methods, and periods of travel not only offered new avenues for the movement’s expansion but also generated novel dynamics and reshaped this religious network. As such, the extension of the Cijiao’s global reach cannot be solely understood through the lens of a single locality. Instead, it must be seen as arising from prolonged engagement with cultural currents and competing interests spanning diverse global regions.

title: Hà Tiên, the Dutch East India Company, and the politics of piracy in eighteenth-century maritime Southeast Asia
abstract: This article reconstructs an eighteenth-century legal dispute involving piracy between two Chinese captains in the Gulf of Siam. In an unprecedented move, Mo Tianci (Mạc Thiên Tứ), the ruler of Hà Tiên, delegated judicial authority over the case to the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in Batavia. This decision reveals his deliberate strategy to integrate into the Company’s sphere of influence to bolster security and trade. Hà Tiên’s agility in navigating multiple sovereignties was essential to its continued prosperity as a commercial crossroads. The Mo’s historical trajectory also illustrates the growing influence of Western power in maritime Asia’s geopolitical order.

title: Colonisation and cultivation: Nutmeg production, labour and ecology on the Banda Islands before and after the conquest of 1621
abstract: In 1621, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) conquered the Banda Islands (Maluku, Indonesia) and killed, expelled and enslaved its indigenous population. The motivation behind this genocide was to establish control over the production of nutmeg and mace, two valuable spices that were grown almost exclusively in Banda. According to most historians, the VOC was successful in radically transforming, intensifying and, rationalising spice production. This paper, by contrast, argues that there was a significant degree of continuity in cultivation methods between the precolonial and (early) colonial periods and that productivity levels stagnated or declined following colonisation.

title: Growing your own: Vegetables and food scarcity in colonial Malaya, c. 1900–1950
abstract: Between 1900 and 1950, colonial Malaya suffered a series of difficulties including trade supply disruptions, economic downturns, warfare and harvest failures. These resulted in short to long-term impacts on the availability of locally produced or imported food, especially rice. Small-scale market gardening and home vegetable growing became critical avenues to ameliorating shortfalls. The subject of vegetable gardening as a means of everyday or crisis subsistence has been little attended to in the Asian context, yet, local vegetable growing played an important role in managing food insecurity, even making the difference between life and death. Taking colonial Malaya as a case-study, this article investigates how small-scale vegetable farming and market gardening were methods of subsistence during periods of minor to acute food insecurity and a means of decreasing reliance on imports. This relatively untapped history reveals government-led strategies to increase food production, including ones that created conflict with communities or individuals already producing their own food. It argues that colonialism had in fact created many of the insecurities that the government now sought to address, and that the production of food was closely connected to — and reinforced — the colonial governments perceptions and stereotypes of different Malayan peoples.

title: Unreading the literary: The Hikayat Anggun Cik Tunggal and Malay oral historical tradition in an age of print
abstract: While Malay Hikayat texts are composed along oral-oriented sensibilities or otherwise originate in the oral medium, what survives of their past recitations are but scant written records of them. Scholars working under these evidentiary limits have often seized on these texts’ fantastical elements to interpret them as myths. I suggest that such flawed interpretations are found on visual readings that ignore Hikayat texts’ oral poetics; and consider instead how a text is historical insofar as its medium is germane to its historical poetics. I demonstrate a methodology to unread Hikaya and re-situate them in their oral medium in which texts were liable to change over time, to appreciate their historicity. In unreading the Hikayat Anggun Cik Tunggal, this article recovers a history which retold Minangkabau experiences of colonialism through the memory of the 1511 Portuguese invasion of Melaka. Finally, I trace the Hikayat into an age of print colonialism, in which print formed a key technology by which European colonists re-moulded meaning-making and intellectual life in the Malay world. By these mores of media consumption, Malay readers came to interpret Hikayat as fictions, and were wrested from a long tradition of history-telling that enabled them to process colonial trauma.

title: Where civilisations converged, where culture languished: A Chinese artist’s wartime travels across South and Southeast Asia, 1939–42
abstract: Amidst the upheaval of the Second World War between 1939 and 1942, renowned Chinese artist Xu Beihong embarked on a journey across Singapore, India, and Malaya, one which would leave an indelible mark on his artistic career. While existing studies typically frame this phase as Xu Beihong’s Nanyang period and foreground his patriotic fundraising endeavours and contributions to China’s War of Resistance Against Japan, his nearly year-long sojourn in India is overshadowed by these fundraising accounts. Drawing on newly discovered primary sources, this study conducts a comparative analysis to explore overlooked aspects such as his everyday linguistic practices, social networks and markedly divergent artistic outputs across the two regions. By examining Xu’s different attitudes towards South and Southeast Asia, this research highlights the limitations of nationalist or bilateral frameworks for interpreting intra-Asian artistic interaction. It also reveals the intricate power dynamics within overseas Chinese communities during the Second World War, which not only shaped the diverse cultural landscape of both regions but also consolidated hierarchies beneath a rhetoric of resistance and solidarity. Through this comparative lens, the study exposes a deeper layer of inequality that foreshadowed regional divergences on the eve of decolonisation.

title: The end of nature in Borneo: A concise contemporary history
authors: David Henley; David Gaveau; Erik Meijaard
abstract: This article provides a concise overview of the history of environmental change in Borneo since 1970, with particular attention to human institutions, actors, and choices, and to the reasons for those choices. It is a political narrative, with an eye for vested interests and for the forces resisting environmental change as well as those driving it. The article deals with the whole of Borneo, including Indonesian Kalimantan, the Malaysian states of Sarawak and Sabah, and the sultanate of Brunei, highlighting parallels and contrasts between their trajectories. In the late twentieth century the appearance of large international markets for tropical timber and palm oil changed the ecological fate of Borneo, leading to an almost uniquely rapid process of environmental destruction. In the early twenty-first century a combination of incipient timber and land exhaustion, stagnating palm oil prices (2010–20), and an internationalisation and monetisation of conservation efforts has slowed down the rate of deforestation. But the close involvement of Indonesian and East Malaysian political elites in extractive industries makes it unlikely that a reversal is imminent. Even if some ecosystem restoration can now be envisaged, the fact that this is most likely to take place under the stewardship of big business raises uncomfortable ethical questions.

journal: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
title: Islamic Sectarianism in China: A Neglected Problem
authors: Mohammed Turki A. Alsudairi; Aaron Nathan Glasserman; Noriko Unno
abstract: This introduction to the special issue dives into the often overlooked and politically charged topic of Islamic sects and sectarianism in China. Although Islam in China is often viewed as a single, uniform block, it has actually been defined over the centuries by fluid borders, shifting labels like "old" and "new" sects, and intricate social and political pressures. Through critical engagement with Ma Tong’s now classic taxonomy of China’s sects, the six papers in this collection adopt a multi-layered perspective on the problem of organized intra-Islamic diversity. They investigate how diverse Muslim groups, religious leaders, and state institutions—ranging from imperial times to the modern era across regions including Xinjiang—have negotiated boundaries and constructed sectarian identities from the top down and the bottom up.

journal: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
title: The Akhunds of Kashgar: Sufi Rivalries in Qing Xinjiang
abstract: The Qing conquest of Xinjiang in the mid-eighteenth century significantly disrupted the region’s established networks of religious authority. With the charismatic “khoja” lineages of the Tarim Basin Naqshbandiyya removed from the scene, networks of “akhund” disciples were left to carry on the tradition. While a persistent White Hat / Black Hat (or White Mountain / Black Mountain) rivalry is a prominent theme in scholarship on Qing Xinjiang, that scholarship is yet to explore the ways this rivalry was expressed in local religious narratives set down during the Qing period itself. The focus of this article is a body of hagiographies written by members of these surviving akhund families, representing the standpoint of rival factions of the Tarim Basin Naqshbandiyya, or ʿIshqiyya as they came to refer to themselves. I ask, firstly, how these texts adapt and reshape a historical narrative of the “khoja period” and the Qing invasion for sectarian purposes. Secondly, I explore how they construct the landscape of tariqat affiliations in Qing Xinjiang and ask what light this sheds on the evolution of Sufi brotherhoods in nineteenth-century Central Asia.

journal: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
title: Unifying (and Dividing) the Believers: The Sectarian Governance of Muslims in the People’s Republic of China
abstract: The article explores how and why the Chinese Party-state manages its Muslim subjects/citizens through sectarian governance—a type of statecraft aimed at safeguarding the inherited sectarian configuration of Muslim communities through various classificatory and sectarianized discourses and practices. It argues that this governance originates from the Party-state’s encounter with the Northwest’s culture of sectarianism, itself born from the ambitious yet violent and traumatic project of the Muslim warlords in the 1920s–1940s to impose confessional unity across the Islamic landscape. The article looks at the Party-state’s discordant efforts to subjugate and manage this culture across the Maoist and post-Maoist eras, and traces how these attempts yielded eventually to a theoretical framework and set of bureaucratic and interventionist practices that, in amalgamation, came to constitute sectarian governance. It contributes a fresh reading of state-religion relations in China and highlights an important yet neglected dimension in understanding how the Party-state has governed and manipulated, both in the past and the present, Muslim heterogeneity.

journal: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
title: The Concept of Ṭarīqa and Its Social Implication: Discourses of the Four Great Sufi Orders and Muslim Fraternity in Northwest China
abstract: This paper explores how and why Sino-phone Muslims developed various interpretations about the four great menhuan s ( ṭarīqa s) during the 19th and 20th centuries. It elucidates how the variation of interpretations about ṭarīqa was correlated with tensions among Chinese Sufi orders and their struggles against anti-Sufi reformists. It also clarifies how Chinese Sufis’ consideration of ṭarīqa involved a kind of union among Muslims beyond a Sufi order. By this case study, I hope to suggest how we may overcome the widespread dichotomy in Sufi studies between doctrinal and sociopolitical aspects of Sufism.

journal: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
title: People of the Mosque: the Social Foundations of Islamic Sectarianism in China
abstract: This article explains why Islamic ritual has long been a source of controversy in China, not just as a marker of Muslim difference from the cultural mainstream but also as a matter of dispute within the Islamic fold. Previous studies examining ritual rules on mosque stelae across late imperial China have interpreted these writings as evidence of scholastic disagreement over scripture. This article shifts the focus from the scriptural basis of ritual rules to the social context in which they were prescribed. Claims about ritual were commonly inscribed alongside contracts and administrative regulations, forming complex sets of agreements. These congregational compacts constituted the mosque congregation as a property-owning corporate entity dominated by local Muslim elites. Where congregations coexisted near one another, distinctive definitions of normative Islamic practice not only symbolized the authority of a congregation’s leadership but also marked boundaries between congregations, the salience of which could be heightened by the arrival of Muslim migrants and by official efforts to control these movements. Ritually marked boundaries between Muslim communities were a common feature of Hui social organization in late imperial China. They also provided a template for thinking about Islamic sectarianism and the challenges to a unified, nationwide Chinese Islam in the modern period.

journal: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
title: A “Sect” for Whom? The Rise of a New Islamic Movement in Taozhou, Gansu (1890–1914)
abstract: At the end of the nineteenth century, an Islamic movement emerged in Taozhou (Gansu), initially rooted in the Jinxingtang School (1890) and formally known as the Xidaotang from 1908 onward. Challenging established Sufi institutions, the movement’s ritual practices and doctrinal positions were soon contested and provoked accusations of heterodoxy. As the movement became institutionalized, these attacks were brought before the judicial courts, casting imperial authorities as arbiters of Muslim orthodoxy. Over time, the movement gradually gained recognition as part of Islamic orthodoxy and emerged as a potential and opportunistic ally to Muslim warlords in broader struggles for religious and politico-economic hegemony. This case study offers an instructive lens with which to examine how local actors deploy the notion of “sect” to delegitimize a new Islamic movement during a period of significant religious transformation. Drawing on a range of primary sources, the study reveals how conflicts generated accusatory dynamics aimed at excluding groups perceived as religious innovators from the local Muslim community. From an epistemological standpoint, it encourages historians to treat “sect” and its derivatives not as analytical categories, but as practical acts through which the boundaries of religious belonging are asserted and negotiated.

title: Kita Ikki and Zeng Qi: National Socialism in East Asia, Late 1910s–Early 1930s
abstract: This article explores emergent radical political discourse in East Asia driven, at least partially, by regionalized national socialism, which was one of the two most influential revolutionary ideologies, alongside communism, in the early twentieth-century world. Despite a wealth of scholarship about national struggles and communist movements in the political radicalization of East Asia from the late 1910s to the early 1930s, it is still difficult to understand the role national socialism played in this radicalization, as seen in the ascendance of Kita Ikki and Zeng Qi, the two leading national socialists in Japan and China in this era. By comparing Kita’s and Zeng’s transformative ideas, this article documents radical discursive changes.

title: The Spanish Naval Station in the Pacific: A Frustrated Project of Global Regeneration (1833–1866)
authors: Rodrigo Escribano Roca; Mikel Gómez Gastiasoro
abstract: The project to install a permanent naval station on the South American shores of the Pacific attracted the consensus of Spain’s political-intellectual, military, and diplomatic elites during the reign of Isabel II (1844–1868). This article reconstructs the constellation of strategic, economic, legal, and political arguments used by the Spanish monarchy’s diplomatic agents to support the need to station warships in its former Pacific dominions. It also identifies these agents’ socioeconomic coordinates, networks, and interests, evaluating the factual consequences of their attempts to create the station. We will argue that Spanish political elites conceived the naval station as a critical element in the new repertoire of instruments of power necessary for configuring a “second Spanish empire” based on the ideological postulates of navalism, pan-Hispanism, and the imperialism of free trade. This case study allows us to make some theoretical contributions to understanding the crucial functions that naval stations performed as elements of imperial power in the nineteenth century.

title: Koreans Skilled Workers in Japan after the East Asian War of 1592–1598: Pak Hoin and Tofu in Early Modern Tosa Domain
abstract: This article analyzes the importance of Korean skilled workers in Japan during and after the East Asian War of 1592–1598. By tracing the story of the Korean Pak Hoin and his descendants, this article demonstrates the close relationship between domains and migrants. In doing so, it demonstrates that migrants were not only widespread throughout early Tokugawa Japan, but also that their experiences were highly varied. By placing Hoin’s experience next to that of other Korean migrants, this article identifies some of the factors that influenced migrant experiences and the varying impact they had on their local environments.

title: Industrial Lessons Abroad: Chinese Engineers in Britain, 1933–1948
abstract: This article explores the dynamic development of the Federation of British Industries Chinese Apprenticeships Scheme from 1933 to 1948, examining how China’s national reconstruction agenda intersected with Britain’s trade-political interests in technology and engineering. It argues that the scheme embodies key features of Sino-British educational, scientific, and cultural initiatives in the 1930s and 1940s—advancing cultural diplomacy while steering China toward purchasing relationships favorable to Britain. Adopting a multi-perspective approach that combines institutional analysis and bio-graphical research, the article moves beyond traditional narratives of modernization, patriotism, and Sino-British friendship to uncover key tensions within this transnational, factory-based initiative, including international competition in foreign manufacturing exports, the mismatch between Chinese engineering graduates and Britain’s apprenticeship system, Britain’s chronic under-resourcing in cultural diplomacy, and Chinese engineers’ frustrations under nationalist statism. It offers insights into Britain’s cultural diplomacy, China’s nation-building efforts, and broader Sino-British trade and cultural exchanges in the twentieth century.

title: Anti-Colonial Activism and Multi-Imperial Entanglements: Reassessing the 1932 Hongkou Bombing Incident in Interwar Shanghai
abstract: This article examines the 1932 Hongkou Park Bombing Incident in Shanghai as a critical episode of anti-colonial resistance that reveals the entangled dynamics of empire, nationalism, and global political activism in the interwar period. Despite its historical significance, the incident remains relatively under-studied in English-language scholarship. This article addresses that gap by situating the bombing within the distinctive urban setting of interwar Shanghai. Drawing on multilingual archival sources and press coverage, this study shows how the bombing incident catalyzed a range of responses: it exposed the contra-dictions of British imperial strategy, prompted Franco-Japanese collaboration in colonial policing, and deepened covert support from the Chinese Nationalist Government. This article argues that the Hongkou Incident not only brought into sharp relief existing power differentials but also served as a catalyst for renegotiating power relations and modes of interaction among agents of multiple empires and local Chinese authorities in the city of Shanghai. In doing so, it contributes to global historiographies of anti-colonialism by demonstrating how interwar Shanghai functioned not only as a site of colonial governance and repression but also as a crucible of trans-Asian political mobilization and media discourse.

Notes from Enlightenment Studio: The Movement and Materiality of Scientific Information in Nineteenth-Century China
abstract: Between 1867 and 1872, a scholar-clerk in Jiangxi Province composed an inventory of scientific and mathematical books. The list records not only their contents, but also the paths they had traced into the scholar's possession. Thus, the inventory preserves a record of how scientific information moved through inland China in the years immediately following the Taiping Rebellion. Analyzing both the physical and metaphorical aspects of this movement, this article argues that scientific knowledge and practice were promoted and constrained by material conditions. The inventory suggests the rarity of certain scientific-mathematical volumes, and underlines that foreign books translated in Shanghai did not circulate easily, even to provincial capitals. In addition to this material movement, information also moved through different representational languages in different texts, for instance through the translation of mathematics from physical forms (counting rod, abacus) to symbolic ones (abstract notation). As illustrated by the scholar's commentaries, material conditions informed intellectual trends. Finally, the inventory shows the continued importance of manuscripts, even in the age of woodblock and moveable type print. The methods of replication of scientific texts shaped what could be known, and in what manner.

title: Concealing and Revealing: Women and Embodied Exemplarity in Late Imperial Chinese Biographies
abstract: This article examines a distinctive subset of Qing-dynasty biographies of exemplary women that foreground forensic-style description alongside supernatural revelation. Tracing this practice to Ming precedents, especially Gui Youguang's writings, the article argues that the combined staging of the maimed female body and miraculous occurrences constituted a deliberate narrative strategy for resolving juridical and moral ambiguity surrounding women killed while resisting sexual violation. Through close textual analysis and contextualization within Qing forensic practice, judicial debates, and religious culture, the article demonstrates that graphic attention to bodily wounds functioned as a form of para-juridical evidence, transforming the injured corpse into legible proof of resistance and moral integrity. Divine dreams and posthumous miracles, meanwhile, operated as supplementary modes of validation, compensating for the perceived insufficiency of formal legal adjudication. In this sense, bodily spectacle and miracle worked in tandem not to undermine Confucian norms prescribed by the nei–wai (inner–outer) divide, but to reaffirm them through their strategic suspension under conditions of inconclusive bureaucratic and judicial judgment. Situated at the intersection of history, law, and literature, the examples studied here reveal the uneasy interweaving of moral judgment, legal reasoning, and narrative sensation in Qing biographical writing.

title: The Rise of a Mountain King: Geopolitics and the Tributary System on the Fifteenth-Century Sichuan-Tibetan Frontier
abstract: In the fifteenth century, the rise of Dongbuhanhu presented a significant political and military challenge for Ming China along its Sichuan-Tibetan frontier. The tributary system played a pivotal role in Dongbuhanhu's development, functioning in different ways at various stages of the polity's rise. From the 1410s to 1430s, Dongbuhanhu employed the tributary system to gain recognition from the Ming, thus consolidating its secular and religious authority. In the 1440s, control over tributary routes became a central element in the power struggle between Dongbuhanhu and Zagu, transforming the system into a strategic tool for geopolitical competition. During the 1450s, the tributary system not only facilitated Dongbuhanhu's accumulation of material wealth but also provided the polity a political framework to establish a hierarchical order in frontier regions. By examining the practical implications of the tributary system in the frontier region, this article traces specific ways through which frontier societies took advantage of imperial policies to negotiate with state authorities for their own interests.

title: Zhongshu in the Grand Secretariat and Everyday Administration of the Qing Empire
abstract: This paper examines the pivotal yet largely invisible role of Han-Chinese secretaries known as zhongshu 中書 (7b) in the everyday administration of the Qing empire. It is generally believed that the influence of the Grand Secretaries significantly waned with the development of the palace memorial ( zouzhe 奏折)system in the eighteenth century, which allowed senior officials to bypass the Grand Secretariat and communicate directly with the emperor. A low-ranking secretary at the Grand Secretariat thus was viewed as a sinecure with dim career prospects. Examining zhongshu's responsibilities and activities, I argue that despite their obscurity they were actually the backbone of the Qing central administration, indispensable to the daily operation of the imperial bureaucracy. Moreover, zhongshu were remarkably well connected and informed, which prepared them for higher positions and more important assignments after their Grand Secretariat career. In this sense, the post of zhongshu not only offered aspirating degree-holders promising paths to climb the ladder of success but also trained them to be capable bureaucrats on behalf of the Qing empire.

title: The “Great Disappearing Act of Success”: Technologies of Speculation in Contemporary Black Financial Fictions
abstract: This article examines how two contemporary works of Black speculative fiction imagine a financialized future, playing with racialized logics of prediction that position whiteness as the watchword for the ceaseless accumulation of value over time. Both Boots Riley’s Sorry to Bother You (2018) and Mateo Askaripour’s Black Buck (2021) depict salesmen on trajectories of individual upward mobility, prospering despite the racial and financial inequalities of their near-future dystopian worlds. Like the tech companies where they work, these characters generate profitable projections, fabricating visions of the future that solicit audience investment. For both protagonists, success involves the strategic performance of whiteness as a tool of financial causality that promises future happiness, security, and unfettered growth. Yet, even as they stage the spectacle of success, Sorry to Bother You and Black Buck formally sabotage the plausibility of their own growth narratives, using flimsy props, temporal acceleration, exaggerated plot twists, and situational irony to render their own storytelling fundamentally absurd. The result, I argue, is speculative fiction that undermines the act of speculation, in both narrative and financial forms. Moving beyond exposure, these texts explore how finance capitalism disciplines desire to foster affective attachments to incredible projections. They invite audiences to disinvest from prediction as the means to secure a happy future, turning instead toward strategic destabilization and radical narrative uncertainty.

title: Postsentimental Horizons in Sui Sin Far’s “In the Land of the Free”
abstract: This article explores the racial politics of sympathy in Sui Sin Far’s short story “In the Land of the Free” (1909). Widely celebrated as the “mother” of Asian American literature, Sui Sin Far dedicated much of her writing career to the advocacy of Chinese immigrant rights. Contrary to the common understanding that presumes the early Asian American writer’s appeal to white sympathy for Chinese immigrants as fundamental to her short stories, I reconsider Sui Sin Far as a trenchant critic of the dominant white sentimental politics of recognition who nonetheless experimented with sentimental tropes to provoke a more liberatory model of social justice that I call “postsentimental allyship.” Building on Lauren Berlant’s formulation of postsentimentalism and Xine Yao’s recent work on unfeeling, I honor this horizon of sociality and its affective reorganization of white-Chinese relations amid the stifling pressure to yield to the terms of white sympathetic recognition during the Chinese Exclusion Era. In analyzing the short story, I locate Sui Sin Far’s dissent from the sentimental politics of recognition through reading practices that attend to Sui Sin Far’s often-overlooked narrative experiments and the Chinese immigrant characters in the story, whose words and gestures express their demand for and enact the practice of alternative politics of advocacy. As sympathy has been normalized into the default affective mode in animating white activism, reading Sui Sin Far’s short story in this way helps us see that there are other possible ways to feel solidarity that do not reinscribe oppression but rather can begin rearranging race relations toward more just dynamics.

title: Beyond “Saving” Life: Biopolitical Dynamics and Virus Narrative in Saving the World
abstract: Julia Alvarez’s Saving the World (2006) employs virus narratives to weave two storylines into a shared account of the entanglement of life, medical intervention, and biopolitics. Reading the novel through the biopolitical transformations of the early nineteenth century, this article examines the 1803 Royal Spanish Smallpox Expedition and its reliance on live carriers to show how an ostensibly humanitarian project was structured by colonial power. It then situates the novel within the context of twenty-first-century globalization to trace the neo-imperial logic of US intervention in the Global South during the AIDS pandemic, particularly at the nexus of biomedical aid, neoliberal governance, and counterterrorism. The article further argues that Alvarez imagines forms of affiliation that exceed colonial and imperial containment through a negative affirmation that moves from immunized individuals to communal life. Saving the World thus reworks the immunitary paradigm by envisioning communities forged across racial, national, and territorial boundaries. In bringing a colonial history of smallpox into dialogue with a fictional AIDS narrative and linking both to questions of care, violence, and survival, the novel reframes biopolitical dynamics transnationally and expands the critical scope of multiethnic US literary study.

title: “A Resurrection That is beyond Death”: African Diasporic Healing Rituals in Toni Morrison’s Paradise
abstract: This article concerns medical racism and sexual trauma in Toni Morrison’s Paradise (1997), but also the innovative African Diasporic healing ceremonies the novel depicts, which are key to understanding the mysterious deaths and seeming rebirth of the women who reside in the Convent and are (in theory) massacred by the men from Ruby at the end of the novel. I argue that the healing figure at the center of this novel (Consolata Sosa) creates a unique boundary-melting ceremony that ties together fragments from three different traditions of Africanist healing to create a new ritual that enables physical and spiritual rebirth. Connie draws on Nigerian Òs∘un healing rituals involving water, Afro-Brazilian practices of repair originating in Candomblé, and a configuration of feminine agency and revivification present in the Gnostic and Egyptian-influenced Christian gospel “The Thunder, Perfect Mind” and its invocation of the Egyptian goddess Isis. This last topic, in particular— Morrison’s use of the Gnostic Gospel and the figure of Isis, who was thought to bring people back to life—is key to comprehension of how the novel creates an innovative ritual that facilitates (in Morrison’s own words) “a resurrection that is beyond death.” The healing ceremony at the heart of the novel engenders new psychic and corporeal restorations even after the “death” of the Convent women. The women can therefore return from death to repair the bonds of their communities and institute ongoing forms of reconciliation and reparative justice.

title: “Playing Latinx” as Settler-Colonial Reenactment
abstract: This is an article about the “problem of the indio” in a transamerican context of migration, and about accounting for the political role of Indigeneity in contemporary Latinx and Latin American literature. The figure of “the Indian” has been a central concept for national literatures in the so-called Americas since the nineteenth century, and its role becomes further complicated when considering the convergence of Indigeneities across the United States and Mexico and their unique nationalist literary traditions. In considering the intersections of these literary traditions in the space of the US-Mexico borderlands, this article identifies the narrative act of “playing Latinx,” whereby texts about the US-Mexico borderlands perform the dual reenactment of mestizaje and settler-colonial history. Using a Critical Latinx Indigeneities framework to analyze Valeria Luiselli’s migration texts—Tell Me How It Ends: An Essay in Forty Questions (2017) and Lost Children Archive (2019), to which I refer jointly as the “Lost Children Project”—this article traces the related but distinct intellectual genealogies that reduce Indigeneity to a cultural trait rather than a political condition.

title: Eva’s (In)visible Man: Reading Gayl Jones through the Lens of Black Male Vulnerability
abstract: Despite its title, Gayl Jones’s novel Eva’s Man (1976) is not a story of a man. Instead, it is a disturbing account of the experiences of an abused woman, Eva Medina Canada, who grotesquely murders Davis Carter, a man she had met a few days prior. While exploring Eva’s Man from the perspective of Black women’s victimization is relevant and necessary, in this article, I read beyond a victim/perpetrator binary and focus attention on the male victim and female perpetrators that are seldom addressed in critical readings of this novel or in scholarship more generally. Drawing on Tommy J. Curry’s theorization of Black male vulnerability (Man-Not), I examine the (in)visibility of Black men as victims and women as perpetrators across the spectrum of intergenerational and interpersonal violence reproduced in society and reflected in the novel. I argue that reading the male character as not only a metonym for masculine aggression against women but also as a victim allows us to understand the novel more deeply. Not only does Davis stand for and remind Eva of her previous abusers but also he is a victim of the same cycle of violence in which Eva is victimized and in which all the characters, men and women, are somehow involved. Rereading the novel through the lens of Black male vulnerability enables us to see beyond racialized gender stereotypes and binaries and focus instead on the spectrum of violence itself to better understand its psychological, social, and political functions and ramifications.

title: “The Logic Is Built Right into the Architecture”: Speculative Architecture in Contemporary Queer-of-Color Science Fiction
abstract: This article studies Rivers Solomon’s An Unkindness of Ghosts (2017) and Larissa Lai’s Salt Fish Girl (2002) to explore a concept that I term speculative architecture, which describes speculative, humanmade spaces and structures onto which authors layer social meaning. I argue that authors such as Solomon and Lai leverage the generic characteristics of speculative fiction to write social ideologies into the physical constructs of the world, posing a challenge to forms of oppression that rely on our understandings of such spaces, and their structuring logics, as natural and innate. In An Unkindness of Ghosts, Solomon transcribes histories of the Middle Passage onto the futuristic spaceship, challenging certain sciencefiction traditions that treat interstellar colonization as an idealized future for humanity without acknowledging the circumstances necessary for such a future to come about. In Salt Fish Girl, Lai critiques the racialized and gendered histories of inclusion and exclusion written into sub/urban borders and the mechanisms of control necessary to maintain those borders. Interestingly, both novels suggest gardens as potentially revolutionary interstitial spaces, in which the protagonists explore possibilities not prescribed by the material structures of oppression that otherwise dictate their lives. Thus, attention to speculative architectures highlights various possibilities for navigating narrative and material spaces, offering alternative epistemologies of both familiar and fantastical structures. Importantly, these characteristics are transferable across other works of speculative fiction, including not only sci-fi but also horror, fantasy, and magical realism, offering an interpretive lens that can be used to broadly articulate representations of spatiality, materiality, and sociality.

title: Dirty Words: Lack and/of Innocence in Toni Morrison’s The Bluest Eye
abstract: Toni Morrison’s The Bluest Eye (1970) depicts a complex interplay of lack and fetishism. While many scholars read narrator Claudia and protagonist Pecola in opposition—emblematic of childhood survival and failure, respectively—this article argues that the novel links the girls insofar as both are excluded from an innocence primarily associated with white childhood. Both girls respond to the shameful sense of lack that emerges from their unfulfilled desire for innocence by fetishizing symbols of the ideal object. While innocence depends on negation, fetishization operates by substituting one love-object for another. As such, fetishization necessarily fails to “produce” innocence for either girl. Claudia, who fetishizes cleanliness and “good grammar,” recognizes the inadequacy of her substitution even as she maintains an attachment to it. She consequently exhibits what David Eng and Shinhee Han call “racial melancholia,” an orientation toward lack that permeates the formal elements of her narrative. Conversely Pecola, who fetishizes the titular blue eyes, uncritically adores her substitution. Enacting the process of incorporation theorized by Nicolas Abraham and Maria Torok allows Pecola to keep innocence “alive” within her unconscious but also requires she compulsively stage the fantasy of the object’s continued existence. Attending to the girls’ shared melancholia alongside the parallels between them ultimately enables a reparative reading that honors their position in Morrison’s lineage of complex girlhood friendships.

title: Political Act and Poetic Act: An Interview with Kimiko Hahn
abstract: This interview with renowned Asian American poet Kimiko Hahn, Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets and New York State Poet Laureate, 2025-27, includes biographical information about her life growing up with artistic parents in a mixed-ethnicity family, the blended influences of Japanese and European poetic forms on her work, her childhood love of language, activism as a young feminist in the 1960s and 70 s, the roles of unconscious processes and formal structures within the creative process, and the place of poetry in our social landscapes.

title: Extravagant Camp: The Queer Abjection of Asian America. Chris A Eng
Colored Women Sittin’ on High: Womanist Sermonic Practice in Literature and Music. Melanie R. Hill
abstract: Melanie R. Hill’s Colored Women Sittin’ on High: Womanist Sermonic Practice in Literature and Music provides a useful interdisciplinary analysis of women’s public speech and performance as it is affiliated with theology and social justice. The book includes discussion of African American literary characters as well as actual women, ordained or not, who have preached and sung their way into local, regional, and national influence. Hill’s argument relies on insights drawn from literary theory, critical race theory, classic and contemporary theology, and musicology. Its coverage sweeps across twentieth- and twenty-first-century America with references to earlier periods. Given the disciplinary isolation within which many scholars work, nearly every reader will find much that is new here. In her introductory chapter, Hill links these disciplines through attention to “sermonic practice.” That is, while most of the figures Hill explores are not literal ministers preaching from a literal pulpit, they all engage with readers and listeners as a preacher might through “prayers, prophecy, and praise” (1). As specifically African American women often communicating with a primarily African American audience, they participate in the ministry of the Black church in America, which understands its call as liberatory. Hill interprets scenes from literature and musical performances as doing the work of sermons, but she also examines sermons—the texts and the delivery—as a literary genre. In this chapter, she devotes extensive space to contextualizing her argument and defining her terms, not only the specifically religious ones such as “sermonic practice” but also more theoretical ones such as “womanist,” a term used primarily within literary studies as an African American elaboration on, amplification of, and critique of feminism. She acknowledges the particularly patriarchal assumptions and practices embedded in many religious traditions, a fact that prompts her analysis and approach.
